questions.e: High pH with high bicarbonate is a metabolic alkalosis, from loss of gastric acid, with a compensatory rise in PaCO2 from hypoventilation. Hypochloraemia and hypokalaemia are typical of prolonged vomiting; a respiratory acidosis would have a low pH.

questions.s: Bilal, a 34-year-old shopkeeper in Multan, has had upper abdominal discomfort and early fullness after meals for 3 months. He takes no regular medicines. He has no weight loss, vomiting, dysphagia or bleeding, and examination is normal. Hb is 14.2 g/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Upper GI endoscopy with gastric biopsies within 2 weeks
Test for H. pylori by stool antigen or breath test
questions.e: A young patient with uninvestigated dyspepsia and no alarm features should have a non-invasive test-and-treat approach for H. pylori, which is highly prevalent in Pakistan. Endoscopy is reserved for alarm features (weight loss, anaemia, dysphagia, bleeding, persistent vomiting) or older age at onset, none of which he has.

questions.s: A 63-year-old retired teacher from Rawalpindi presents with 2 months of epigastric pain and loss of appetite. He has lost 6 kg. Hb is 9.4 g/dL with MCV 71 fL. He has no melaena. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks
H. pylori stool antigen and treat if positive
Oral iron and review in 4 weeks
questions.e: New dyspepsia in an older patient with weight loss and iron deficiency anaemia is an alarm presentation for gastric cancer, so urgent endoscopy with biopsy is needed. An empirical PPI trial or test-and-treat could mask or delay the diagnosis of a malignancy.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man with heartburn for over 10 years has an upper GI endoscopy. A salmon-pink tongue of mucosa extends 4 cm above the gastro-oesophageal junction. Biopsies are taken. Which histological finding confirms the most likely diagnosis?
o: Stratified squamous epithelium with basal cell hyperplasia
Eosinophils more than 15 per high-power field
Columnar epithelium with intestinal-type goblet cells
questions.e: Barrett's oesophagus is replacement of the normal squamous lining of the distal oesophagus by columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells), driven by chronic acid reflux. Basal cell hyperplasia is seen in simple reflux oesophagitis, and dense eosinophils suggest eosinophilic oesophagitis rather than Barrett's.

questions.s: Ayesha, a 29-year-old office worker, has burning retrosternal pain after large meals and when lying flat at night, with an acid taste in her mouth. She has no dysphagia, weight loss or vomiting. She has tried antacids with brief relief. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Full-dose proton pump inhibitor for 4 to 8 weeks
Referral for laparoscopic Nissen fundoplication surgery
questions.e: Typical GORD without alarm features is treated with lifestyle advice and a full-dose PPI for 4 to 8 weeks. Prokinetics and sucralfate are less effective, and fundoplication is reserved for patients who do not respond to, or cannot tolerate, adequate medical therapy.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man from Faisalabad has epigastric pain that wakes him at night and is relieved by eating. Endoscopy shows a clean-based ulcer in the duodenal bulb, and a rapid urease test on the gastric biopsy is positive. He has no drug allergies. Which regimen is most appropriate?
o: Proton pump inhibitor alone for 8 weeks
Ranitidine with metronidazole and bismuth for 14 days
Proton pump inhibitor, amoxicillin and clarithromycin
questions.e: H. pylori-positive peptic ulcer disease needs eradication with a PPI plus two antibiotics, most commonly amoxicillin and clarithromycin (or metronidazole), given for 7 to 14 days. A PPI alone heals the ulcer but leaves the infection, so the ulcer is likely to recur.

questions.s: Rukhsana, 67, has taken diclofenac daily for knee osteoarthritis for a year. She now has a gastric ulcer on endoscopy; H. pylori testing is negative. By which mechanism did the drug most likely cause the ulcer?
o: Reduced mucosal prostaglandins through COX-1 inhibition
Increased gastrin release from antral G cells
Direct stimulation of parietal cell histamine H2 receptors
Reduced gastric emptying with prolonged acid contact
questions.e: NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, lowering gastric prostaglandins that maintain mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow, so the mucosa becomes vulnerable to acid. Gastrin excess causes ulcers in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, not with NSAID use.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man from Lahore has had bloody diarrhoea 4-5 times a day with urgency for 4 weeks. He is afebrile with a pulse of 82/min, Hb 12.8 g/dL and a mildly raised CRP. Stool cultures are negative. Colonoscopy shows continuous mucosal inflammation from the rectum to the sigmoid colon, and biopsies confirm ulcerative colitis. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Mild to moderate ulcerative colitis (fewer than six stools a day, no fever or tachycardia) is treated first with an aminosalicylate such as mesalazine, given rectally and/or orally depending on extent, which also maintains remission. Oral prednisolone is added if this fails, and intravenous hydrocortisone is for acute severe colitis. Azathioprine is a steroid-sparing maintenance drug, not first-line induction.

questions.s: A 41-year-old woman has had recurrent peptic ulcers despite H. pylori eradication and no NSAID use. Endoscopy now shows ulcers in the second and third parts of the duodenum and the proximal jejunum. She also has chronic watery diarrhoea that improves on a PPI. Which test is most appropriate next?
o: Serum calcium with intact parathyroid hormone level
Fasting serum gastrin off acid suppression
Repeat H. pylori urea breath test
questions.e: Multiple distal duodenal and jejunal ulcers with diarrhoea that responds to acid suppression suggest a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome); the first test is a fasting gastrin, ideally off PPI because PPIs raise gastrin. Calcium and PTH are relevant later to look for MEN1, but they do not make the diagnosis.

questions.s: A 36-year-old woman completed 14 days of H. pylori eradication therapy for a duodenal ulcer. She feels well and wants to know if the infection is gone. She has stopped all medicines. When is the urea breath test most appropriately done?
o: One week after finishing the antibiotics
4 weeks after antibiotics and 2 weeks off the PPI
Only if her epigastric symptoms return at any later stage
questions.e: Antibiotics and PPIs suppress H. pylori and cause false-negative breath or stool antigen tests, so testing for cure is done at least 4 weeks after antibiotics and 2 weeks after stopping the PPI. Testing earlier risks falsely reassuring results; serology is not used because antibodies persist after cure.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man presents to the emergency department of a DHQ hospital after one episode of melaena. Pulse is 84/min, BP 128/78 mmHg, Hb 13.8 g/dL, urea normal. He has no comorbidity. Which scoring system best identifies whether he could be managed as an outpatient before endoscopy?
questions.e: The Glasgow-Blatchford score uses urea, Hb, blood pressure, pulse and clinical features before endoscopy; a score of 0 (or 1 in some guidance) identifies patients safe for outpatient care. The Forrest classification describes ulcer appearance at endoscopy and so cannot be used before the procedure.

questions.s: Imran, 50, has known hepatitis C cirrhosis. He presents with vomiting of fresh blood. Pulse 118/min, BP 92/60 mmHg. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and blood is cross-matched. Apart from IV antibiotics, which drug should be given before endoscopy?
questions.e: Suspected variceal bleeding in cirrhosis is treated with a vasoconstrictor such as terlipressin (or octreotide) plus prophylactic antibiotics, followed by endoscopic band ligation. Propranolol is used for prevention, not for an acute bleed with hypotension, and tranexamic acid has not been shown to help GI bleeding.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man vomited repeatedly after eating at a wedding. After several forceful retches he vomited a small amount of bright red blood. He is now well, with pulse 80/min and normal blood pressure. Hb is 14.5 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Haematemesis after repeated forceful retching in a stable young patient suggests a mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction, which usually stops on its own. Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness rupture with chest pain, shock and surgical emphysema rather than minor bleeding.

questions.s: A 76-year-old man passes a large amount of painless bright red and maroon blood per rectum. He had no previous bowel symptoms. Pulse is 96/min, BP 124/76 mmHg. Urea is normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Sudden painless large-volume rectal bleeding in an elderly patient is most often from colonic diverticula, where a vessel at the neck of a diverticulum ruptures. Ischaemic colitis usually gives crampy abdominal pain with smaller-volume bloody diarrhoea, and haemorrhoids rarely cause bleeding of this volume.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man with a bleeding duodenal ulcer has had successful endoscopic therapy. His Hb is 7.6 g/dL, pulse 88/min, BP 120/76 mmHg. He has no ischaemic heart disease and is no longer bleeding. When is red cell transfusion most appropriate for him?
o: Now, to bring Hb above 12 g/dL
questions.e: In stable upper GI bleeding, a restrictive transfusion threshold of about 7 g/dL (target 7 to 9 g/dL) reduces rebleeding and mortality compared with a liberal threshold. A higher threshold is used for patients with significant cardiovascular disease or ongoing massive haemorrhage.

questions.s: Saima, a 26-year-old from Peshawar, has 6 months of right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, weight loss and alternating bowel habit. Colonoscopy shows ileocaecal ulcers with a deformed, gaping ileocaecal valve. Biopsies are taken. Which finding most favours intestinal tuberculosis over Crohn's disease?
o: Large confluent granulomas with caseous necrosis
Deep fissuring ulcers with skip lesions and cobblestoning
questions.e: Large, confluent, caseating granulomas (often with acid-fast bacilli) point to intestinal TB, which is common in Pakistan and must be excluded before immunosuppression for Crohn's. Small, sparse non-caseating granulomas, skip lesions and fissuring ulcers favour Crohn's disease.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman with known ulcerative colitis has 9 bloody stools a day. Temperature 38.1 °C, pulse 104/min. Hb 10.1 g/dL, CRP 64 mg/L. Stool cultures and C. difficile toxin are sent. Abdominal X-ray shows no colonic dilatation. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Six or more bloody stools a day with fever, tachycardia, anaemia or raised CRP is acute severe ulcerative colitis, treated in hospital with IV corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone, plus VTE prophylaxis. Antimotility drugs can precipitate toxic megacolon, and colectomy is reserved for failure of medical rescue or complications.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man with extensive ulcerative colitis is admitted with a severe flare. On day 3 he becomes more unwell with abdominal distension and tenderness. Pulse 124/min. Abdominal X-ray shows the transverse colon measuring 8 cm in diameter. What is the most likely complication?
questions.e: A dilated transverse colon over 6 cm with systemic toxicity in a severe colitis flare is toxic megacolon, which carries a high risk of perforation and usually needs surgical review. Carcinoma is a long-term risk of colitis and does not present acutely with colonic dilatation.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man with ulcerative colitis for 8 years has fatigue and itching. ALP is 480 U/L (normal 40-130), ALT 62 U/L, bilirubin normal. Ultrasound shows no gallstones. MRCP shows multifocal strictures and dilatations of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A cholestatic picture with beaded bile ducts on MRCP in a man with ulcerative colitis is typical of primary sclerosing cholangitis. Primary biliary cholangitis mainly affects middle-aged women, is positive for antimitochondrial antibodies and spares the large ducts on imaging.

questions.s: A 22-year-old university student is diagnosed with ileal Crohn's disease after colonoscopy and biopsy; TB has been excluded. He has diarrhoea, abdominal pain and mild weight loss, without fistulae or obstruction. Which drug is most appropriate to induce remission?
questions.e: Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone (or budesonide for ileocaecal disease) are first-line to induce remission in a first presentation of Crohn's disease. Azathioprine works too slowly to induce remission and is used to maintain it, and mesalazine has little effect in Crohn's.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman has iron deficiency anaemia that has not responded to oral iron, with bloating and loose stools. She eats chapati made from wheat daily. Which is the most appropriate first test for the likely diagnosis?
o: Stool microscopy for ova, cysts and parasites
questions.e: Refractory iron deficiency with bloating and loose stools suggests coeliac disease; the first test is IgA anti-tTG with total IgA, taken while the patient is still eating gluten. Faecal calprotectin helps separate IBD from functional disease but is not specific for coeliac disease.

questions.s: A 31-year-old woman with positive tissue transglutaminase antibodies has a duodenal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. She has been eating a normal diet. Which histological picture is expected?
o: PAS-positive foamy macrophages in the lamina propria
Villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and lymphocytes
questions.e: Coeliac disease shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes in the duodenum, which improve on a gluten-free diet. PAS-positive macrophages are seen in Whipple's disease and a thickened collagen band in collagenous colitis.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy returned from a summer trip to Gilgit 3 weeks ago. Since then he has had bloating, flatulence and pale, greasy, foul-smelling stools with no blood. He has lost a little weight. Stool microscopy shows pear-shaped trophozoites. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Steatorrhoea and bloating with pear-shaped flagellate trophozoites are giardiasis, often acquired from untreated water in northern Pakistan, and treated with metronidazole (or tinidazole). Albendazole is mainly for roundworms, praziquantel for flukes and tapeworms, and ciprofloxacin has no role.

questions.s: A 46-year-old man with years of heavy alcohol use has recurrent epigastric pain radiating to the back, weight loss and bulky, pale, floating stools. Abdominal X-ray shows calcification in the region of the pancreas. Which test best confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency?
questions.e: Chronic pancreatitis with steatorrhoea indicates exocrine insufficiency, best shown by a low faecal elastase. Serum amylase and lipase are often normal in chronic pancreatitis because little functioning tissue remains, so they are useful mainly in acute attacks.

questions.s: An 11-year-old girl has had bloating, cramps and watery diarrhoea after drinking milk or lassi since a bout of gastroenteritis 2 months ago. She is otherwise well and growing normally. Coeliac serology is negative. Which test best supports the likely diagnosis?
o: Hydrogen breath test after a lactose load
Serum specific IgE to cow's milk protein
questions.e: Symptoms after dairy following gastroenteritis suggest secondary lactase deficiency; undigested lactose is fermented by colonic bacteria, raising breath hydrogen. Serum IgE tests are for IgE-mediated milk allergy, which gives urticaria or wheeze soon after exposure rather than delayed fermentative symptoms.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man with Crohn's disease had 80 cm of terminal ileum resected 2 years ago. He now has fatigue, numbness in both feet and a smooth red tongue. Hb is 9.0 g/dL, MCV 112 fL. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.e: The intrinsic factor-B12 complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum, so ileal resection causes B12 deficiency with macrocytic anaemia, glossitis and neuropathy. Folate is absorbed in the proximal small bowel and its deficiency does not cause peripheral neuropathy.

questions.s: A 27-year-old man presents with 10 days of jaundice, nausea and dark urine. ALT is 1,850 U/L. He had a dental extraction at a roadside clinic 3 months ago. Serology: HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative, anti-HCV negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Chronic hepatitis B with a flare
questions.e: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc in a patient with recent onset of hepatitis indicates acute HBV infection; the dental procedure with unsterile instruments is the likely source. A flare of chronic hepatitis B can also give low-titre IgM anti-HBc, but the short history and clear exposure make acute infection most likely.

questions.s: A 23-year-old nursing student at a Karachi teaching hospital has pre-employment screening. Results: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs 140 mIU/mL, total anti-HBc negative. What do these results indicate?
o: Immunity after natural hepatitis B infection
Acute hepatitis B in the window period
questions.e: Anti-HBs alone, without anti-HBc, means the immunity came from vaccination, because the vaccine contains only surface antigen. Natural infection produces anti-HBc as well, and the window period is defined by a positive IgM anti-HBc with negative HBsAg and anti-HBs.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man has been HBsAg positive for 2 years. HBeAg is negative, HBV DNA is 85,000 IU/mL and ALT has been above twice the upper limit on repeated tests. Ultrasound shows a coarse liver without cirrhosis. Anti-HDV is negative. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Chronic HBV with high viral load and persistently raised ALT needs antiviral treatment, and the first-line oral agents are tenofovir or entecavir because of their potency and low resistance. Sofosbuvir and daclatasvir are direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C and have no activity against HBV.

questions.s: Nasreen delivers a healthy term baby at a THQ hospital. Her antenatal screening showed she is HBsAg positive. What is the most appropriate management of the baby?
o: Hepatitis B vaccine at 6 weeks with the EPI schedule
Hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin only, with no vaccine
Advise mother to avoid breastfeeding until 6 months
questions.e: Babies of HBsAg-positive mothers should receive the birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine plus HBIG within 12 hours, then complete the vaccine course, which prevents most vertical transmission. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated, and delaying the vaccine to 6 weeks misses the window for preventing perinatal infection.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man from rural Sindh has been a known HBsAg carrier with normal liver tests for 5 years. He now has 2 weeks of jaundice and confusion. ALT 1,420 U/L, INR 2.1. IgM anti-HAV, anti-HEV IgM and anti-HCV are negative; anti-HDV IgM is positive. What is the most likely cause of his deterioration?
questions.e: Acute severe hepatitis in a known HBsAg carrier with IgM anti-HDV indicates hepatitis D superinfection; HDV is a defective virus that needs HBsAg, and superinfection often causes severe disease. HBV reactivation is possible in a carrier but would not explain the positive anti-HDV IgM.

questions.s: A 39-year-old man is found to be anti-HCV positive on screening before donating blood. He feels well, and ALT is 58 U/L. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: A positive anti-HCV shows exposure but cannot separate current infection from spontaneous clearance, so HCV RNA by PCR is needed to confirm active infection before treatment. Liver biopsy has largely been replaced by non-invasive fibrosis assessment such as elastography.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman in Lahore has chronic hepatitis C with detectable HCV RNA. Elastography shows no cirrhosis. She is not pregnant and has no other illness. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Chronic hepatitis C is now treated with oral direct-acting antivirals, such as sofosbuvir with daclatasvir or velpatasvir, which cure most patients in 12 weeks with few side effects. Interferon-based regimens are less effective and poorly tolerated, and entecavir, lamivudine and tenofovir are hepatitis B drugs.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man from a village near Sargodha is found to have chronic hepatitis C. He has never had a blood transfusion or surgery and has one sexual partner. Which route of transmission is most likely in his case?
o: Reused syringes for injections by local practitioners
questions.e: Unsafe injection practice, especially reuse of syringes and needles by informal practitioners, is the main driver of hepatitis C in Pakistan. Sexual and vertical transmission of HCV are uncommon, and faeco-oral spread occurs with hepatitis A and E, not C.

questions.s: Zainab, 25, is 32 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. She lives in an area of Hyderabad where several people have recently had jaundice after a sewage leak into the water supply. She now has jaundice, confusion and an INR of 2.6. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: An outbreak linked to contaminated water with fulminant hepatitis in a third-trimester woman is typical of hepatitis E, which has a high mortality in pregnancy. Hepatitis A spreads the same way but rarely causes liver failure in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy has had 4 days of fever and vomiting followed by jaundice. Several classmates had jaundice last month. He is alert, drinking well and has no bleeding. ALT is 1,200 U/L, INR 1.1, glucose normal. IgM anti-HAV is positive. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Supportive care at home with review
questions.e: Acute hepatitis A in a child is usually self-limiting, and with a normal INR, normal glucose and normal conscious level he can be managed at home with fluids, rest and hygiene advice. Signs of liver failure such as prolonged INR, hypoglycaemia or drowsiness would need admission; antivirals and steroids have no role.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man has compensated cirrhosis due to hepatitis C, now cured with direct-acting antivirals. He feels well. What is the most appropriate long-term surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma?
o: CT of the abdomen every year
No surveillance as the virus has been cleared
Liver ultrasound, with or without AFP, every 6 months
questions.e: Patients with cirrhosis remain at risk of hepatocellular carcinoma even after HCV cure, so they need 6-monthly ultrasound (often with alpha-fetoprotein). Annual CT adds radiation without clear benefit as a routine test, and stopping surveillance after viral clearance misses cancers that still develop.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man with hepatitis B cirrhosis has a screening endoscopy that shows large oesophageal varices without red signs. He has never bled. Pulse 84/min, BP 126/78 mmHg; he has no asthma. Which drug is most appropriate to prevent a first bleed?
questions.e: Primary prophylaxis of large varices is with a non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol or carvedilol, which lowers portal pressure, or with band ligation. Nitrates alone do not reduce first bleeds and may increase mortality, and PPIs do not prevent variceal haemorrhage.

questions.s: A 17-year-old boy has a tremor, slurred speech and declining school performance. He was treated for jaundice a year ago. ALT is 140 U/L. Slit-lamp examination shows a golden-brown ring at the edge of the cornea. Which result best supports the likely diagnosis?
o: Raised serum ferritin with transferrin saturation of 80 %
questions.e: Liver disease with neuropsychiatric features and Kayser-Fleischer rings in a young person indicates Wilson disease, in which serum caeruloplasmin is usually low and 24-hour urinary copper high. Raised ferritin and transferrin saturation suggest haemochromatosis, which does not cause corneal rings or movement disorders in teenagers.

questions.s: A 54-year-old man has diabetes, erectile dysfunction, joint pain in the second and third MCP joints and grey-brown skin. ALT is 88 U/L. Ferritin is 2,400 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 78 %. He drinks no alcohol and has had no transfusions. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Diabetes, hypogonadism, MCP arthropathy, pigmentation and iron overload without transfusion suggest hereditary haemochromatosis, treated with regular venesection until ferritin is normal. Chelators such as deferasirox are used for transfusional iron overload (as in thalassaemia) or when venesection is not possible; penicillamine is for Wilson disease.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man presents with abdominal distension. He has spider naevi and palmar erythema. Diagnostic paracentesis shows straw-coloured fluid with albumin 0.9 g/dL; serum albumin is 2.7 g/dL. Ascitic total protein is 1.1 g/dL and neutrophils 60/mm³. What is the most likely cause of his ascites?
questions.e: The serum-ascites albumin gradient is 1.8 g/dL; a gradient of 1.1 or more indicates portal hypertension, and the stigmata of chronic liver disease point to cirrhosis. TB peritonitis and carcinomatosis give a low gradient with high protein, and nephrotic syndrome gives a low gradient.

questions.s: Fatima, a 24-year-old from Quetta, has 2 months of evening fever, weight loss and abdominal swelling. There are no signs of chronic liver disease. Ascitic fluid: protein 4.6 g/dL, SAAG 0.6 g/dL, white cells 900/mm³ mostly lymphocytes, adenosine deaminase raised. Gram stain is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Exudative low-gradient ascites with lymphocytes and a raised ADA in a young woman with constitutional symptoms is typical of tuberculous peritonitis, common in Pakistan. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in cirrhotic high-gradient ascites and has a neutrophil-predominant count.

questions.s: A 56-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis has moderate ascites causing discomfort. Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L. She has stopped drinking. Apart from salt restriction, which is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Ascites in cirrhosis is driven by secondary hyperaldosteronism, so the aldosterone antagonist spironolactone is first-line, with furosemide added if response is inadequate. Furosemide alone is less effective and causes more electrolyte disturbance.

questions.s: A 61-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has mild abdominal pain and new confusion. Temperature 37.8 °C. Diagnostic paracentesis shows a neutrophil count of 480/mm³; culture is pending. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: An ascitic neutrophil count of 250/mm³ or more diagnoses spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is treated at once with an IV third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime, plus IV albumin to reduce renal failure. Laparotomy is needed only for secondary peritonitis from a perforation, which is suggested by multiple organisms or very high protein.

questions.s: A 49-year-old man with cirrhosis and tense ascites undergoes therapeutic paracentesis, and 8 litres are drained. Which measure most reduces the risk of circulatory dysfunction and renal impairment after the procedure?
questions.e: After large-volume paracentesis (more than 5 litres), IV human albumin (about 8 g per litre removed) prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, hyponatraemia and renal impairment. Saline is a less effective volume expander and worsens sodium retention in cirrhosis.

questions.s: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has a creatinine that has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL over a week. Diuretics were stopped and IV albumin given for 2 days without improvement. He is not shocked and has had no nephrotoxic drugs. Urine sodium is very low, urinalysis is bland and ultrasound shows normal kidneys. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute kidney injury in cirrhosis that does not respond to stopping diuretics and albumin, with no shock, nephrotoxins, proteinuria or structural kidney disease, meets criteria for hepatorenal syndrome. Simple prerenal injury from diuretics would have improved with volume expansion, and ATN usually gives granular casts and a higher urine sodium.

questions.s: A 64-year-old man with known cirrhosis is brought in by his son because he has been drowsy and muddled for 2 days. He has a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands. He has been constipated for a week. Glucose is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Hepatic encephalopathy is treated by correcting precipitants (here constipation) and giving lactulose titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools a day, which reduces ammonia absorption. Protein restriction is no longer advised because it worsens malnutrition, and neomycin has more toxicity and less evidence.

questions.s: A 59-year-old woman with cirrhosis becomes confused with asterixis. Temperature is normal. She has passed black stools for 2 days. Hb has fallen from 11.4 to 8.6 g/dL, and urea is raised with a normal creatinine. What is the most likely precipitant of her encephalopathy?
questions.e: Melaena with a falling Hb and a raised urea out of proportion to creatinine indicate upper GI bleeding, where digested blood provides a large protein load that raises ammonia. Infection such as SBP is another common precipitant but she has no fever, and glucose and sodium should still be checked.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man with cirrhosis has had a second episode of hepatic encephalopathy despite regular lactulose. No precipitating cause was found. Which drug is most appropriate to add to reduce further episodes?
questions.e: Rifaximin, a poorly absorbed antibiotic, added to lactulose reduces recurrent hepatic encephalopathy and hospital admissions. Metronidazole has neurotoxicity with long-term use, and benzodiazepines can precipitate encephalopathy.

questions.s: Shazia, a 44-year-old woman, presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting for 8 hours. She does not drink alcohol. Serum lipase is 6 times the upper limit of normal. Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
o: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen today
questions.e: Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis, especially in women who do not drink, and abdominal ultrasound is the first test to look for them. Early CT is not needed when the diagnosis is already clear from pain and lipase, and ERCP is reserved for pancreatitis with cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man is admitted with acute alcohol-related pancreatitis. Pulse 112/min, BP 104/66 mmHg, urine output low. Temperature 37.6 °C. What is the most important initial management?
o: Keep nil by mouth for at least a week
questions.e: Early goal-directed IV crystalloid resuscitation, with analgesia and close monitoring, is the key initial treatment of acute pancreatitis with hypovolaemia. Prophylactic antibiotics do not improve outcome in sterile pancreatitis, early oral or enteral feeding is preferred, and surgery is avoided early.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman has taken omeprazole daily for 6 years for reflux. She now has muscle cramps and palpitations. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. Her calcium is low-normal and her other medicines are amlodipine and paracetamol. Which electrolyte abnormality is most likely linked to her long-term medicine?
questions.e: Long-term proton pump inhibitors can reduce intestinal magnesium absorption, causing hypomagnesaemia with cramps, arrhythmia and secondary hypocalcaemia or hypokalaemia. Hyperkalaemia is not a recognised effect of PPIs.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man had a bleeding duodenal ulcer treated with endoscopic adrenaline injection and clips, followed by a proton pump inhibitor infusion. He takes no NSAIDs or aspirin, and the biopsy urease test is positive. Which measure will most reduce his long-term risk of the ulcer bleeding again?
questions.e: In a Helicobacter pylori-positive ulcer, eradication therapy heals the ulcer and markedly reduces recurrence and rebleeding, and cure should be confirmed with a test afterwards. Tranexamic acid does not reduce rebleeding and adds thrombotic risk, and acid-reducing surgery is now rarely needed because eradication prevents most recurrences.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man on aspirin presents with melaena and Hb 8.2 g/dL. After resuscitation, endoscopy within 24 hours shows a 1 cm duodenal ulcer with a non-bleeding visible vessel. What is the most appropriate management at this endoscopy?
o: Adrenaline injection combined with clips or thermal therapy
No endoscopic treatment, start oral PPI
Biopsy of the ulcer edge only
questions.e: A non-bleeding visible vessel has a high risk of rebleeding and needs endoscopic haemostasis; adrenaline injection should be combined with a second method (clips, thermal coagulation) because adrenaline alone is less effective. A high-dose PPI is then given after endoscopic therapy.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with Crohn's colitis asks which of her problems are likely to improve once her bowel inflammation is controlled. Which extraintestinal manifestation most closely follows the activity of the bowel disease?
questions.e: Erythema nodosum and peripheral large-joint arthritis typically flare with active bowel disease and settle when it is controlled. Primary sclerosing cholangitis and ankylosing spondylitis run a course independent of bowel activity, and uveitis may also occur independently.

questions.s: A 29-year-old man with extensive ileal Crohn's disease and fat malabsorption presents with right loin pain radiating to the groin and haematuria. CT shows a 6 mm stone in the right ureter. What is the most likely composition of the stone?
questions.e: In ileal disease, unabsorbed fat binds calcium in the gut, leaving free oxalate to be absorbed in the colon (enteric hyperoxaluria), which leads to calcium oxalate stones. Uric acid stones can also occur from dehydration in IBD, but oxalate stones are the classic link with fat malabsorption.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man has an intensely itchy rash of grouped small blisters over his elbows, knees and buttocks. Skin biopsy shows granular IgA deposits in the dermal papillae. With which condition is this rash most strongly associated?
questions.e: Dermatitis herpetiformis, with itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces and granular IgA in the dermal papillae, is a skin manifestation of coeliac disease and responds to a gluten-free diet (with dapsone for symptoms). Hepatitis C is linked to lichen planus and porphyria cutanea tarda rather than this rash.

questions.s: A 48-year-old man with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is about to start chemotherapy that includes rituximab. Screening shows HBsAg positive, HBV DNA 600 IU/mL, ALT normal. What is the most appropriate action regarding his hepatitis B?
o: No action, as his liver tests are normal
Check HBV DNA only if ALT rises
Give hepatitis B vaccine before chemotherapy
Start entecavir or tenofovir before chemotherapy
questions.e: Rituximab and other strong immunosuppression can reactivate hepatitis B, causing severe or fatal hepatitis, so HBsAg-positive patients need prophylactic entecavir or tenofovir started before and continued after treatment. Waiting for ALT to rise risks a flare that may not respond, and vaccination has no role in someone already infected.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C has increasing breathlessness that is worse when he sits or stands and eases when he lies down. Oxygen saturation is 95 % lying and 88 % sitting up. He has clubbing and spider naevi, and the chest X-ray is clear. On contrast echocardiography, bubbles appear in the left heart after four cardiac cycles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Platypnoea and orthodeoxia with a clear chest X-ray in cirrhosis suggest hepatopulmonary syndrome, caused by intrapulmonary vascular dilatation; the delayed appearance of bubbles in the left heart confirms an intrapulmonary rather than intracardiac shunt. Portopulmonary hypertension is pulmonary arterial hypertension with a raised pulmonary pressure on echocardiography, and hepatic hydrothorax shows an effusion on the X-ray.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman with untreated chronic hepatitis C has palpable purpura on her legs, joint pain, proteinuria and haematuria. Complement C4 is low and rheumatoid factor is positive. What is the most likely cause of her rash and renal findings?
questions.e: Hepatitis C is the main cause of mixed cryoglobulinaemia, which gives palpable purpura, arthralgia and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with low C4 and positive rheumatoid factor. IgA vasculitis gives purpura and nephritis too, but complement is normal and it is not linked with hepatitis C.

questions.s: A 46-year-old man who drinks heavily presents with jaundice, fever 38.0 °C and tender hepatomegaly. Bilirubin 9.8 mg/dL, AST 210 U/L, ALT 85 U/L, INR 1.9, white cells 15 x 10⁹/L. Blood and urine cultures are negative and ultrasound shows no biliary dilatation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Jaundice, fever, tender hepatomegaly and leucocytosis in a heavy drinker with AST more than twice ALT (both under about 300 U/L) is typical of alcoholic hepatitis. Acute viral hepatitis usually gives transaminases in the thousands, and cholangitis would show biliary dilatation.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has recovered from his first episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. He still has moderate ascites. What is the most appropriate measure to prevent recurrence?
questions.e: After one episode of SBP the recurrence risk is high, so long-term secondary prophylaxis with an oral quinolone such as norfloxacin or ciprofloxacin is given. Regular paracentesis and weekly albumin do not prevent infection.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with compensated cirrhosis has trouble sleeping and asks his GP for a sleeping tablet. Which drug is most likely to precipitate hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.e: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam are metabolised by the liver and have prolonged sedative effects in cirrhosis, a classic precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy. Lactulose is used to treat encephalopathy, and paracetamol in reduced doses is the preferred analgesic in liver disease.

questions.s: A 41-year-old man had acute alcohol-related pancreatitis 6 weeks ago. He now has early satiety, epigastric fullness and a vague epigastric mass. Amylase is persistently raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Carcinoma of the head of pancreas
Gastric outlet obstruction from a peptic ulcer
questions.e: A peripancreatic fluid collection that persists beyond 4 weeks after pancreatitis and becomes encapsulated is a pseudocyst; it causes epigastric fullness, early satiety and persistently raised amylase. Pancreatic carcinoma is unlikely at this age and timing and usually presents with painless jaundice and weight loss.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman with gallstone pancreatitis is in her second day in hospital. She now has a temperature of 39.2 °C with rigors, and bilirubin has risen from 2.1 to 5.6 mg/dL. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: CT of the abdomen in one week
questions.e: Gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis (fever, rising bilirubin, dilated duct) needs urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy and stone extraction, along with antibiotics. Cholecystectomy is done later in the same admission or soon after recovery, not during acute cholangitis.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man is on day 2 of severe acute pancreatitis. He complains of tingling around his mouth, and tapping over the facial nerve makes his lip twitch. Serum calcium is 6.8 mg/dL with albumin 3.6 g/dL. What is the most likely mechanism of his low calcium?
o: Reduced parathyroid hormone release from low magnesium
Renal calcium wasting caused by loop diuretics
Low albumin causing a falsely low total calcium
Calcium deposition in areas of fat necrosis
questions.e: In acute pancreatitis, released lipase digests fat to fatty acids that bind calcium as soaps in areas of fat necrosis, lowering serum calcium; this is a marker of severity. The albumin is near normal, so the low calcium is genuine rather than an artefact of hypoalbuminaemia.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman in Hyderabad has had profuse diarrhoea for 3 days. She is dizzy on standing with dry mucosa, BP 92/60 mmHg. Creatinine is 2.3 mg/dL (baseline 0.9). Urine sodium is 10 mmol/L, fractional excretion of sodium is below 1%, and urine microscopy is bland. What is the most likely type of kidney injury?
o: Post-renal obstruction at the bladder outlet
questions.e: Volume depletion with avid sodium retention (low urine sodium, FENa below 1%) and bland urine indicates prerenal AKI, which should reverse quickly with fluid replacement. In acute tubular necrosis the damaged tubules cannot conserve sodium, so urine sodium and FENa are high, with granular casts.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man had prolonged hypotension during septic shock from a perforated bowel. Two days later his urine output is 300 mL/day and creatinine is rising despite restored BP. Urine microscopy is most likely to show which finding?
o: Fatty casts and oval fat bodies
questions.e: Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis sheds tubular epithelial cells that form muddy brown granular casts. Red cell casts indicate glomerulonephritis, and fatty casts are typical of nephrotic syndrome.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman develops fever, a maculopapular rash and joint pains 10 days after starting a course of a penicillin. Her creatinine has risen from 0.8 to 2.6 mg/dL. Urine shows white cells and white cell casts with a sterile culture, and blood count shows eosinophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, rash, eosinophilia and sterile pyuria with white cell casts after a new drug suggest drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis; the drug should be stopped. Pyelonephritis would give a positive urine culture and loin pain without rash or eosinophilia.

questions.s: A 76-year-old man with a long history of poor urinary stream has not passed urine for 12 hours and is restless. A smooth, tender midline mass is palpable above the pubis. Creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). What is the most appropriate first step?
o: CT scan of the kidneys with contrast
questions.e: Acute retention from prostatic obstruction is causing post-renal AKI, and bladder catheterisation relieves the obstruction and usually allows renal function to recover. Furosemide does nothing for obstruction, and contrast CT would add nephrotoxic risk without changing first management.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man is pulled from a collapsed building after 18 hours trapped under rubble with his legs crushed. His urine is dark brown; dipstick is strongly positive for blood but microscopy shows no red cells. Creatine kinase is 85,000 U/L. What is the most important initial treatment to protect his kidneys?
o: Restriction of all fluids to 500 mL/day
questions.e: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin, which is toxic to the tubules; early, generous IV isotonic fluid to maintain a high urine output is the key preventive treatment. Fluid restriction would increase myoglobin concentration in the tubules and worsen injury.

questions.s: A 35-year-old farmer from Tharparkar is brought in 10 hours after a snake bite on the foot while harvesting at dusk. The foot is swollen, his gums are bleeding, blood in a glass tube has not clotted after 20 minutes, and he has passed only 100 mL of urine since admission. What is the most important specific treatment?
questions.e: Viper envenoming causing coagulopathy (positive 20-minute whole blood clotting test) and acute kidney injury needs polyvalent antivenom, which neutralises the venom; dialysis may later be needed for established renal failure. Plasma or vitamin K alone cannot correct a venom-induced consumptive coagulopathy while venom is still active.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has fatigue and a normocytic, normochromic anaemia (Hb 8.9 g/dL). Iron studies, B12 and folate are normal. What is the main cause of his anaemia?
o: Chronic blood loss from the gut
questions.e: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney produce erythropoietin, and loss of renal mass in CKD reduces its production, causing normocytic anaemia. Uraemia shortens red cell survival somewhat, but this is a minor contributor.

questions.s: Bilal, 34, has hypertension, intermittent flank pain and episodes of visible haematuria. Both kidneys are palpable and ballotable. His father started dialysis at 50 and his uncle died of a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Creatinine is 1.3 mg/dL. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral palpable kidneys, hypertension, haematuria and a family history of kidney failure and subarachnoid haemorrhage point to autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, and ultrasound showing multiple bilateral cysts confirms it in an at-risk adult. Renal biopsy is unnecessary and risky in cystic kidneys, and cystoscopy looks for a bladder source of haematuria, which this picture does not suggest.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man with CKD stage 4 not yet on dialysis has a haemoglobin of 8.6 g/dL. Ferritin is 60 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 14%. B12 and folate are normal and there is no bleeding. What is the most appropriate next step for his anaemia?
o: Transfuse two units of packed red cells
Give iron, usually intravenously, before considering an ESA
Start oral folic acid and recheck in three months
questions.e: Iron deficiency must be corrected before or alongside an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, because ESAs work poorly without adequate iron; IV iron is often preferred in advanced CKD. Starting an ESA alone with low iron stores would give a poor response.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 8 years. Her creatinine and eGFR are normal. Which test is the most useful for early detection of diabetic kidney disease?
o: Renal ultrasound with Doppler of renal arteries
questions.e: Moderately increased albuminuria on the urine albumin:creatinine ratio is the earliest practical marker of diabetic kidney disease, appearing before the GFR falls. Serum urea and creatinine stay normal until a large amount of renal function has been lost.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man has hypertension, intermittent loin pain and episodes of visible haematuria. Both kidneys are palpable and enlarged, and his father needed dialysis at 55. Ultrasound shows multiple cysts in both kidneys and the liver. Which associated condition should he be specifically asked about?
questions.e: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is associated with intracranial berry aneurysms, which can cause subarachnoid haemorrhage; screening is considered when there is a family history of aneurysm or haemorrhage. Liver cysts and mitral valve prolapse are other associations, but not retinal detachment.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has CKD with an eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73 m². He takes metformin, linagliptin, insulin glargine and amlodipine. Which drug should be stopped because of his kidney function?
questions.e: Metformin should be stopped when the eGFR falls below 30 because accumulation increases the risk of lactic acidosis. Linagliptin is excreted mainly through bile and needs no dose change in CKD.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has puffy eyes in the morning that have spread to his legs over a week. BP is normal. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ with no blood, serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and cholesterol is high. Complement levels are normal. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Nephrotic syndrome in a young child with normal BP, no haematuria and normal complement is most likely minimal change disease, which usually responds to oral corticosteroids, so steroids are started without biopsy. Cyclophosphamide and ciclosporin are reserved for frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease.

questions.s: An 8-year-old girl from a village near Larkana had infected sores on her legs 3 weeks ago. She now has cola-coloured urine, puffy eyelids and a BP of 140/95 mmHg. Urine shows red cell casts and serum C3 is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A nephritic illness 2 to 4 weeks after streptococcal skin or throat infection, with low C3, is post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. IgA nephropathy causes haematuria within a day or two of an upper respiratory infection and complement is normal.

questions.s: A 23-year-old man notices dark red urine one day after the onset of a sore throat. This has happened twice before. BP is normal, creatinine is normal and serum complement levels are normal. Urine shows dysmorphic red cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent visible haematuria within one to two days of an upper respiratory infection, with normal complement, is typical of IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis appears after a latent period of weeks and causes a low C3.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man has 2 months of increasing leg oedema. Urine protein is 7 g/day with a few red cells, serum albumin 2.1 g/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Complement is normal, hepatitis B and C serology are negative, and serum anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Anti-PLA2R antibodies are highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy, the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in older white adults and common in adults elsewhere. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis usually has low complement and is often linked to hepatitis C.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman with nephrotic syndrome develops sudden left loin pain and visible haematuria. Doppler ultrasound shows a left renal vein thrombosis. What is the main mechanism of the hypercoagulable state in nephrotic syndrome?
o: Increased platelet destruction in the spleen
Excess hepatic production of protein C
Reduced fibrinogen synthesis by the liver
questions.e: Antithrombin III and other small anticoagulant proteins are lost in the urine, while the liver increases production of fibrinogen and other clotting factors, causing hypercoagulability. Fibrinogen is increased, not reduced, in nephrotic syndrome.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man who smokes has coughed up blood several times this week. His creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 4.5 mg/dL in 10 days and urine shows red cell casts. Renal biopsy shows crescents in most glomeruli. Which immunofluorescence pattern is expected?
o: Granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls
Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
questions.e: Pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis suggests anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture), which shows linear IgG along the basement membrane. Little or no immune deposits (pauci-immune) is typical of ANCA-associated vasculitis, which can mimic it clinically.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man on haemodialysis missed two sessions. Serum potassium is 7.2 mmol/L and ECG shows tall peaked T waves and widening QRS complexes. What should be given first?
questions.e: With ECG changes, IV calcium gluconate (or chloride) is given first to stabilise the myocardial membrane within minutes; it does not lower potassium. Salbutamol and insulin-dextrose then shift potassium into cells, and dialysis removes it.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman with AKI has a serum potassium of 6.9 mmol/L. IV calcium gluconate has been given for ECG changes. Which treatment most reliably shifts potassium into cells and lowers the serum level within 30 minutes?
questions.e: Insulin stimulates the Na-K ATPase and moves potassium into cells, lowering serum potassium within 15 to 30 minutes; glucose is given to prevent hypoglycaemia. Calcium resonium removes potassium through the gut but takes hours to act.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing alcohol misuse is admitted with confusion and serum sodium of 108 mmol/L. Her sodium rises to 128 mmol/L within the first 24 hours. Three days later she develops dysarthria, difficulty swallowing and weakness of all four limbs. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatraemia causes osmotic demyelination, typically in the pons, with dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis days later; alcohol misuse and malnutrition increase the risk. Wernicke encephalopathy causes confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia rather than quadriparesis.

questions.s: A 72-year-old man recovering from pneumonia has a serum sodium of 126 mmol/L. He is asymptomatic and clinically euvolaemic. Serum osmolality is low, urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg and urine sodium is 50 mmol/L. Thyroid and adrenal function are normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: These findings indicate SIADH, and the first-line treatment for mild asymptomatic SIADH is fluid restriction while the cause settles. Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatraemia in SIADH because the sodium is excreted while the water is retained.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman with prolonged diarrhoea has a serum potassium of 2.6 mmol/L. Which ECG change is most characteristic of hypokalaemia?
o: Prominent U waves with flattened T waves
Delta waves with a short PR interval
questions.e: Hypokalaemia produces flattened or inverted T waves, ST depression and prominent U waves. Tall peaked T waves are the earliest sign of hyperkalaemia.

questions.s: A 65-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is drowsy, thirsty and constipated. Serum calcium is 14.5 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.5) and creatinine is mildly raised. She looks dehydrated. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.e: Severe hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and dehydration, so the first step is IV rehydration with 0.9% saline, followed by an IV bisphosphonate once hydrated. Loop diuretics are no longer used routinely and can worsen dehydration if given before fluid replacement.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman collapses with a generalised seizure after a long charity walk during which she drank large volumes of water. Serum sodium is 118 mmol/L. She is now drowsy with a GCS of 12. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or reduced consciousness needs urgent IV hypertonic saline boluses to raise sodium by a few mmol/L and reduce cerebral oedema, with careful limits on the 24-hour rise. Fluid restriction is far too slow for a life-threatening presentation.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has had profuse watery diarrhoea for 4 days. Results: sodium 136 mmol/L, chloride 114 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, potassium 3.0 mmol/L; arterial pH 7.26. How is this acid-base disorder best classified?
questions.e: The anion gap is 136 − (114 + 12) = 10 mmol/L, which is normal, so this is a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis from loss of bicarbonate in diarrhoeal stool. A high anion gap would point to added acids such as lactate or ketones.

questions.s: A patient has a metabolic acidosis with an anion gap of 26 mmol/L. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Lactic acidosis adds an unmeasured anion (lactate), raising the anion gap. Diarrhoea, acetazolamide and renal tubular acidosis cause bicarbonate loss or reduced acid excretion with chloride retention, giving a normal anion gap.

questions.s: Several men are brought to a hospital in Punjab after drinking illicitly brewed liquor. One has blurred vision, abdominal pain and rapid deep breathing. He has a severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis and a raised osmolar gap. Besides supportive care and haemodialysis, which treatment specifically prevents formation of the toxic metabolite?
questions.e: Methanol is converted by alcohol dehydrogenase to formic acid, which causes acidosis and optic nerve damage; fomepizole or ethanol blocks this enzyme. N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol poisoning and has no role here.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman with Sjögren syndrome has recurrent kidney stones and muscle weakness. Blood tests show a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with potassium 2.9 mmol/L. Urine pH remains 6.5 despite the acidosis, and X-ray shows nephrocalcinosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5 during systemic acidosis, with hypokalaemia, stones and nephrocalcinosis, is distal (type 1) RTA, which is associated with Sjögren syndrome. In proximal RTA the urine can still be acidified once serum bicarbonate falls, and stones are uncommon.

questions.s: A 17-year-old girl took a large number of aspirin tablets 4 hours ago. She has tinnitus, sweating and rapid breathing. Which acid-base picture is most typical at this stage?
o: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalaemia
questions.e: Salicylates stimulate the respiratory centre, causing an early respiratory alkalosis, and then uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, producing a high anion gap metabolic acidosis; adults often show this mixed picture. A pure respiratory acidosis would need hypoventilation, which occurs only late with severe CNS depression.

questions.s: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 3 has a persistent serum potassium of 6.0 mmol/L and a mild normal anion gap metabolic acidosis. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both low. He takes no potassium-sparing drugs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Type 4 RTA, from hyporeninaemic hypoaldosteronism, is common in diabetic kidney disease and causes hyperkalaemia with a mild normal anion gap acidosis. Primary adrenal insufficiency also lowers aldosterone, but renin is high, and patients usually have hyponatraemia and hypotension.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man with AKI is being reviewed on the medical ward. Which finding is an indication for urgent dialysis?
o: Uraemic pericarditis with a pericardial rub
Serum creatinine of 4.0 mg/dL with good urine output
Serum potassium of 5.6 mmol/L with a normal ECG
Blood urea of 90 mg/dL with no symptoms
questions.e: Uraemic complications such as pericarditis or encephalopathy are indications for urgent dialysis, along with refractory hyperkalaemia, refractory fluid overload and severe acidosis. A creatinine or urea value alone, without complications, does not by itself require emergency dialysis.

questions.s: A 59-year-old woman with AKI after sepsis has passed less than 100 mL of urine in 24 hours. She is now breathless with SpO2 86% on 40% oxygen and widespread crackles. She has received two large doses of IV furosemide without any increase in urine output. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: A third, higher dose of IV furosemide
questions.e: Pulmonary oedema that does not respond to diuretics in oliguric AKI is an indication for urgent renal replacement therapy to remove fluid. Further diuretic doses are unlikely to work in established oliguria and risk ototoxicity.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis has diffuse abdominal pain and notices that her drained dialysis fluid has become cloudy. She is mildly febrile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cloudy effluent with abdominal pain in a patient on peritoneal dialysis is peritonitis until proven otherwise; effluent cell count and culture are sent and intraperitoneal antibiotics started. An exit-site infection alone causes redness and discharge at the catheter exit without cloudy effluent.

questions.s: A 26-year-old non-pregnant woman has 2 days of dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort. She has no fever or loin pain. Urine dipstick is positive for nitrites and leucocytes. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
questions.e: Uncomplicated lower UTI in a non-pregnant woman is treated with a short course of nitrofurantoin, which reaches high concentration in urine and has low resistance rates. Fluoroquinolones are reserved for more serious infections because of side effects and resistance.

questions.s: At her first antenatal visit at 12 weeks, a 24-year-old woman has a routine urine culture growing more than 10^5 colonies/mL of E. coli on two samples. She has no urinary symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Treat with an antibiotic safe in pregnancy and repeat culture
Treat only if pyuria is present on microscopy
Advise increased oral fluids and daily cranberry juice until delivery
questions.e: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated because it carries a significant risk of pyelonephritis and preterm birth; a test of cure culture follows. In non-pregnant adults it is usually left untreated, which makes the first option tempting.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has 2 days of fever of 39.5 °C, rigors, right loin pain and vomiting. She has right renal angle tenderness. Urine dipstick shows nitrites and leucocytes. She cannot keep tablets down. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Oral nitrofurantoin for 3 days and review at home in a week
IV ceftriaxone after sending urine and blood cultures
questions.e: Acute pyelonephritis with vomiting needs admission and IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone after cultures are sent. Nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate kidney tissue levels and is not suitable for pyelonephritis.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has her third episode of uncomplicated cystitis this year. Which organism is responsible for most community-acquired urinary tract infections?
questions.e: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli causes the large majority of community-acquired UTIs. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a recognised second cause in young sexually active women but is much less common.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has recurrent urinary infections. Urine pH is 8.0 and contains crystals shaped like coffin lids. X-ray shows a large stone filling the left renal pelvis and calyces. Which organism is most likely involved?
questions.e: Proteus produces urease, which splits urea into ammonia, making urine alkaline and promoting magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) staghorn stones. E. coli does not produce urease and does not cause struvite stones in this way.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man from Bannu has had dysuria, frequency and occasional haematuria for 3 months, with evening fevers. Repeated urine microscopy shows many pus cells, but routine cultures are sterile. He has not taken antibiotics. Which investigation is most appropriate next?
o: Repeat routine urine culture on a midstream sample after another 48 hours
Three early-morning urine samples for acid-fast bacilli culture
questions.e: Sterile pyuria with chronic urinary symptoms and constitutional features in a TB-endemic area suggests genitourinary tuberculosis, investigated with three early-morning urine samples for mycobacterial culture and molecular testing. Repeating routine culture will remain negative because M. tuberculosis does not grow on standard media.

questions.s: A 67-year-old woman takes ramipril and a thiazide diuretic for hypertension. She bought diclofenac for knee pain a week ago and now has a creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.0). How does the NSAID contribute to her kidney injury?
o: It causes direct crystal deposition and obstruction within the renal tubules
It blocks aldosterone at the collecting duct
It blocks prostaglandin-mediated dilatation of the afferent arteriole
questions.e: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins that keep the afferent arteriole dilated when renal perfusion is threatened, so glomerular filtration falls, especially combined with an ACE inhibitor (efferent dilatation) and a diuretic (volume depletion). ACE inhibitors, not NSAIDs, cause efferent arteriolar dilatation.

questions.s: Which of the following meets the KDIGO criteria for acute kidney injury?
o: Creatinine rise from 1.0 to 1.4 mg/dL within 48 hours
Creatinine rise from 1.0 to 1.2 mg/dL over 3 weeks
Urine output of 0.8 mL/kg/h for 12 hours
Stable creatinine of 1.6 mg/dL for 6 months
questions.e: KDIGO defines AKI as a creatinine rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. A stable raised creatinine over months suggests CKD rather than AKI.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man is found to have a creatinine of 4.2 mg/dL on his first ever blood test. No previous results exist. Which finding most strongly suggests chronic rather than acute kidney disease?
o: Bilateral small kidneys of 8 cm on ultrasound
Urine output of 1.5 litres per day
questions.e: Small, echogenic kidneys on ultrasound indicate long-standing damage and favour CKD. Normal haemoglobin argues against long-standing disease, and a normal urine output or mildly raised potassium do not separate acute from chronic disease.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man on maintenance haemodialysis has a serum phosphate of 7.5 mg/dL despite dietary advice. Calcium is normal. Which treatment is most appropriate to lower his phosphate?
o: Oral vitamin D supplement taken at night
questions.e: Phosphate binders such as calcium acetate or sevelamer bind dietary phosphate in the gut and must be taken with meals to work. Vitamin D increases gut absorption of both calcium and phosphate, which could raise phosphate further.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman has a malar rash, painful joints and oral ulcers. Urine shows protein 3+ and red cell casts, creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL, C3 and C4 are low and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are positive. What is the most likely kidney diagnosis?
questions.e: Nephritic urine with low C3 and C4 and positive anti-dsDNA in a young woman with skin and joint features indicates lupus nephritis, which needs biopsy to guide immunosuppression. IgA nephropathy has normal complement levels.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has 2 months of nasal crusting with bloody discharge, sinus pain and cough with haemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows cavitating nodules, urine contains red cell casts, and creatinine has risen to 3.0 mg/dL. Which antibody is most likely positive?
questions.e: Upper airway disease, cavitating lung nodules and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis are typical of granulomatosis with polyangiitis, associated with c-ANCA (PR3). Anti-GBM disease causes lung haemorrhage and nephritis but not sinus disease or cavitating nodules.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man on long-term omeprazole and a loop diuretic has a serum potassium of 2.8 mmol/L that has not risen despite 3 days of adequate potassium replacement. Which additional abnormality is most likely preventing correction?
questions.e: Magnesium deficiency, which both proton pump inhibitors and loop diuretics can cause, increases renal potassium wasting, so hypokalaemia cannot be corrected until magnesium is replaced. Hypophosphataemia also occurs with malnutrition but does not cause refractory potassium loss in this way.

questions.s: The day after a total thyroidectomy, a 38-year-old woman has tingling around the mouth and in her fingertips. Tapping over the facial nerve causes twitching at the corner of the mouth. Her serum calcium is 6.8 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy, usually from parathyroid injury or ischaemia, is treated with IV calcium gluconate, followed by oral calcium and active vitamin D. Oral vitamin D alone acts too slowly for symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

questions.s: In a patient with chronic metabolic acidosis, the kidneys increase acid excretion over several days. Which renal process generates most of the new bicarbonate in this adaptation?
o: Ammonia production from glutamine in proximal tubular cells
Increased filtration of bicarbonate at the glomerulus
Secretion of bicarbonate by type B intercalated cells
Reabsorption of chloride in the thick ascending limb
questions.e: Proximal tubular cells metabolise glutamine to ammonium and new bicarbonate; the ammonium is excreted in urine and the bicarbonate returned to blood, and this process increases greatly in chronic acidosis. Type B intercalated cells secrete bicarbonate, which would worsen acidosis rather than correct it.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man with CKD stage 4 and a declining eGFR is expected to need haemodialysis within the next year. Which form of vascular access is preferred for long-term haemodialysis?
o: Arteriovenous fistula created in the arm
questions.e: A native arteriovenous fistula, such as radiocephalic at the wrist, has the lowest rates of infection and thrombosis and is created months ahead so it can mature. Tunnelled catheters carry higher risks of bloodstream infection and central vein stenosis.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman has mild dysuria. Her urine culture report shows a mixed growth of three different organisms with many squamous epithelial cells. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Treat for all three organisms with combined antibiotics
Repeat the test on a properly collected midstream sample
questions.e: A mixed growth with many squamous cells indicates contamination from skin or the vagina, so the result is unreliable and a clean midstream sample should be sent. Treating every organism in a contaminated sample exposes her to needless antibiotics and resistance.

questions.s: A 27-year-old woman at 9 weeks of gestation has symptoms of cystitis. Which antibiotic is best avoided at this stage of pregnancy because it is a folate antagonist?
questions.e: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase and is avoided in the first trimester because of the risk of neural tube defects. Nitrofurantoin is acceptable in early pregnancy but avoided near term because of the risk of neonatal haemolysis.

questions.s: Tariq, a 46-year-old bank manager with a BMI of 31 kg/m², attends a screening camp in Lahore. He has no symptoms. A random capillary glucose is 168 mg/dL. Which result would confirm a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus?
o: A second random glucose of 170 mg/dL
A fasting plasma glucose of 112 mg/dL
questions.e: In an asymptomatic person, diabetes is confirmed by two abnormal tests, such as HbA1c of 6.5 % or more on two occasions or fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more. A fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL indicates impaired fasting glucose, and glycosuria is not diagnostic because renal thresholds vary.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. HbA1c is 7.6 %, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL (eGFR above 90), BMI 29 kg/m². She has no heart failure or cardiovascular disease. Diet advice has been given. Which drug is most appropriate to start?
questions.e: Metformin is first-line for type 2 diabetes because it is effective, weight-neutral, does not cause hypoglycaemia on its own and is cheap. Glibenclamide causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain, and insulin is not first-line at this HbA1c without symptoms of severe hyperglycaemia.

questions.s: A 67-year-old man with type 2 diabetes takes metformin 1 g twice daily. His creatinine has risen over a year and his eGFR is now 26 mL/min/1.73 m². He is clinically well. What is the most appropriate change to his metformin?
o: Reduce it to 500 mg twice daily
Switch to extended-release metformin at the same dose
questions.e: Metformin should be stopped when eGFR falls below 30 because accumulation increases the risk of lactic acidosis; the dose is reduced when eGFR is between 30 and 45. Changing to extended-release metformin does not remove the risk of accumulation.

questions.s: A 74-year-old widow living alone in Gujranwala is brought in at 6 am sweating and confused. Capillary glucose is 38 mg/dL. She takes glibenclamide for diabetes and has been eating poorly with a cold. Creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. Why is this drug a particular problem for her?
o: It causes lactic acidosis when the kidney function falls
It causes urinary loss of glucose and fluid
Its active metabolites accumulate in renal impairment
It increases insulin resistance in the liver
questions.e: Glibenclamide is a long-acting sulfonylurea with active metabolites cleared by the kidney, so elderly people with reduced renal function and poor intake are at high risk of prolonged hypoglycaemia. Lactic acidosis is linked with metformin, and urinary glucose loss describes SGLT2 inhibitors.

questions.s: A 10-year-old girl from Abbottabad has had increased thirst, frequent urination and bedwetting for 3 weeks, with 3 kg weight loss. She is alert and well hydrated. Random glucose is 342 mg/dL; urine shows glucose 3+ and ketones 1+. Venous pH is 7.37. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start metformin and review in a month
Dietary advice and repeat glucose in a week
Start subcutaneous insulin the same day
questions.e: A thin child with osmotic symptoms, weight loss, hyperglycaemia and ketonuria has type 1 diabetes and needs insulin started the same day under a specialist team, to prevent progression to DKA. Oral agents have no role in type 1 diabetes.

questions.s: A 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and had a myocardial infarction last year. HbA1c is 8.1 %, eGFR 58 mL/min/1.73 m². Which class of drug is most appropriate to add?
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin or dapagliflozin lower glucose and reduce heart failure admissions, cardiovascular death and progression of kidney disease, so they are preferred in heart failure and atherosclerotic disease. Thiazolidinediones cause fluid retention and are contraindicated in heart failure.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 7 years. Her blood pressure and creatinine are normal and urine dipstick shows no protein. Which test is most appropriate for annual screening for diabetic kidney disease?
questions.e: Annual screening for diabetic kidney disease uses a spot urine albumin:creatinine ratio, which detects moderately increased albuminuria long before dipstick proteinuria, together with eGFR. A 24-hour collection is cumbersome and urea is an insensitive marker of kidney function.

questions.s: Sana, a 26-year-old with type 1 diabetes on basal-bolus insulin, has had vomiting and diarrhoea for a day and is eating very little, though she can keep fluids down. Her glucose is 250 mg/dL and blood ketones 0.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate advice about her insulin?
o: Stop all insulin until she is eating normally again
Stop the basal insulin and give rapid-acting insulin only with each meal
Continue basal insulin and check glucose and ketones every 2-4 hours
Halve all insulin doses and check her glucose once a day
questions.e: During illness the stress response raises glucose even when little is eaten, so basal insulin must never be stopped in type 1 diabetes; glucose and ketones are checked every few hours and extra rapid-acting insulin is given if they rise. Stopping insulin is a classic precipitant of diabetic ketoacidosis. She needs urgent review if she cannot keep fluids down or her ketones keep rising.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes for 15 years has his annual eye check. Fundoscopy shows fine new vessels on the optic disc and dot-blot haemorrhages in all quadrants. His vision is 6/9 in both eyes. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: New vessels on the disc indicate proliferative diabetic retinopathy, which can bleed into the vitreous or cause tractional detachment, so urgent ophthalmology referral for panretinal photocoagulation (or anti-VEGF injection) is needed. Waiting 12 months risks sudden visual loss.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has a hot, red, swollen right foot for 2 weeks after twisting it. The skin is intact with no ulcer, she has no fever, and pedal pulses are bounding. The foot is 3 °C warmer than the left. CRP is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Deep vein thrombosis of the calf
questions.e: A warm, swollen, red foot with intact skin and good pulses in a person with neuropathy, often after minor trauma, is acute Charcot neuroarthropathy; it needs urgent offloading in a cast to prevent collapse of the midfoot. Cellulitis usually has a portal of entry, fever and raised inflammatory markers.

questions.s: At an annual diabetes review in a BHU, the medical officer wants to identify patients at risk of foot ulceration. Which bedside test best detects loss of protective sensation?
o: Joint position sense at the big toe
questions.e: Inability to feel a 10 g monofilament at standard sites on the sole identifies loss of protective sensation and a high risk of ulceration. Ankle reflexes and joint position sense may be reduced in neuropathy but are not the standard screening tool.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has had vomiting and abdominal pain for a day after missing insulin. He is breathing deeply. Glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.12, bicarbonate 9 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.8 mmol/L, potassium 5.1 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hyperglycaemia, acidosis (pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 15) and raised ketones define diabetic ketoacidosis, here precipitated by missed insulin; deep Kussmaul breathing is respiratory compensation. HHS has marked hyperosmolality with little or no ketosis or acidosis.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes arrives in the emergency department with DKA. Pulse 118/min, BP 96/60 mmHg. Glucose 520 mg/dL, pH 7.10, potassium 4.8 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate first step?
questions.e: The first priority in DKA is restoring circulating volume with IV 0.9 % saline, followed by a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion and potassium replacement guided by levels. Bicarbonate is not routinely given and can worsen hypokalaemia and cerebral oedema.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man is being treated for DKA with IV fluids and a fixed-rate IV insulin infusion. After 6 hours his glucose has fallen to 230 mg/dL, but blood ketones are still 2.8 mmol/L and pH 7.24. What is the most appropriate change?
o: Stop the insulin infusion and start subcutaneous insulin
Add IV 10 % dextrose and continue the insulin infusion
questions.e: Ketosis and acidosis have not resolved, so insulin must continue to switch off ketogenesis; dextrose is added when glucose falls below about 250 mg/dL (14 mmol/L) to prevent hypoglycaemia. Stopping or reducing the insulin because glucose has fallen is a common error that prolongs DKA.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy is 5 hours into treatment for severe DKA. He now complains of headache, becomes irritable, and his pulse falls from 120 to 64/min with a rise in blood pressure. Glucose is 260 mg/dL. What is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Headache, irritability, falling heart rate and rising blood pressure during DKA treatment in a child suggest cerebral oedema, the main cause of death in paediatric DKA; it is treated urgently with mannitol or hypertonic saline. The glucose is not low, and hypokalaemia causes arrhythmia and weakness rather than these signs.

questions.s: A 72-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is brought from her home in Sukkur during a heatwave. She has been drowsy for 3 days with poor fluid intake.
