Glucose 920 mg/dL, sodium 148 mmol/L, urea high, serum osmolality 356 mOsm/kg, pH 7.36, blood ketones 0.6 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Very high glucose, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and marked dehydration without significant acidosis or ketosis define hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, typical in elderly people with type 2 diabetes. In DKA the pH would be below 7.3 with ketones above 3 mmol/L.

questions.s: A 36-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department unconscious after a long football match. Capillary glucose is 32 mg/dL. He has a working intravenous cannula. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
o: Oral glucose gel between the gums
questions.e: Severe hypoglycaemia in an unconscious patient with IV access is treated with IV glucose (for example 10 % glucose), then a long-acting carbohydrate once awake. Oral glucose is unsafe when consciousness is impaired; IM glucagon is the alternative when there is no IV access.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman on insulin feels shaky and sweaty at work. She is fully alert and able to swallow. Capillary glucose is 58 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
o: 15 to 20 g of glucose tablets or juice
A full meal of rice and curry
A chocolate bar and recheck glucose in an hour
questions.e: Conscious hypoglycaemia is treated with 15 to 20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets, juice), rechecking after 10 to 15 minutes and following with a longer-acting snack. Chocolate and full meals contain fat that slows glucose absorption, and glucagon is for patients who cannot take oral treatment.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has palpitations, heat intolerance and weight loss. She has a diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, proptosis and lid lag. TSH is undetectable and free T4 is raised. Which test best confirms the cause?
questions.e: A diffuse goitre with bruit and eye signs in a hyperthyroid young woman is Graves disease, confirmed by TSH receptor (stimulating) antibodies. Anti-TPO antibodies are found in Graves but are much more typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis and are not specific.

questions.s: Sana, 32, was started on carbimazole for Graves disease 5 weeks ago. She now has a sore throat and fever of 38.6 °C. She has no cough. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Start oral amoxicillin and continue the carbimazole
Throat swab and review in 3 days
Stop carbimazole and check a full blood count
questions.e: Sore throat or fever on an antithyroid drug may signal agranulocytosis, so the drug is stopped and an urgent full blood count checked. Propylthiouracil can also cause agranulocytosis, so switching to it is unsafe.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has had a painful, tender swelling in the front of her neck, fever and palpitations for 10 days, beginning two weeks after a sore throat. ESR is 78 mm/h, free T4 is raised and TSH is suppressed. A technetium scan shows very low thyroid uptake. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, with a high ESR, thyrotoxicosis and low isotope uptake, is subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: hormone leaks from damaged follicles rather than being overproduced. It is treated with NSAIDs and a beta-blocker, not antithyroid drugs. Graves disease is painless and shows diffusely increased uptake.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease is admitted after a cholecystectomy with temperature 40.1 °C, agitation, vomiting and atrial fibrillation at 164/min. Propranolol is started. Which additional drug most directly blocks both new hormone synthesis and peripheral conversion of T4 to T3?
questions.e: In thyroid storm, propylthiouracil is preferred because it blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3; iodide is given at least an hour later to block release. Carbimazole blocks synthesis only, and iodide given first could fuel further hormone production.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman had a sore throat 2 weeks ago. She now has fever, neck pain radiating to the jaw, palpitations and a very tender thyroid. ESR is 92 mm/h, TSH is suppressed and free T4 high. Technetium scan shows almost no uptake. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Painful thyroid, high ESR, thyrotoxicosis and low uptake after a viral illness indicate subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis; the thyrotoxicosis comes from release of stored hormone, so NSAIDs (or steroids if severe) and beta-blockers are used. Antithyroid drugs do not help because new hormone synthesis is not increased.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman has tiredness, weight gain, constipation and heavy periods. She has a firm, non-tender diffuse goitre. TSH is 38 mU/L (normal 0.4-4.0) and free T4 is low. Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Hypothyroidism with a firm goitre and positive anti-TPO antibodies is Hashimoto thyroiditis, treated with lifelong levothyroxine titrated to TSH. Iodide does not treat autoimmune hypothyroidism and can worsen it, and liothyronine is not used as standard replacement.

questions.s: A 76-year-old man with stable angina is found to have primary hypothyroidism. TSH is 24 mU/L and free T4 is low. What is the most appropriate way to start treatment?
o: Full replacement dose of levothyroxine from the first day
Delay treatment until his angina is revascularised
questions.e: In elderly patients and those with ischaemic heart disease, levothyroxine is started at a low dose (such as 25 micrograms daily) and increased gradually, because a rapid rise in metabolic rate can provoke angina or arrhythmia. A full dose from the start is appropriate only for younger, fit patients.

questions.s: A 39-year-old woman had thyroid tests during a health check. She has no symptoms and is not pregnant or planning pregnancy. TSH is 7.2 mU/L (normal 0.4-4.0) and free T4 is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat TSH and free T4 in about 3 months
questions.e: A mildly raised TSH with normal free T4 is subclinical hypothyroidism; a single result may be transient, so tests are repeated in about 3 months (often with anti-TPO antibodies) before deciding on treatment. Levothyroxine is usually considered for persistent TSH above 10 or in pregnancy, and ultrasound is not needed without a palpable abnormality.

questions.s: A 37-year-old woman has a 2 cm painless lump in the right lobe of the thyroid. TSH is normal. Ultrasound shows a solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: A euthyroid nodule with suspicious ultrasound features (hypoechoic, microcalcification, irregular margins) needs fine-needle aspiration cytology. Isotope scanning is used when TSH is low to look for a hot nodule, and thyroglobulin is used for follow-up after cancer treatment, not diagnosis.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman from Karachi has a slowly growing thyroid nodule and a firm 1.5 cm lymph node in the same side of the neck. She is euthyroid. Fine-needle aspiration shows cells with nuclear grooves, pale 'Orphan Annie' nuclei and intranuclear inclusions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Nuclear grooves, clear nuclei and intranuclear inclusions are characteristic of papillary carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, which typically spreads to cervical lymph nodes in young women. Follicular carcinoma cannot be diagnosed on cytology because it requires capsular or vascular invasion on histology and spreads by blood.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man with Graves disease has gritty eyes, mild proptosis and periorbital swelling. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and is controlled on carbimazole. He asks what he can do to protect his eyes. Which measure most reduces the risk of his eye disease worsening?
questions.e: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for developing and worsening thyroid eye disease, and stopping smoking improves outcome and response to treatment. Tinted glasses help symptoms of photophobia but do not change the course of the disease, and switching antithyroid drugs has no effect on the eyes.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man has taken amiodarone for 18 months for recurrent ventricular tachycardia. He now has fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. TSH is 19 mU/L and free T4 is low. His cardiologist says amiodarone is essential. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop amiodarone and recheck thyroid tests in 3 months
questions.e: Amiodarone's high iodine content can cause hypothyroidism through the Wolff-Chaikoff effect, especially in people with underlying autoimmune thyroiditis; it is treated with levothyroxine while continuing amiodarone if it is needed. Carbimazole and perchlorate are used for amiodarone-induced thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism.

questions.s: A 33-year-old woman has 4 months of fatigue, weight loss, dizziness on standing and darkening of her palmar creases and gums. BP is 92/60 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing. Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L. Which test best confirms the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hyperpigmentation, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia suggest primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), confirmed by a failure of cortisol to rise after synthetic ACTH in a short Synacthen test. The dexamethasone suppression test is used to screen for cortisol excess, the opposite problem.

questions.s: A 41-year-old man with known Addison disease is brought in after 2 days of vomiting and diarrhoea, unable to keep down his tablets. He is drowsy; BP 78/44 mmHg, glucose 62 mg/dL, sodium 124 mmol/L. What is the most important immediate treatment?
o: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg after a Synacthen test
questions.e: Adrenal crisis is treated immediately with IV (or IM) hydrocortisone 100 mg, IV 0.9 % saline and glucose as needed. Oral treatment cannot be absorbed with vomiting, and delaying steroid for a Synacthen test is unnecessary in a known patient and dangerous.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man from a village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has Addison disease confirmed by a short Synacthen test. He was treated for pulmonary TB 15 years ago. CT shows small, bilaterally calcified adrenal glands. What is the most likely cause of his adrenal failure?
questions.e: Bilateral adrenal calcification with a history of TB points to tuberculous adrenalitis, still an important cause of Addison disease in countries with high TB burden. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the commonest cause worldwide, but it produces small adrenals without calcification.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man who smokes 40 cigarettes a day has 6 weeks of rapidly worsening weakness, ankle swelling and weight loss. BP 168/98 mmHg. Potassium 2.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 34 mmol/L, glucose 240 mg/dL. Cortisol is high and ACTH markedly raised. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Cushing disease from an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Ectopic ACTH secretion from small cell lung cancer
questions.e: Rapid onset of hypokalaemic alkalosis, weakness, hyperglycaemia and very high ACTH in a heavy smoker suggests ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer; there is often little time for classic Cushingoid features to develop. An adrenal adenoma would suppress ACTH, and pituitary Cushing disease usually gives only moderately raised ACTH and a slower course.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has central obesity, purple abdominal striae, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness and new hypertension. She takes no steroid medicines, creams or injections. Which is the most appropriate first-line screening test?
questions.e: Suspected Cushing syndrome is screened with the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (or late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol); failure to suppress cortisol suggests excess. A random cortisol is unhelpful because of diurnal variation, and ACTH and imaging are used only after cortisol excess is confirmed.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman from rural Punjab has a round face, central obesity, thin skin and bruises. For a year she has taken powders from a local hakeem for joint pain. 9 am cortisol is low and ACTH is low. What is the most likely cause of her features?
questions.e: Cushingoid features with suppressed cortisol and ACTH mean the glucocorticoid is coming from outside; unlabelled remedies containing steroids are a well-known cause in Pakistan. She is at risk of adrenal crisis if the remedy is stopped suddenly. An adrenal carcinoma would give high cortisol with low ACTH.

questions.s: A 39-year-old man has hypertension of 168/102 mmHg despite amlodipine and ramipril. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L without diuretics or vomiting. Sodium is 143 mmol/L. Which is the most appropriate initial investigation for the likely cause?
questions.e: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia suggests primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome), screened with the aldosterone:renin ratio. ACE inhibitors raise renin and can give false negatives, so results are interpreted with this in mind; metanephrines are for phaeochromocytoma, which causes paroxysmal symptoms.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman has episodes of pounding headache, palpitations, sweating and pallor. BP between attacks is 162/104 mmHg. Plasma free metanephrines are markedly raised and CT shows a 4 cm right adrenal mass. Surgery is planned. Which drug should be started first?
questions.e: Phaeochromocytoma needs alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 1 to 2 weeks before surgery, with a beta-blocker added only after alpha-blockade if tachycardia persists. Starting a beta-blocker first leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can cause a hypertensive crisis.

questions.s: A 44-year-old man from Faisalabad notices that his rings and shoes no longer fit. He has coarse facial features, a large tongue, sweaty doughy hands and recently diagnosed hypertension. What is the most appropriate initial blood test?
questions.e: Enlarging hands and feet with coarse features suggest acromegaly, and serum IGF-1 is the best screening test because it reflects average growth hormone secretion over the day. A random growth hormone level is unreliable because secretion is pulsatile; failure of growth hormone to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test confirms the diagnosis.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man notices his rings and shoes no longer fit. He has coarse facial features, a protruding jaw, sweating, carpal tunnel syndrome and new hypertension. Which test best confirms the likely diagnosis?
o: Growth hormone after a 75 g oral glucose load
questions.e: Acromegaly is confirmed by failure of growth hormone to suppress after a 75 g oral glucose load, usually with a raised IGF-1. A random GH is unreliable because secretion is pulsatile, and prolactin may be raised but does not confirm GH excess.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man keeps bumping into door frames on both sides. MRI shows a large pituitary macroadenoma extending upwards. Which visual field defect is most likely?
questions.e: A pituitary tumour growing upwards compresses the optic chiasm from below, damaging the crossing nasal fibres and causing bitemporal hemianopia, often starting in the upper quadrants. Homonymous hemianopia arises from lesions behind the chiasm, such as in the optic tract or occipital cortex.

questions.s: Parveen, 30, delivered at home in rural Balochistan 6 months ago and had a severe postpartum haemorrhage needing transfusion. She could not breastfeed, has had no periods since, and feels tired and cold. BP 96/60 mmHg, sodium 129 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Massive postpartum haemorrhage can cause ischaemic necrosis of the enlarged pituitary (Sheehan syndrome), shown by failure of lactation, amenorrhoea and features of secondary hypothyroidism and cortisol deficiency. Asherman syndrome causes amenorrhoea from uterine scarring but does not affect lactation or cause hypotension and hyponatraemia.

questions.s: A 66-year-old smoker with a newly found lung mass is mildly confused. He is clinically euvolaemic. Sodium 122 mmol/L, serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 48 mmol/L. TSH and cortisol are normal. He has no seizures. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.e: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, is SIADH, here likely from small cell lung cancer; first-line treatment of mild symptoms is fluid restriction. Normal saline can worsen hyponatraemia in SIADH, and hypertonic saline is for severe symptoms such as seizures.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman on long-term lithium for bipolar disorder passes 6 litres of dilute urine a day. Glucose and calcium are normal. During a water deprivation test her urine osmolality stays low, and after desmopressin it rises by less than 10 %. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Failure to concentrate urine with water deprivation and no response to desmopressin indicates nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, a recognised effect of lithium on the collecting ducts. In cranial DI the urine concentrates well after desmopressin, and in primary polydipsia it concentrates with water deprivation alone.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman has a corrected calcium of 11.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5-10.2) found on routine tests, with low phosphate. Parathyroid hormone is raised. She had a renal stone last year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: High calcium with an inappropriately raised PTH and low phosphate is primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a single parathyroid adenoma; renal stones are a classic complication. In malignancy and vitamin D toxicity PTH is suppressed, and secondary hyperparathyroidism has a low or normal calcium.

questions.s: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer is drowsy, thirsty and constipated. Corrected calcium is 14.2 mg/dL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, PTH suppressed. She is clinically dehydrated. What is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.e: Severe hypercalcaemia causes dehydration through nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, so the first step is IV saline rehydration, followed by an IV bisphosphonate. Loop diuretics are no longer used routinely and can worsen dehydration, and steroids help mainly in lymphoma or vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia.

questions.s: A 54-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has bone pain and itching. Which pattern of results is most likely?
o: Calcium high, phosphate low, PTH high
Calcium low, phosphate high, PTH high
Calcium high, phosphate high, PTH low
Calcium normal, phosphate low, PTH low
questions.e: In CKD, phosphate retention and reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D lower calcium, which drives secondary hyperparathyroidism with high PTH. High calcium with low phosphate and high PTH is the pattern of primary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.s: Nusrat, a 34-year-old mother of four who keeps purdah and rarely goes outdoors, has aching bones, a waddling gait and difficulty climbing stairs. Calcium is low, phosphate low, alkaline phosphatase raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency
questions.e: Bone pain, proximal myopathy and low calcium and phosphate with raised ALP are typical of osteomalacia, common in Pakistani women with little sun exposure and repeated pregnancies. Osteoporosis causes no symptoms until fracture and has normal biochemistry.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman had a total thyroidectomy for a large goitre yesterday. She now has tingling of the fingers and lips and painful spasms of the hands. Corrected calcium is 6.6 mg/dL. ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany and QT prolongation after thyroidectomy, from damage to the parathyroids, needs slow IV calcium gluconate, followed by oral calcium and active vitamin D. Oral treatment alone is too slow for symptomatic severe hypocalcaemia.

questions.s: A 36-year-old man has recurrent renal stones with raised calcium and PTH. He also has galactorrhoea with a raised prolactin and has had several peptic ulcers with a high fasting gastrin. His father had a 'gland operation in the neck'. Which condition is most likely?
questions.e: Primary hyperparathyroidism with a pituitary tumour (here a prolactinoma) and a pancreatic or duodenal tumour (gastrinoma) is MEN1, inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. MEN2A combines medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism, without pituitary or gastrinoma tumours.

questions.s: A 38-year-old slim man was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 9 months ago and started on metformin, then gliclazide. Despite good adherence, his HbA1c has risen from 7.4 % to 10.2 % and he has lost weight. GAD antibodies are strongly positive and C-peptide is low. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Rapid failure of oral agents in a slim adult with positive GAD antibodies and low C-peptide indicates latent autoimmune diabetes in adults, a slowly progressive form of type 1 diabetes that needs insulin. Further oral agents depend on beta-cell function that is being lost.

questions.s: A 47-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes for 25 years has early fullness, bloating and vomiting of food eaten many hours earlier. Her glucose readings have become erratic, with unexpected lows after meals. Endoscopy shows food residue but no obstruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Autonomic neuropathy in long-standing diabetes delays gastric emptying, causing early satiety, vomiting of old food and mismatched insulin timing with post-meal hypoglycaemia. Endoscopy excluding obstruction makes pyloric stricture and malignancy unlikely; a gastric emptying study confirms the diagnosis.

questions.s: Kiran, 31, received 4 units of red cells for a postpartum haemorrhage 5 weeks ago. She had gestational diabetes and her home fasting glucose readings are now 130 to 150 mg/dL. Her HbA1c is 5.3 %. What is the best explanation for this discrepancy?
o: Home glucose meters read falsely high after delivery
Gestational diabetes has fully resolved since the delivery
HbA1c is falsely high after transfusion
Young and transfused red cells are less glycated
questions.e: HbA1c reflects glycation of haemoglobin over the lifespan of red cells; after blood loss and transfusion, the circulating cells are younger or donor-derived, so HbA1c is falsely low. Glucose readings or an oral glucose tolerance test should be used to assess her glycaemia instead.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man with DKA has a serum potassium of 5.2 mmol/L on arrival. The registrar plans to add potassium chloride to the IV fluids once insulin is running and potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L. Why is this necessary?
o: Saline infusion causes renal potassium retention
Acidosis worsens as the serum potassium falls further
Ketones bind potassium in the blood
questions.e: In DKA total body potassium is depleted through osmotic diuresis and vomiting, but acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells so the serum level looks normal or high. Insulin moves potassium back into cells, so serum potassium falls quickly and replacement is needed to avoid dangerous hypokalaemia.

questions.s: A 71-year-old woman has palpitations and weight loss. She has had a lumpy goitre for many years. TSH is suppressed and free T3 high. TSH receptor antibodies are negative. Technetium scan shows several areas of increased uptake with suppression of the rest of the gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Patchy uptake in several autonomous nodules with suppression of the rest of the gland in an older woman with a long-standing nodular goitre is toxic multinodular goitre. Graves disease shows diffuse uniform uptake with positive TSH receptor antibodies, and subacute thyroiditis shows low uptake.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man has a hard thyroid nodule. His brother had an adrenal tumour removed after attacks of high blood pressure. Histology after thyroidectomy shows nests of cells in an amyloid-containing stroma. Which serum marker is most useful for follow-up?
questions.e: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, shows amyloid stroma and secretes calcitonin (and CEA), which is used to monitor for recurrence; the family history suggests MEN2. Thyroglobulin is the follow-up marker for papillary and follicular cancers, which arise from follicular cells.

questions.s: A 78-year-old woman is found drowsy at home in winter. Temperature 33.8 °C, pulse 46/min, BP 94/58 mmHg. She has periorbital puffiness and slow-relaxing reflexes. Sodium 122 mmol/L, glucose 64 mg/dL. TSH is very high. Adrenal function has not been tested. Which drug should be given together with thyroid hormone replacement?
questions.e: Myxoedema coma is treated with IV thyroid hormone plus IV hydrocortisone, because coexisting adrenal insufficiency is possible and thyroid hormone increases cortisol clearance, which can precipitate adrenal crisis. Supportive warming, glucose and ventilation as needed are also given.

questions.s: A 36-year-old teacher with Addison disease takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. She now has influenza with fever of 38.6 °C but is eating and drinking normally. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop fludrocortisone until she is well
Double the hydrocortisone dose during the fever
Switch to intravenous hydrocortisone given at home by a relative
questions.e: Sick day rules for adrenal insufficiency are to double the oral glucocorticoid dose during fever or significant illness, and to use injectable hydrocortisone and seek help if vomiting. Continuing the usual dose risks adrenal crisis because cortisol needs rise with illness.

questions.s: A 56-year-old man with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma develops a sudden severe headache, vomiting and double vision. He has a third nerve palsy and BP 86/52 mmHg. CT shows haemorrhage within an enlarged pituitary. What is the most urgent treatment?
questions.e: Pituitary apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary tumour; acute ACTH deficiency causes life-threatening adrenal insufficiency, so IV hydrocortisone is given urgently, with neurosurgical review for decompression. Lumbar puncture is not needed once imaging shows the cause and is risky with raised pressure.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman recovering from removal of a pituitary macroadenoma has low free T4 with a low TSH, and low 9 am cortisol. She is clinically stable. What is the most appropriate order of hormone replacement?
o: Levothyroxine first, then hydrocortisone after a week
Levothyroxine only, as cortisol will recover
questions.e: Glucocorticoid replacement must begin before thyroxine, because thyroxine speeds cortisol metabolism and can precipitate adrenal crisis in untreated ACTH deficiency. Mineralocorticoid is usually not needed in pituitary disease because the renin-angiotensin system still drives aldosterone.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy from a poor area of Karachi was exclusively breastfed until 18 months and rarely goes outside. He has bowed legs, swollen wrists and a row of bumps along the costochondral junctions. ALP is raised and phosphate low. Which X-ray finding at the wrist is most expected?
o: Cupping and fraying of the metaphyses
Periosteal new bone with subperiosteal haemorrhage
questions.e: Nutritional rickets from vitamin D deficiency causes widened, cupped and frayed metaphyses at the wrist, matching the clinical wrist widening and rachitic rosary. Subperiosteal haemorrhage suggests scurvy, and dense metaphyseal bands are seen in lead poisoning.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man has a corrected calcium of 10.9 mg/dL and a PTH at the upper limit of normal. He has no symptoms, no stones and normal bone density. His mother and uncle had 'high calcium' that was never treated. Which test best distinguishes the likely diagnosis from primary hyperparathyroidism?
questions.e: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, an autosomal dominant defect of the calcium-sensing receptor, gives mild lifelong hypercalcaemia with very low urinary calcium excretion (clearance ratio below 0.01); it needs no surgery. A sestamibi scan localises an adenoma but cannot separate the two conditions.

questions.s: A 14-year-old girl is short with a round face and short fourth and fifth metacarpals. She has had cramps and tingling. Calcium is low, phosphate high and PTH markedly raised. Magnesium and vitamin D are normal, and kidney function is normal. What is the underlying problem?
questions.e: Low calcium and high phosphate despite a high PTH with normal kidneys mean the tissues are not responding to PTH (pseudohypoparathyroidism); the body habitus is Albright hereditary osteodystrophy. In true hypoparathyroidism PTH would be low.

questions.s: A medical officer at a BHU in a remote valley of Gilgit-Baltistan notices that many women and schoolchildren have diffuse, painless goitres. Most are clinically euthyroid. Which public health measure is most appropriate?
o: Referral of all goitres for thyroidectomy
questions.e: Endemic diffuse goitre in mountainous areas of northern Pakistan is due to iodine deficiency, best prevented by universal salt iodisation. Levothyroxine for everyone and routine surgery treat individuals but do not address the cause, and mass ultrasound adds cost without benefit.

questions.s: A 57-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is admitted 2 days after a hernia repair with vomiting and rapid breathing. Glucose 196 mg/dL, pH 7.14, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L, blood ketones 5.6 mmol/L. His diabetes medicines were continued around surgery. Which drug most likely contributed?
questions.e: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin can cause euglycaemic DKA, with ketoacidosis at only modestly raised glucose, especially around surgery, fasting or acute illness; they are usually withheld before operations. Metformin is associated with lactic acidosis, not ketoacidosis.

questions.s: A 64-year-old hypertensive man, Ghulam Rasool, is brought to a THQ hospital 90 minutes after sudden weakness of his right arm and leg and difficulty speaking. BP is 170/95 mmHg, capillary glucose 132 mg/dL. Which investigation should be done first?
o: Non-contrast CT scan of the head
questions.e: In suspected acute stroke, an urgent non-contrast CT head excludes haemorrhage and decides eligibility for thrombolysis within the time window. MRI is more sensitive for early infarction but is slower and less available, so it must not delay the decision; carotid and cardiac imaging belong to the later search for a cause.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden left-sided weakness. CT head 2 hours after onset shows no haemorrhage. BP is 165/90 mmHg, glucose 140 mg/dL, platelets normal and she takes no anticoagulant. Symptoms are disabling and persisting. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Lower the BP to below 120/80 mmHg first
questions.e: A disabling ischaemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours with no haemorrhage on CT and no contraindication should receive intravenous thrombolysis. Aspirin is given later (24 hours after thrombolysis, or immediately if thrombolysis is not given); aggressive BP lowering is harmful, and thrombolysis only requires BP below 185/110 mmHg.

questions.s: A 70-year-old right-handed man has sudden weakness and sensory loss of the right face and arm, with the leg relatively spared, and he cannot produce fluent speech although he understands commands. Which artery is most likely occluded?
questions.e: Face and arm more affected than leg, with expressive (Broca) aphasia, localises to the dominant (left) middle cerebral artery territory. Anterior cerebral artery occlusion affects the leg more than the arm, and posterior cerebral artery occlusion causes a contralateral homonymous hemianopia.

questions.s: A 66-year-old woman had 20 minutes of weakness of her left hand and slurred speech yesterday, which resolved fully. She has atrial fibrillation and takes no medication. ECG confirms AF. CT head is normal. Which long-term treatment best reduces her risk of stroke?
questions.e: A transient ischaemic attack in a patient with atrial fibrillation is cardioembolic; oral anticoagulation (a DOAC or warfarin) reduces stroke risk far more than antiplatelet therapy. Aspirin is not recommended for stroke prevention in AF, and dual antiplatelet therapy carries bleeding risk without the benefit of anticoagulation.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man presents with vertigo, vomiting and hiccups. On examination he has right-sided Horner syndrome, loss of pain and temperature over the right face and the left side of the body, hoarseness and right limb ataxia. Which vessel is most likely involved?
o: Right anterior spinal artery in the medulla
questions.e: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome causes ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, bulbar weakness and ataxia, with contralateral body sensory loss; it results from vertebral or PICA occlusion on the side of the facial signs. AICA infarction affects the lateral pons and typically causes facial weakness and deafness rather than hoarseness.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman develops a sudden, severe occipital headache while lifting a heavy pot, followed by vomiting and neck stiffness. She says it is the worst headache of her life. GCS is 15 and there is no focal deficit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds, with vomiting and meningism, is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise, usually from a ruptured berry aneurysm. Meningitis develops over hours with fever, and migraine builds gradually and is not described as the worst ever.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man has a sudden severe headache. Non-contrast CT head done 14 hours after onset is normal. He is alert with mild neck stiffness. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat non-contrast CT head after 48 hours
questions.e: CT sensitivity for subarachnoid haemorrhage falls after the first 6 hours, so a normal CT does not exclude it; a lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset looking for xanthochromia is the next step. Waiting 48 hours for repeat CT would risk a fatal rebleed, and EEG has no role.

questions.s: A 76-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension is found drowsy with right hemiparesis. CT head shows a 25 mL haematoma in the left basal ganglia. BP is 200/110 mmHg. He takes no anticoagulant. Which immediate measure is most appropriate?
o: Intravenous mannitol for all such patients
questions.e: In acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage with very high BP, controlled lowering of systolic pressure to about 140 mmHg is recommended to limit haematoma growth. Thrombolysis and antiplatelets are contraindicated in haemorrhage, and mannitol is reserved for raised intracranial pressure with deterioration rather than used routinely.

questions.s: A 19-year-old university student, Hamza, is witnessed to fall, stiffen and then have rhythmic jerking of all limbs for 2 minutes, with tongue biting and urinary incontinence, followed by 30 minutes of confusion. This is his second such episode. What type of seizure is this?
questions.e: Stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all limbs, lateral tongue biting, incontinence and prolonged post-ictal confusion are typical of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. Syncope can cause a few brief jerks but recovery is rapid without prolonged confusion.

questions.s: A 7-year-old girl's teacher reports that she 'switches off' many times a day for a few seconds, staring blankly with eyelid flickering, then carries on as if nothing happened. Hyperventilation in clinic provokes an episode. EEG shows 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. Which drug is the first-line treatment?
questions.e: Childhood absence epilepsy, with brief frequent absences provoked by hyperventilation and 3 Hz spike-and-wave, is treated first line with ethosuximide (sodium valproate is an alternative). Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence seizures.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy has jerks of his arms in the morning, often dropping his teacup shortly after waking. Last month he had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure after a night without sleep. Neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Morning myoclonic jerks in a teenager with tonic-clonic seizures triggered by sleep deprivation are typical of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, a lifelong generalised epilepsy that responds well to valproate in males. Rolandic epilepsy causes nocturnal focal facial seizures in younger children.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has been having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure for 7 minutes in the emergency department. His airway is supported, oxygen is given and glucose is 98 mg/dL. Intravenous access is available. What is the most appropriate first drug?
questions.e: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus; the first-line drug with IV access is a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam (buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam without access). Phenytoin, valproate or levetiracetam are second-line if seizures continue after two benzodiazepine doses.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman with focal epilepsy controlled on sodium valproate tells you she is planning a pregnancy in the next year. Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue valproate, as changing drugs risks breakthrough seizures
Stop all antiepileptic drugs once pregnant
Specialist review to switch to lamotrigine before conception
Continue valproate and add folic acid 400 micrograms
questions.e: Valproate carries a high risk of major malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders, so women of childbearing potential should be switched, under specialist review and before conception, to a safer drug such as lamotrigine or levetiracetam, with high-dose folic acid. Stopping all drugs abruptly risks status epilepticus, which is dangerous to mother and fetus.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man reports episodes beginning with a rising feeling in his stomach and a smell of burning rubber, followed by lip-smacking and fumbling with his clothes for a minute; he does not respond and has no memory of it afterwards. Where does the seizure most likely originate?
questions.e: Epigastric rising sensation, olfactory hallucination and automatisms with impaired awareness are characteristic of focal impaired-awareness seizures from the temporal lobe (often mesial temporal sclerosis). Occipital seizures produce visual phenomena, and frontal motor seizures cause clonic jerking of a limb.

questions.s: A 28-year-old female bank officer in Karachi has recurrent throbbing unilateral headaches lasting about a day, with nausea and dislike of light and noise. She lies in a dark room during attacks. Examination between attacks is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent unilateral pulsating headaches lasting 4-72 hours with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia that worsen with activity fit migraine without aura. Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing and without nausea, while cluster attacks are short and accompanied by autonomic features.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man, a smoker, is woken at about 2 am each night for the past 3 weeks by excruciating pain around his right eye lasting 45 minutes, with a watering red eye and a blocked nostril on that side. He paces the room during attacks. Which treatment is most effective for an acute attack?
questions.e: Cluster headache is aborted acutely by high-flow 100% oxygen or subcutaneous sumatriptan. Paracetamol is too slow to help, and propranolol and amitriptyline are migraine and tension-type prophylactics; verapamil is the cluster preventive.

questions.s: A 72-year-old woman has had a new headache over her right temple for 2 weeks, pain in her jaw when chewing and aching stiff shoulders in the morning. ESR is 92 mm/h. The right temporal artery is tender. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
o: Arrange temporal artery biopsy and treat only if positive
Start ibuprofen and review in a week
questions.e: Suspected giant cell arteritis must be treated immediately with high-dose glucocorticoids to prevent irreversible visual loss; biopsy can still be done within the following 1-2 weeks. Delaying steroids until a biopsy result risks blindness.

questions.s: A 26-year-old obese woman has daily headaches worse on lying down and transient blurring of vision on bending. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. Neurological examination is otherwise normal apart from a sixth nerve palsy. MRI and MR venography are normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 35 cm H2O with normal CSF. What is the most appropriate first-line drug?
questions.e: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is treated with weight loss and acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that reduces CSF production. Corticosteroids are not used long term, and propranolol is a migraine preventive that does not lower intracranial pressure.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has had a progressively worsening headache for 6 weeks, worse in the morning and on coughing, with vomiting. Over the past week his family noticed personality change. Which feature in this history most strongly indicates raised intracranial pressure from a space-occupying lesion?
o: Headache relieved by simple analgesia such as paracetamol
Headache worse on waking and on coughing, with vomiting
questions.e: Headache that is worse on waking and with Valsalva (coughing, straining), with early-morning vomiting, suggests raised intracranial pressure; with progressive course and personality change, urgent imaging is needed. Band-like tightness suggests tension-type headache and photophobia is common in migraine.

questions.s: A 20-year-old male student from a hostel in Lahore has fever, severe headache, vomiting and neck stiffness for 12 hours. He has a non-blanching purpuric rash on his legs. BP is 95/60 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Lumbar puncture, then antibiotics according to the Gram stain
Oral amoxicillin and review in 24 hours
questions.e: Fever, meningism and a purpuric rash indicate meningococcal disease; give parenteral ceftriaxone immediately (after blood cultures if they do not cause delay). Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with shock and purpura, and waiting for CT or LP would delay life-saving treatment.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man has 3 weeks of fever, headache and lethargy, and now has a left sixth nerve palsy and drowsiness. CSF shows protein 210 mg/dL, glucose 28 mg/dL (blood 110 mg/dL), white cells 280/µL with 85% lymphocytes. Gram stain is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A subacute course over weeks with cranial nerve palsy, very high CSF protein, low glucose and a lymphocytic picture is typical of tuberculous meningitis, common in Pakistan. Viral meningitis has a normal glucose and only mildly raised protein, and acute bacterial meningitis is neutrophilic with a rapid onset.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with tuberculous meningitis and started on four-drug antituberculous therapy. Which additional drug reduces mortality in this condition?
questions.e: Adjunctive corticosteroids (dexamethasone or prednisolone) reduce mortality in tuberculous meningitis and are recommended with antituberculous therapy. Pyridoxine prevents isoniazid neuropathy but does not change survival, and mannitol and phenytoin are given only for specific complications.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has 3 days of fever, headache and confusion, and today had a focal seizure. He keeps smelling strange odours. MRI shows bilateral asymmetric high signal in the medial temporal lobes. CSF shows a lymphocytosis with normal glucose and some red cells. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Fever, confusion, seizures and temporal lobe involvement on MRI with lymphocytic CSF indicate herpes simplex encephalitis; intravenous aciclovir should be started immediately as it greatly reduces mortality. Ceftriaxone covers bacterial meningitis but does not treat HSV.

questions.s: An adult with suspected bacterial meningitis is drowsy (GCS 10) and has a new left hemiparesis. Which sequence of management is most appropriate?
o: Lumbar puncture first, then CT, then antibiotics
CT head, then lumbar puncture, then antibiotics
Blood cultures, IV antibiotics and dexamethasone, then CT head
Await CT and lumbar puncture results before giving any antibiotic
questions.e: With reduced consciousness and a focal deficit, CT is needed before lumbar puncture, but antibiotics (with dexamethasone) must not be delayed: blood cultures are taken and treatment started immediately, then CT is done. Doing the LP first risks coning, and waiting for imaging delays treatment and worsens outcome.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy from rural Punjab is admitted in August with 3 days of high fever, then altered sensorium, abnormal movements and seizures. Several children in his village were similarly affected. MRI shows bilateral thalamic lesions. Which mosquito-borne infection is most likely?
o: Cerebral malaria due to Plasmodium vivax
questions.e: Japanese encephalitis, spread by Culex mosquitoes in rice-growing areas in the monsoon season, typically causes encephalitis in children with bilateral thalamic involvement and movement disorders. Rabies is not mosquito-borne and typically follows an animal bite, and cerebral malaria is mainly due to P. falciparum.

questions.s: A 23-year-old man has had fever, headache and photophobia for 2 days. He is alert with mild neck stiffness and no rash. CSF: clear, white cells 150/µL mostly lymphocytes, protein 60 mg/dL, glucose 65 mg/dL (blood 100 mg/dL). Gram stain is negative. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: An acute illness in an alert young adult with a lymphocytic CSF, only mildly raised protein and normal CSF:blood glucose ratio is typical of viral meningitis, most often enteroviral. Tuberculous and cryptococcal meningitis cause low glucose and a subacute course, and pneumococcal meningitis gives a neutrophilic CSF with low glucose.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man had diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. Over 4 days he has developed tingling in his feet and progressive weakness of both legs, now spreading to his arms. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent. Sensation is only mildly reduced. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Ascending symmetrical weakness with areflexia and mild sensory symptoms after a diarrhoeal illness (often Campylobacter) is Guillain-Barré syndrome. Transverse myelitis causes a sensory level and sphincter disturbance, and myasthenia spares reflexes and sensation.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman is admitted with Guillain-Barré syndrome. She is still able to walk with help but her weakness is progressing. Which bedside measurement best guides the need for ventilatory support?
questions.e: Serial forced vital capacity monitors neuromuscular respiratory failure in GBS; a falling FVC (around 20 mL/kg or less) indicates the need for intensive care and ventilation. Oxygen saturation stays normal until late, so it is falsely reassuring, and peak flow measures airway obstruction rather than muscle strength.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome diagnosed 4 days ago can no longer walk unaided. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.e: Intravenous immunoglobulin (or plasma exchange) started within about 2 weeks of onset speeds recovery in GBS patients who cannot walk unaided. Corticosteroids have not shown benefit in GBS, and pyridostigmine is used for myasthenia gravis.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man presents with acute progressive weakness of all four limbs and areflexia. Lumbar puncture on day 10 is reviewed. Which CSF result is most typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
o: Protein 40 mg/dL, low glucose and lymphocytosis
questions.e: Albuminocytological dissociation, a raised CSF protein with a normal cell count, is characteristic of GBS, especially after the first week. A high white cell count should prompt consideration of other diagnoses such as HIV, infection or lymphoma.

questions.s: A 42-year-old man develops double vision, unsteady gait and loss of reflexes over a few days, after a respiratory infection. He has no limb weakness. Which antibody is most associated with this variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
questions.e: The triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia is Miller Fisher syndrome, strongly associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies. Anti-aquaporin-4 is the marker of neuromyelitis optica, and anti-VGCC antibodies are found in Lambert-Eaton syndrome.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman, Sana, has drooping eyelids and double vision that are worse in the evening, and difficulty chewing towards the end of a meal. On sustained upward gaze her ptosis worsens. Reflexes and sensation are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia and bulbar weakness worse later in the day with normal reflexes and sensation are typical of myasthenia gravis. A third nerve palsy is constant and not fatigable, and myotonic dystrophy has myotonia and distal weakness.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has suspected generalised myasthenia gravis. Which test is most specific for the diagnosis?
questions.e: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are present in most patients with generalised myasthenia gravis and are highly specific. Creatine kinase is normal in myasthenia, and routine nerve conduction velocity is normal; repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG is the electrophysiological test.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman is diagnosed with myasthenia gravis. Which investigation should be arranged next because of a recognised associated condition?
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and thymic hyperplasia, so CT of the chest (anterior mediastinum) is done at diagnosis; thymectomy is indicated for thymoma and benefits many patients with generalised disease. The other investigations do not look for a known association.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis develops increasing difficulty swallowing and breathlessness over 2 days after a chest infection. Her forced vital capacity is falling. Which drug used for her infection could have worsened her myasthenia?
questions.e: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin, aminoglycosides and macrolides can impair neuromuscular transmission and precipitate a myasthenic crisis. Amoxicillin is generally safe, and paracetamol and salbutamol do not affect the neuromuscular junction in a clinically important way.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man who smokes heavily has weakness of his thighs and difficulty rising from a chair, a dry mouth and constipation. Reflexes are reduced but improve after a few seconds of maximal contraction. Chest X-ray shows a hilar mass. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Motor neurone disease with bulbar onset
questions.e: Proximal leg weakness, autonomic features and reflexes that are reduced but improve after sustained contraction are typical of Lambert-Eaton syndrome, caused by antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels and associated with small cell lung cancer. Myasthenia typically starts with ocular and bulbar weakness and worsens with exercise.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man has a 'pill-rolling' tremor of his right hand at rest, which improves when he reaches for a cup. His handwriting has become small and he walks with short shuffling steps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Asymmetric rest tremor, bradykinesia (micrographia, shuffling gait) and rigidity are the hallmarks of Parkinson's disease. Essential tremor is postural and action tremor, usually bilateral and improved by alcohol, and cerebellar tremor is an intention tremor.

questions.s: A 72-year-old man with Parkinson's disease has motor symptoms that interfere with his daily life. Which drug gives the greatest improvement in motor symptoms?
questions.e: Levodopa combined with carbidopa or benserazide is the most effective treatment for the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease and is preferred when symptoms affect quality of life. MAO-B inhibitors and amantadine are less potent, and anticholinergics cause confusion in older people.

questions.s: A 52-year-old woman with schizophrenia has been on haloperidol for 3 months. She now has a slow shuffling gait, reduced arm swing and stiffness of both arms. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Start levodopa with carbidopa and continue the haloperidol
Reduce the dose or switch to an atypical antipsychotic
Add a dopamine agonist such as ropinirole
Arrange a DaT scan before changing any medication
questions.e: Symmetrical parkinsonism developing on a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic is drug-induced; the management is to reduce the dose or switch to an atypical antipsychotic, with an anticholinergic if needed. Levodopa and dopamine agonists can worsen psychosis and are not appropriate.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man with presumed Parkinson's disease has falls early in the illness and difficulty looking downwards. He has axial rigidity and little tremor, and levodopa has given no benefit. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Early falls, vertical (especially downward) gaze palsy, axial rigidity and poor levodopa response suggest progressive supranuclear palsy. Multiple system atrophy features prominent autonomic failure or cerebellar signs, and Lewy body dementia presents with fluctuating cognition and visual hallucinations.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man with Parkinson's disease on levodopa has started having vivid visual hallucinations of people in his room. His family wants to know which drug class is most likely to make this worse if added. Which is it?
questions.e: Dopamine agonists such as pramipexole and ropinirole commonly cause hallucinations, confusion and impulse-control disorders, especially in older patients. Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors are already combined with levodopa to reduce its peripheral side effects.

questions.s: A 27-year-old woman has had pain on moving her right eye and blurred vision for 4 days. Visual acuity on the right is 6/36 with reduced colour vision and a right relative afferent pupillary defect. The fundus looks normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Painful eye movements with subacute visual loss, impaired colour vision and a relative afferent pupillary defect in a young woman indicate optic neuritis, a common first presentation of multiple sclerosis. Retinal artery occlusion is sudden and painless with a pale retina, and papilloedema rarely affects acuity early.

questions.s: A 31-year-old woman had optic neuritis 2 years ago and now has numbness of both legs and urinary urgency. Which investigation best supports a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
o: MRI of brain and spinal cord
Nerve conduction studies of the legs
questions.e: MRI of the brain and spinal cord shows demyelinating lesions disseminated in space and time, which is the key investigation for MS; CSF oligoclonal bands support it. CT is insensitive for demyelinating plaques, and nerve conduction studies examine peripheral nerves.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops weakness of her left leg and unsteadiness over 3 days, severe enough to limit walking. Urinary infection has been excluded. What is the most appropriate treatment for this relapse?
o: Plasma exchange as the first-choice treatment
questions.e: A disabling MS relapse is treated with a short course of high-dose methylprednisolone (oral or IV), which speeds recovery but does not change long-term outcome. Long-term steroids are not used for MS, and plasma exchange is reserved for severe relapses that do not respond to steroids.

questions.s: A 33-year-old woman with MS describes an electric-shock sensation running down her spine and into her legs when she bends her neck forward. What is this sign called?
questions.e: Lhermitte sign is an electric-shock sensation down the spine on neck flexion, caused by demyelination in the cervical cord. Uhthoff phenomenon is worsening of symptoms with heat, such as a hot bath, and Kernig sign indicates meningeal irritation.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man is brought in after a road traffic accident. He opens his eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and withdraws his arm from a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.e: Eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds score 2 (verbal), and withdrawal from pain scores 4 (motor), giving a GCS of 8. A GCS of 8 or less generally means the airway is at risk and needs protection.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man is found unconscious at home. He has pinpoint pupils, respiratory rate 6/min and no focal signs. Glucose is 110 mg/dL. Which drug is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Coma with pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression is typical of opioid toxicity, reversed by naloxone. Organophosphate poisoning also causes small pupils but with prominent secretions, sweating and fasciculations, which are absent here; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man is drowsy after a fall 6 hours ago. On examination his right pupil is dilated and unreactive, and he has a left hemiparesis. Which process best explains these signs?
o: Right uncal herniation compressing the third nerve
Tonsillar herniation compressing the medulla oblongata
questions.e: A unilateral fixed dilated pupil with declining consciousness indicates uncal herniation compressing the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve, here from a right-sided mass lesion such as an extradural or subdural haematoma, causing a contralateral hemiparesis. Tonsillar herniation causes respiratory arrest and neck stiffness without a third nerve palsy first.

questions.s: A 41-year-old man has had migraine for years. He now has headache on most days of the month and takes paracetamol and codeine on 20 days each month. The headache is worst on waking. Examination is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Headache on 15 or more days a month in someone taking analgesics (especially opioids) on 10 or more days a month suggests medication-overuse headache; the treatment is to stop the overused drugs, with migraine prophylaxis if needed. Adding more analgesia perpetuates the problem, and with a normal examination imaging is not urgent.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is to start an antiepileptic drug. She has no plans for pregnancy now but is sexually active. Which drug is the most appropriate first choice for her?
questions.e: For women of childbearing potential with generalised epilepsy, lamotrigine or levetiracetam is preferred because valproate is highly teratogenic. Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonic seizures and are not suitable for juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

questions.s: A 59-year-old diabetic woman wakes with a weak right leg; her arm is much less affected. She is also unusually apathetic and has urinary incontinence. Which artery is most likely affected?
questions.e: Contralateral leg weakness greater than arm, with abulia and urinary incontinence from frontal lobe involvement, indicates anterior cerebral artery territory infarction. Middle cerebral artery infarction affects the face and arm more than the leg.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man is seen 3 days after a minor ischaemic stroke with full recovery. He is in sinus rhythm. Carotid Doppler shows 80% stenosis of the symptomatic internal carotid artery. What is the most appropriate further management?
o: Aspirin alone and repeat Doppler in a year
Carotid endarterectomy as soon as possible
Carotid surgery only if a second event occurs
questions.e: Symptomatic carotid stenosis of 50-99% (by NASCET criteria) should be referred for carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks, alongside antiplatelet and statin therapy. Waiting for a second event loses the benefit, as the risk of recurrent stroke is highest early.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man has a generalised seizure for the first time after staying awake all night before exams. Examination and blood tests are normal. He drives a motorcycle to university. What is the most appropriate advice about driving?
o: He may drive as long as he takes medication
He should stop driving and notify the licensing authority
He may drive in daylight only
He need not change anything after a single seizure
questions.e: After a first unprovoked or provoked seizure, the patient must stop driving for a period set by the licensing authority and should be advised to inform it; this protects him and others. Taking medication does not by itself allow immediate driving.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman on carbamazepine for focal epilepsy asks for contraception. Which method is least affected by her antiepileptic drug?
questions.e: Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces the effectiveness of combined and progestogen-only pills and implants; the copper IUD (or levonorgestrel IUS, or depot injection) is not affected. The implant is often chosen for reliability but loses efficacy with enzyme inducers.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has had bilateral, band-like, pressing headaches on most days for 3 months, worse at the end of a working day. There is no nausea, photophobia or neurological symptom, and examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Bilateral pressing or tightening headache of mild to moderate intensity without nausea or photophobia is tension-type headache. Migraine is typically throbbing with nausea and sensitivity to light, and trigeminal neuralgia causes brief electric-shock facial pains.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman has brief, stabbing, electric-shock pains in her right cheek and jaw lasting seconds, triggered by brushing her teeth or a cold breeze. Neurological examination is normal. What is the first-line drug treatment?
questions.e: Trigeminal neuralgia causes paroxysmal shock-like pain in the maxillary or mandibular divisions provoked by light touch; carbamazepine is the first-line treatment. Amitriptyline helps some neuropathic pain but is not first choice here, and triptans treat migraine.

questions.s: A 6-year-old child is diagnosed with meningococcal meningitis. Which group should be offered chemoprophylaxis?
o: All children in the same town
Only staff who examined the child
Nobody, as contacts are vaccinated by EPI
questions.e: Close (household and kissing) contacts of a case of meningococcal disease should receive chemoprophylaxis, such as single-dose ciprofloxacin or rifampicin, regardless of vaccination status. Healthcare workers need it only if exposed to respiratory secretions, for example during intubation without a mask.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man with advanced HIV has 2 weeks of headache and fever. He is alert with no neck stiffness. CSF opening pressure is high and India ink staining shows encapsulated yeasts. What is the most appropriate induction treatment?
questions.e: Cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV is treated with induction amphotericin B plus flucytosine (or high-dose fluconazole when flucytosine is unavailable), followed by fluconazole consolidation and maintenance. Fluconazole monotherapy is inferior for induction; raised pressure is managed with repeated lumbar punctures.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has had progressive weakness of both legs for 5 days after a cough and cold, and now cannot stand. He has lost his knee and ankle reflexes. There is no fever and sensation is near normal. Which condition is most likely?
o: Acute flaccid paralysis due to poliomyelitis
questions.e: Symmetrical ascending weakness with areflexia after a viral illness and without fever is typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Every case of acute flaccid paralysis in a child under 15 in Pakistan must still be notified and stool tested for polio, but polio typically causes asymmetric paralysis during a febrile illness.

questions.s: A 47-year-old man is recovering from Guillain-Barré syndrome in the ward. His pulse varies between 45 and 130/min and his BP swings widely. Which complication explains this?
questions.e: Autonomic involvement in GBS causes labile blood pressure and heart rate and arrhythmias, and is a major cause of death, so patients need cardiac monitoring. Pulmonary embolism is a risk from immobility but presents with sudden breathlessness and tachycardia rather than swings of bradycardia and tachycardia.

questions.s: A 36-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis wants symptomatic treatment for her fatigable ptosis and diplopia. Which drug is first-line for symptom control?
questions.e: Oral pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is first-line symptomatic treatment for myasthenia gravis; immunosuppression is added if needed. Edrophonium is very short acting and was used only as a diagnostic test.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis on high-dose pyridostigmine has increasing weakness, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, excessive salivation and small pupils. What is the most likely cause of her worsening weakness?
o: Cholinergic crisis due to excess anticholinesterase
questions.e: Weakness with muscarinic features (cramps, diarrhoea, salivation, miosis) in a patient on high-dose pyridostigmine suggests a cholinergic crisis from excess anticholinesterase. Myasthenic crisis from undertreatment does not cause these cholinergic features.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man with Parkinson's disease on levodopa for 6 years notices that his medication wears off before the next dose is due, and he has writhing movements at peak dose. What are these writhing movements called?
questions.e: Peak-dose choreiform or writhing movements after years of levodopa are levodopa-induced dyskinesias, often accompanied by end-of-dose wearing off. Tardive dyskinesia follows long-term dopamine-blocking drugs, and akathisia is inner restlessness.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman with known multiple sclerosis develops horizontal double vision. On looking to the right, her left eye fails to adduct while the right eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence is normal. Where is the lesion?
questions.e: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, with failure of adduction of one eye and nystagmus of the abducting eye on lateral gaze, localises to the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the side of the eye that fails to adduct (left here). Preserved convergence distinguishes it from a third nerve palsy; bilateral INO in a young adult strongly suggests MS.

questions.s: A 67-year-old man with chronic liver disease due to hepatitis C is brought in confused and drowsy. He has a flapping tremor, a fetor and constipation for 4 days. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Lactulose to produce 2-3 soft stools daily
questions.e: Confusion with asterixis and fetor hepaticus in cirrhosis is hepatic encephalopathy, here precipitated by constipation; lactulose (with rifaximin if needed) is first-line, along with searching for other triggers such as infection or bleeding. Sedatives such as haloperidol worsen encephalopathy.

questions.s: Rubina, a 32-year-old mother of five from Multan, has fatigue and breathlessness on climbing stairs. Her periods are heavy. Hb is 8.6 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, MCH 21 pg, platelets 460 x 10⁹/L. Which single test best confirms the most likely cause of her anaemia?
questions.e: Microcytic hypochromic anaemia with reactive thrombocytosis in a multiparous woman with menorrhagia suggests iron deficiency, best confirmed by a low serum ferritin. Haemoglobin electrophoresis is used for suspected thalassaemia trait, but that is unlikely with this history and a raised platelet count.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy from a farming village in Sindh walks barefoot in the fields. He is pale and tired, with poor school performance. Hb 7.9 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, eosinophils 1.2 x 10⁹/L. Stool shows oval thin-shelled ova. What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
o: Malabsorption of iron from chronic giardiasis
questions.e: Hookworms penetrate bare skin, attach to the small bowel mucosa and cause chronic blood loss, producing iron deficiency anaemia with eosinophilia; treatment is albendazole plus iron. Malaria causes normocytic haemolytic anaemia, and folate deficiency causes macrocytosis.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man has fatigue. Hb is 9.8 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL. He has no visible bleeding and his diet is good. Coeliac serology is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral iron and recheck the blood count in 3 months
questions.e: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older man is assumed to be from gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, so he needs both upper and lower GI endoscopy to look for cancer. Iron replacement alone may mask a bleeding tumour, and a negative occult blood test does not exclude one.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman with active rheumatoid arthritis for 10 years has Hb 9.9 g/dL, MCV 79 fL, serum iron low, total iron-binding capacity low, ferritin 420 ng/mL and CRP 46 mg/L. What is the most likely cause of her anaemia?
questions.e: In anaemia of chronic disease, hepcidin raised by inflammation traps iron in macrophages, giving low serum iron with low TIBC and a normal or high ferritin. In iron deficiency TIBC is high and ferritin low; ferritin is an acute-phase protein, so it is raised here by inflammation.

questions.s: A 3-year-old girl in Lahore has had poor appetite, abdominal pain and irritability for months. Her mother applies homemade surma to her eyes daily. Hb is 8.8 g/dL, MCV 66 fL, ferritin normal. The blood film shows coarse basophilic stippling of red cells. Which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.e: Microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling, abdominal pain and behaviour change in a child exposed to traditional surma (which often contains lead sulphide) suggests lead poisoning, confirmed by a blood lead level. A normal ferritin makes iron deficiency unlikely, and thalassaemia trait would not explain the systemic symptoms.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has fatigue, a sore smooth tongue and tingling in her feet. Hb is 8.4 g/dL, MCV 118 fL, B12 low. The film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. She eats meat regularly. Which test best confirms the cause of her B12 deficiency?
questions.e: Pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune gastritis often linked with other autoimmune disease such as hypothyroidism, is the commonest cause of B12 deficiency with an adequate diet; intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific. The Schilling test is no longer used in practice.

questions.s: A 64-year-old man has macrocytic anaemia with numbness of both feet and an unsteady gait. Vibration and joint position sense are lost in the legs, and plantar responses are extensor. B12 is low and folate is low-normal. Which treatment should be started first?
o: Red cell transfusion of two units
questions.e: Posterior column loss with upper motor neuron signs is subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency, treated with IM hydroxocobalamin straight away. Giving folic acid alone can correct the blood picture while worsening the neurological damage, so B12 must be started first.

questions.s: A 63-year-old man has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years and takes metformin 1 g twice daily and gliclazide. He has worsening burning feet and fatigue. Hb 10.9 g/dL, MCV 106 fL. Which deficiency is his diabetes medicine most likely to have caused?
questions.e: Long-term metformin reduces ileal B12 absorption, causing macrocytosis and neuropathy that can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy; B12 should be checked in long-term users with these symptoms. Folate deficiency also causes macrocytosis but is not linked with metformin and does not cause neuropathy.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man with epilepsy has taken phenytoin for 6 years. He now has fatigue. Hb 9.6 g/dL, MCV 112 fL, hypersegmented neutrophils. B12 is normal. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.e: Phenytoin interferes with folate absorption and metabolism, causing megaloblastic anaemia with a normal B12. Iron deficiency causes microcytosis, and vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding gums rather than macrocytic anaemia.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man from Bannu was given primaquine after treatment for vivax malaria. Two days later he has dark urine, jaundice and Hb 7.8 g/dL (from 12.6). The film shows bite cells, and Heinz bodies are seen on supravital staining. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Acute intravascular haemolysis with bite cells and Heinz bodies after an oxidant drug such as primaquine is typical of G6PD deficiency, which is why G6PD testing is advised before primaquine. Blackwater fever occurs with severe falciparum malaria, not after treated vivax malaria.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy has had intermittent jaundice and a palpable spleen since childhood. His father had his spleen removed. Hb 10.6 g/dL, reticulocytes 9 %, MCHC raised. The film shows many small dense round red cells without central pallor. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which test best confirms the diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic haemolysis with spherocytes, raised MCHC, a negative DAT and autosomal dominant family history indicate hereditary spherocytosis, confirmed by reduced EMA binding on flow cytometry. The negative DAT excludes autoimmune haemolysis, which also shows spherocytes.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has jaundice and fatigue. Hb 7.4 g/dL, reticulocytes 12 %, bilirubin raised (mainly unconjugated), LDH high. The film shows spherocytes. Which test is most likely to be positive?
questions.e: Spherocytic haemolysis in a patient with SLE suggests warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, in which IgG coats the red cells and the direct antiglobulin test is positive. Osmotic fragility is increased with any spherocytes and cannot separate immune from hereditary causes.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman has fever, confusion and petechiae. Hb 8.1 g/dL, platelets 14 x 10⁹/L, many schistocytes on the film, LDH very high, creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. PT and APTT are normal. What is the most appropriate urgent treatment?
o: Fresh frozen plasma alone at 15 mL/kg once
questions.e: Microangiopathic haemolysis with severe thrombocytopenia, neurological features and fever with normal clotting suggests thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, caused by ADAMTS13 deficiency; urgent plasma exchange (with steroids) is life-saving. Platelet transfusion may worsen thrombosis and is avoided unless bleeding is life-threatening.

questions.s: A 22-year-old student has gum bleeding, recurrent infections and fatigue for a month. Hb 6.8 g/dL, white cells 1.4 x 10⁹/L (neutrophils 0.4), platelets 12 x 10⁹/L, reticulocytes 0.2 %. There is no splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, and no blasts on the film. Bone marrow trephine shows a hypocellular marrow replaced by fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pancytopenia with low reticulocytes, no organomegaly and a hypocellular fatty marrow is aplastic anaemia. Acute leukaemia gives a hypercellular marrow full of blasts, and myelofibrosis typically causes massive splenomegaly with a leucoerythroblastic film.

questions.s: A 7-year-old girl with known hereditary spherocytosis has been unusually pale and tired for 5 days after a febrile illness with a 'slapped cheek' rash in her brother. Hb is 4.2 g/dL (her usual is 10), and reticulocytes are 0.1 %. The spleen is not larger than usual. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Acute folate deficiency from increased demand
questions.e: Parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and briefly halts production; in chronic haemolysis this causes a sudden severe fall in Hb with very low reticulocytes. A haemolytic crisis would show a high reticulocyte count and more jaundice, and sequestration causes rapid splenic enlargement.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy with sickle cell anaemia presents with severe pain in his back and legs after a cold, wet day. Temperature 37.4 °C, oxygen saturation 97 % on air. Chest is clear. What is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Prompt analgesia, including opioids, and fluids
Start hydroxycarbamide and discharge him home today
questions.e: A vaso-occlusive crisis is treated with rapid, adequate analgesia (often opioids) within 30 minutes, hydration and oxygen only if hypoxic, while looking for triggers. Exchange transfusion is reserved for severe complications such as acute chest syndrome or stroke.

questions.s: An 8-month-old boy from Peshawar is brought with increasing pallor, poor feeding and abdominal swelling. His parents are first cousins. Hb is 5.2 g/dL, MCV 58 fL, and he has hepatosplenomegaly. The film shows target cells and nucleated red cells. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows mostly HbF with no HbA. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe microcytic anaemia with hepatosplenomegaly appearing after 6 months, as fetal haemoglobin production falls, and absent HbA on electrophoresis indicate beta thalassaemia major, common in Pakistan especially with consanguinity. Iron deficiency would not cause hepatosplenomegaly or absent HbA.

questions.s: A 23-year-old woman is screened before marriage. She is well. Hb 11.2 g/dL, MCV 62 fL, MCH 20 pg, red cell count 5.9 x 10¹²/L. Ferritin is normal. Which result would confirm the most likely diagnosis?
o: Raised serum iron with low iron-binding capacity
questions.e: Marked microcytosis with mild anaemia, a high red cell count and normal ferritin suggest beta thalassaemia trait, confirmed by a raised HbA2 (above 3.5 %). Iron deficiency causes a low red cell count and low ferritin, and iron studies alone do not confirm the trait.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy with beta thalassaemia major has received monthly transfusions since infancy. Serum ferritin is 3,100 ng/mL. He has no chelation therapy. Creatinine is normal. Which treatment is most appropriate for his iron status?
questions.e: Transfusional iron overload damages the heart, liver and endocrine glands and needs chelation, for example oral deferasirox or subcutaneous desferrioxamine. Venesection is impossible in a transfusion-dependent anaemic child, and dietary restriction cannot remove the iron load from transfusion.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl with beta thalassaemia major attends a thalassaemia centre in Rawalpindi for regular transfusions. The doctor is reviewing her plan to allow normal growth and suppress marrow expansion. What pre-transfusion haemoglobin should be maintained?
questions.e: In transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, a pre-transfusion Hb of about 9 to 10.5 g/dL allows normal growth, suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis and bone deformity, and limits iron loading. A lower threshold allows marrow expansion and skeletal changes, while a higher target increases iron overload.

questions.s: Ali and his fiancée Hira are cousins. Both are found to have beta thalassaemia trait on premarital screening. They ask about the chance that each of their children will have thalassaemia major. What is the risk in each pregnancy?
