questions.e: Beta thalassaemia is autosomal recessive; when both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a 25 % chance of thalassaemia major, 50 % chance of trait and 25 % chance of being unaffected. Prenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling can be offered.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy with thalassaemia intermedia has massive splenomegaly and rising transfusion needs. An elective splenectomy is planned. Which measure is most important beforehand?
o: Stopping iron chelation for a month before surgery
questions.e: After splenectomy, patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming infection by encapsulated bacteria, so vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae type b is given at least 2 weeks before elective surgery, with antibiotic prophylaxis afterwards. Thrombocytosis after splenectomy is common but routine warfarin is not used.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl has had bruises on her legs and a few petechiae for 2 days. She had a cold 2 weeks ago. She is playful, with no mucosal bleeding and no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Platelets 15 x 10⁹/L; Hb and white cells are normal and the film is otherwise normal. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Acute childhood ITP after a viral infection usually resolves within weeks; children with only skin bleeding are managed with observation and advice regardless of the platelet count. Treatment such as IVIG or steroids is for significant bleeding, and marrow examination is needed only if the film or examination suggests another diagnosis.

questions.s: A 36-year-old woman has gum bleeding and heavy periods for 3 weeks. Platelets are 11 x 10⁹/L, with normal Hb, white cells and clotting. The film shows large platelets only. HIV, hepatitis C and H. pylori tests are negative. She is not pregnant. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Adult ITP with mucosal bleeding and a very low platelet count is treated first with corticosteroids such as prednisolone (or dexamethasone), with IVIG if a rapid rise is needed. Platelet transfusion is used only for life-threatening bleeding because transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed, and splenectomy and rituximab are second-line.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy has a hot, swollen, painful knee after a minor fall. He had prolonged bleeding after circumcision. His maternal uncle had similar problems. Platelets and PT are normal; APTT is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Haemarthrosis in a boy with an X-linked family history and an isolated prolonged APTT suggests haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency), the commonest haemophilia. Von Willebrand disease mainly causes mucosal bleeding and affects both sexes, and vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT.

questions.s: Imran, a 45-year-old shopkeeper from Multan, has headaches and itching after hot baths. He has a ruddy face and a palpable spleen. Hb is 19.4 g/dL with a haematocrit of 58 %, and a JAK2 V617F mutation is detected. He has never had a thrombosis. Alongside low-dose aspirin, what is the most appropriate first treatment?
questions.e: Polycythaemia vera is confirmed by the raised haematocrit and JAK2 mutation, and in a low-risk patient (under 60, no previous thrombosis) regular venesection to a haematocrit below 45 % with low-dose aspirin reduces thrombotic risk. Hydroxycarbamide is added for high-risk patients or those who cannot tolerate venesection. Imatinib targets BCR-ABL1 in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

questions.s: Shabana, 30, has a placental abruption with an intrauterine death at 36 weeks. She is now oozing from cannula sites. Platelets 42 x 10⁹/L, PT and APTT prolonged, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, D-dimer very high. The film shows fragmented red cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen and high D-dimer after placental abruption indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation, caused by release of tissue factor into the circulation. TTP and HELLP cause thrombocytopenia with haemolysis but do not consume fibrinogen to this degree or prolong clotting times so markedly.

questions.s: A 5-day-old boy born at home in rural Tharparkar, exclusively breastfed, is brought with bleeding from the umbilical stump and blood in his stools. He received no injections after birth. He is otherwise well. Platelets normal; PT markedly prolonged. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Bleeding in the first week in a breastfed baby who missed vitamin K prophylaxis, with a prolonged PT and normal platelets, is vitamin K deficiency bleeding; it responds to vitamin K, with fresh frozen plasma if bleeding is severe. Factor VIII is for haemophilia A, which prolongs the APTT rather than the PT.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man in Lahore is on day 5 of dengue fever. He is drinking well, has no bleeding and no warning signs. Pulse 82/min, BP 118/76 mmHg, haematocrit stable. Platelets have fallen to 18 x 10⁹/L. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: In dengue, prophylactic platelet transfusion in a stable patient without bleeding does not prevent bleeding and can cause fluid overload, so management is careful monitoring of vital signs, haematocrit and fluid balance. Platelets recover on their own during recovery; steroids and IVIG have no proven benefit.

questions.s: A 40-year-old farmer from interior Sindh was bitten on the foot by a small snake 6 hours ago. The foot is swollen and his gums are bleeding. Blood placed in a clean dry glass tube has not clotted after 20 minutes. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Tight tourniquet applied above the bite site
questions.e: Local swelling, gum bleeding and a positive 20-minute whole blood clotting test indicate venom-induced consumption coagulopathy (for example from a saw-scaled viper), which needs IV polyvalent anti-snake venom. Clotting factors alone are consumed by circulating venom, and tight tourniquets cause ischaemia without benefit.

questions.s: A 46-year-old woman has a painful swollen left calf 10 days after a hip fracture repair. The left calf is 4 cm larger than the right, with pitting oedema. Her Wells score indicates that DVT is likely. What is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: When DVT is clinically likely, the investigation of choice is a proximal leg vein ultrasound; D-dimer is useful only to rule out DVT when the probability is low, and it will be raised after recent surgery anyway. Venography is invasive and rarely used now.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man has a confirmed pulmonary embolism. He is haemodynamically stable with BP 132/80 mmHg, normal right ventricle on echo and normal troponin. Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. He is not pregnant and has no cancer. Which is the most appropriate anticoagulant?
questions.e: Haemodynamically stable PE without contraindications is treated with an oral anticoagulant, usually a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban or rivaroxaban. Thrombolysis is reserved for PE with shock, and aspirin is not adequate treatment for venous thromboembolism.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman on warfarin for atrial fibrillation took a course of an antibiotic for a chest infection. Her INR is now 8.4. She has no bleeding and feels well. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Withhold warfarin, give oral vitamin K
Continue warfarin at a lower dose with no other change
questions.e: With an INR above 8 and no bleeding, warfarin is withheld and a small dose of oral vitamin K is given, then warfarin is restarted when the INR is below 5. Prothrombin complex concentrate is for major bleeding, and simply lowering the dose leaves her at high bleeding risk for days.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve presents with sudden headache and left-sided weakness. CT shows an intracerebral haemorrhage. INR is 3.6. What is the most appropriate immediate management, in addition to stopping warfarin?
o: Fresh frozen plasma alone at 15 mL/kg, repeated as needed
Prothrombin complex concentrate with IV vitamin K
questions.e: Life-threatening bleeding on warfarin needs immediate reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate, which replaces factors II, VII, IX and X within minutes, plus IV vitamin K for sustained effect. FFP is slower, needs large volumes and gives incomplete reversal; protamine reverses heparin, not warfarin.

questions.s: A 63-year-old woman was started on unfractionated heparin after a knee replacement. On day 8 her platelets have fallen from 260 to 90 x 10⁹/L and she develops a new DVT in the other leg. She is not bleeding. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Switch to low molecular weight heparin
Start warfarin and stop the heparin on the same day
questions.e: A fall in platelets of more than 50 % 5 to 10 days after starting heparin with new thrombosis suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, in which all heparin must be stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant started. LMWH cross-reacts with the antibodies, and starting warfarin alone in acute HIT can cause venous limb gangrene.

questions.s: A 31-year-old woman has had three miscarriages before 10 weeks and now presents with a DVT. Her APTT is prolonged and does not correct with mixing with normal plasma. Lupus anticoagulant is positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent early miscarriage with venous thrombosis and persistent lupus anticoagulant meets criteria for antiphospholipid syndrome; the antibody prolongs the APTT in the laboratory but causes thrombosis in the body. Factor V Leiden and protein C deficiency cause thrombosis but do not prolong the APTT.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl has had fever, pallor, bone pain and easy bruising for 3 weeks. She has generalised lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Hb 6.9 g/dL, white cells 48 x 10⁹/L, platelets 22 x 10⁹/L. Marrow shows blasts that are TdT and CD10 positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: ALL is the commonest childhood cancer and presents with marrow failure, bone pain, lymphadenopathy and organomegaly; TdT and CD10 positivity identify precursor B lymphoblasts. AML is less common in children and its blasts are myeloperoxidase positive, often with Auer rods.

questions.s: A 57-year-old man has fatigue, fever and gum bleeding. Hb 7.6 g/dL, white cells 34 x 10⁹/L, platelets 26 x 10⁹/L. The film shows large blasts with fine nuclear chromatin and red rod-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions. The blasts are myeloperoxidase positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Myeloperoxidase-positive blasts with Auer rods are diagnostic of acute myeloid leukaemia, the commonest acute leukaemia in adults. Lymphoblasts in ALL are myeloperoxidase negative and lack Auer rods, and chronic leukaemias show mature cells rather than blasts.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has gum bleeding and large bruises. Platelets 18 x 10⁹/L, fibrinogen 0.9 g/L, PT prolonged. The marrow is full of abnormal promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods. Cytogenetics are pending. Which treatment should be started immediately?
questions.e: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia, typically with t(15;17), causes severe DIC and early haemorrhagic deaths, so all-trans retinoic acid is started as soon as APL is suspected, before genetic confirmation, along with blood product support. Imatinib targets BCR-ABL in CML and Ph-positive ALL.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has left upper abdominal fullness and night sweats. His spleen is palpable 12 cm below the costal margin. White cells 186 x 10⁹/L with neutrophils, myelocytes and basophilia; few blasts. PCR detects the BCR-ABL fusion gene. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Allogeneic stem cell transplant at once
questions.e: Chronic myeloid leukaemia in chronic phase, with a massive spleen, neutrophilia with left shift, basophilia and BCR-ABL, is treated with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as imatinib, which gives long-term control in most patients. Transplant is reserved for resistance or advanced phases.

questions.s: A 72-year-old man has a routine blood count before cataract surgery. He feels well. White cells 38 x 10⁹/L with lymphocytes 33 x 10⁹/L; Hb and platelets are normal. The film shows small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells. There is no lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly or B symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Early-stage chronic lymphocytic leukaemia without symptoms, cytopenias or bulky disease is managed by watch and wait, because early treatment does not improve survival. Treatment is started for progressive disease, B symptoms, marrow failure or troublesome lymphadenopathy.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy with a large abdominal Burkitt lymphoma and high white count starts chemotherapy. Twelve hours later his urine output falls and he has muscle cramps. Which pattern of results is most likely?
o: High potassium, high phosphate, low calcium, high uric acid
Low potassium, low phosphate, high calcium, high uric acid
High potassium, low phosphate, high calcium, low uric acid
Low potassium, high phosphate, low calcium, low uric acid
questions.e: Tumour lysis syndrome releases intracellular potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids (metabolised to uric acid); phosphate binds calcium, causing hypocalcaemia and cramps. It is prevented with hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase, especially in fast-growing tumours such as Burkitt lymphoma.

questions.s: A 48-year-old woman had chemotherapy for breast cancer 9 days ago. She now has a temperature of 38.6 °C and rigors. Pulse 108/min, BP 104/68 mmHg. Neutrophils 0.2 x 10⁹/L. There is no obvious source of infection. What is the most appropriate immediate step after taking blood cultures?
o: Wait for culture results before antibiotics
Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor alone, without antibiotics
questions.e: Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency; after cultures, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics with antipseudomonal cover, such as piperacillin-tazobactam, must be given within an hour of arrival. Delaying antibiotics for culture results greatly increases mortality, and G-CSF is not a substitute for antibiotics.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man has a painless rubbery lump in the left side of his neck for 2 months, with night sweats and 6 kg weight loss. Chest X-ray shows mediastinal widening. Node biopsy shows large binucleate cells with prominent 'owl's eye' nucleoli, CD15 and CD30 positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Reed-Sternberg cells (binucleate, owl's eye, CD15 and CD30 positive) in a young adult with cervical and mediastinal nodes and B symptoms indicate Hodgkin lymphoma. TB lymphadenitis is common in Pakistan and must be considered, but biopsy would show caseating granulomas, not Reed-Sternberg cells.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man has persistent low back pain and fatigue. Hb 9.2 g/dL, ESR 110 mm/h, corrected calcium 11.8 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, total protein raised with low albumin. X-ray of the spine shows lytic lesions. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the likely diagnosis?
o: Whole-body technetium bone scintigraphy with SPECT
Serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains
questions.e: Bone pain, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and anaemia with a high globulin gap suggest multiple myeloma; serum protein electrophoresis with free light chains (and urine for Bence Jones protein) detects the paraprotein, with marrow biopsy to confirm. Isotope bone scans are often normal in myeloma because the lesions are purely lytic.

questions.s: A 59-year-old man has headaches, a ruddy face and itching after hot baths. He does not smoke and has normal oxygen saturation. Hb 19.6 g/dL, haematocrit 58 %, platelets 520 x 10⁹/L, white cells 13 x 10⁹/L. The spleen is just palpable. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Raised haematocrit with aquagenic pruritus, splenomegaly and raised platelets and white cells, without hypoxia, suggests polycythaemia vera; over 95 % carry a JAK2 mutation. Erythropoietin is typically low in PV and helps, but on its own it does not confirm the diagnosis.

questions.s: Ten minutes into a blood transfusion after surgery, a 42-year-old woman complains of loin pain and a burning sensation in her arm. Temperature 39 °C, pulse 128/min, BP 84/50 mmHg. She later passes dark red urine. What is the most appropriate first action?
questions.e: Fever, loin pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria within minutes of starting a transfusion suggest an acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility, usually a clerical error; the transfusion must be stopped at once, the line kept open with saline and the unit and patient identity checked. Continuing at any rate exposes her to more incompatible cells.

questions.s: An 81-year-old woman with heart failure is given 2 units of red cells over 2 hours for Hb 6.9 g/dL. Near the end she becomes breathless, with BP 176/98 mmHg, raised JVP and bibasal crackles. Temperature is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Breathlessness with hypertension, raised JVP and crackles in an elderly patient with heart failure after rapid transfusion is circulatory overload, treated by stopping the transfusion and giving a diuretic. TRALI also causes pulmonary oedema but typically with hypotension, fever and a normal JVP.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man is given fresh frozen plasma during surgery. Within minutes he develops stridor, wheeze, urticaria and BP 70/40 mmHg. He has had recurrent chest infections and giardiasis in the past. Which underlying condition most likely explains this reaction?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis to plasma-containing products, in a patient with recurrent sinopulmonary infections and giardiasis, suggests IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies; future transfusions should use IgA-deficient or washed products. ABO incompatibility with plasma causes haemolysis with fever and loin pain rather than urticaria and stridor.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman developed hepatitis C 3 months after receiving a unit of blood at a district hospital. Records show the donor unit had tested negative for anti-HCV. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Donation during the antibody window period
A false-positive HCV RNA result in the recipient
Contamination of the unit with bacteria
Reactivation of her own previously cleared hepatitis C infection
questions.e: A donor recently infected may have virus in the blood before antibodies are detectable; this window period is why antibody-only screening misses some infections and nucleic acid testing reduces the risk. Blood transfusion is a well-known route of hepatitis C transmission.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy from Quetta has a rapidly growing abdominal mass over 3 weeks. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized lymphoid cells with many scattered pale macrophages giving a 'starry sky' appearance, and a very high proliferation index. Which genetic change is most characteristic of this tumour?
questions.e: Burkitt lymphoma is an extremely fast-growing B-cell lymphoma with a starry-sky pattern, driven by MYC translocation, most often t(8;14). The t(14;18) BCL2 translocation is typical of follicular lymphoma, and t(15;17) of acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

questions.s: A 64-year-old man is found to have a serum IgG paraprotein of 12 g/L during investigation of a raised total protein. Hb, calcium and creatinine are normal, there are no bone lesions, and marrow plasma cells are 6 %. He has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: A paraprotein below 30 g/L with fewer than 10 % marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining features (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions) is MGUS, which is monitored because about 1 % a year progress to myeloma. Treatment is not given because it does not benefit people with MGUS.

questions.s: A 69-year-old woman with known multiple myeloma has worsening thoracic back pain for a week and now has weakness of both legs and difficulty passing urine. There is reduced sensation below the umbilicus. Which investigation is most urgent?
o: Plain X-ray of the thoracic spine
questions.e: Back pain with leg weakness, a sensory level and bladder symptoms in myeloma suggest metastatic spinal cord compression, which needs urgent whole-spine MRI and high-dose dexamethasone, with radiotherapy or surgery. Plain X-rays cannot show cord compression, and bone scans are often negative in myeloma.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with chronic kidney disease is given a unit of red cells. After 40 minutes his temperature rises from 36.9 to 38.2 °C with mild shivering. Pulse 92/min, BP 132/80 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98 %. He has no rash, breathlessness or loin pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An isolated rise in temperature with mild rigors and stable observations is most often a febrile non-haemolytic reaction, caused by cytokines or donor white cells; the transfusion is paused, the patient assessed, and paracetamol given. Haemolytic reactions cause hypotension, loin pain and haemoglobinuria.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman receives fresh frozen plasma for liver-related coagulopathy. Two hours later she becomes acutely breathless with oxygen saturation 84 %, temperature 38.3 °C and BP 88/56 mmHg. JVP is not raised. Chest X-ray shows new bilateral infiltrates; echo shows normal heart function. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute hypoxia with bilateral infiltrates within 6 hours of a plasma-rich product, with fever, hypotension and normal cardiac function, suggests TRALI, caused by donor antibodies against recipient white cells. Circulatory overload would cause hypertension and a raised JVP and responds to diuretics.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department of a tertiary hospital after a road traffic accident with massive haemorrhage. Her blood group is unknown and there is no time for cross-matching. Which red cells should be given?
questions.e: Group O red cells lack A and B antigens and can be given to any ABO group in an emergency; RhD negative units are used in girls and women of childbearing age to avoid sensitisation and later haemolytic disease of the newborn. Group AB red cells would be destroyed by anti-A or anti-B in most recipients.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man on an unfractionated heparin infusion for an acute limb ischaemia develops heavy bleeding from his groin puncture site. APTT is markedly prolonged. Which drug most rapidly reverses the anticoagulant?
questions.e: Protamine sulfate binds heparin and neutralises it rapidly; it fully reverses unfractionated heparin and partly reverses LMWH. Vitamin K reverses warfarin and has no effect on heparin.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman has been stable on warfarin for a mechanical aortic valve, with an INR of 2.5 to 3.0. She is diagnosed with pulmonary TB and starts standard treatment. Two weeks later her INR is 1.3 on the same warfarin dose. Which drug most likely explains this change?
questions.e: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes and speeds warfarin metabolism, so the INR falls and much higher warfarin doses with close monitoring are needed. Isoniazid, if anything, inhibits these enzymes, and ethambutol and pyrazinamide have little effect on warfarin.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man on treatment for tuberculosis for 3 months has fatigue and pallor. Hb 8.6 g/dL, MCV 74 fL, ferritin 480 ng/mL. A bone marrow aspirate stained with Prussian blue shows erythroblasts with a ring of iron granules around the nucleus. Which drug should be added to prevent this complication?
questions.e: Ring sideroblasts in a patient on isoniazid indicate acquired sideroblastic anaemia, as isoniazid antagonises pyridoxine (vitamin B6), a cofactor for haem synthesis; pyridoxine prevents and treats it and also prevents isoniazid neuropathy. Oral iron would worsen iron loading because ferritin is already high.

questions.s: A 13-year-old girl with sickle cell anaemia has had five admissions for painful crises in the past year and one episode of acute chest syndrome. Her haematologist starts hydroxycarbamide. By which main mechanism does it reduce crises?
o: Reducing intestinal iron absorption and iron loading
questions.e: Hydroxycarbamide raises fetal haemoglobin, which does not polymerise with HbS, so sickling, painful crises and acute chest syndrome become less frequent; it also lowers neutrophil counts and adhesion. It cannot increase HbA production, as the beta-globin gene is mutated.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy had bloody diarrhoea for 4 days after eating at a roadside stall. A week later he is pale and puffy, with very little urine. Hb 6.8 g/dL with schistocytes, platelets 38 x 10⁹/L, creatinine 2.8 mg/dL. PT and APTT are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury after bloody diarrhoea in a young child is typical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, usually from Shiga toxin-producing E. coli such as O157:H7. In DIC the PT and APTT would be prolonged, and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis does not cause haemolysis or thrombocytopenia.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man has enlarged cervical lymph nodes. He mentions that the nodes ache within minutes of drinking alcohol at a party abroad. He also has itching and evening fevers. Which diagnosis is most strongly suggested by the alcohol-related pain?
questions.e: Pain in involved lymph nodes after drinking alcohol is an uncommon but characteristic symptom of Hodgkin lymphoma, which also causes itching and B symptoms. Tuberculous lymphadenitis also causes fevers and neck nodes in Pakistan, but not alcohol-induced node pain; a biopsy separates the two.

questions.s: A 27-year-old woman is started on oral ferrous sulfate for iron deficiency anaemia after heavy periods. She is worried about side effects. Which effect is most common with oral iron?
questions.e: Oral iron commonly causes gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, epigastric pain, constipation or diarrhoea, and dark stools, which can reduce adherence; taking it on alternate days or with food may help. Neuropathy and hypertension are not side effects of oral iron.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy with known severe haemophilia A presents 2 hours after a fall with a painful, swollen, warm right knee that he cannot bend. He has no inhibitors. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: An acute haemarthrosis in haemophilia A needs prompt factor VIII replacement to stop bleeding and protect the joint, along with rest, ice and analgesia. IM injections can cause muscle haematomas, and joint aspiration is not routine and risks further bleeding without factor cover.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy with poorly transfused beta thalassaemia major has frontal bossing, prominent cheekbones and an overbite. A skull X-ray is taken. Which finding is most expected?
o: Calcification of the basal ganglia on both sides
questions.e: Expansion of the marrow cavity from ineffective erythropoiesis in under-transfused thalassaemia widens the diploic space and produces a 'hair-on-end' skull and thalassaemic facies. Punched-out lytic lesions are typical of multiple myeloma.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man from Hyderabad, Sindh, has had a stepwise rising fever for 8 days, headache, abdominal discomfort and constipation. Pulse is 84/min with a temperature of 39.5 °C. He has a coated tongue and mild splenomegaly. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis at this stage?
questions.e: Enteric fever is best confirmed by blood culture, which is most often positive in the first week or two of illness. The Widal test is unreliable in endemic areas such as Pakistan because of background antibodies and cross-reactions, while stool and urine cultures become positive later.

questions.s: A 9-year-old girl in Karachi has 10 days of fever. Blood culture grows Salmonella Typhi resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole, fluoroquinolones and ceftriaxone. She is not severely ill and can take tablets. What is the most appropriate oral antibiotic?
questions.e: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid, first reported from Sindh, is resistant to first-line drugs, fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins; uncomplicated cases are treated with oral azithromycin, and severe cases with a carbapenem. Cefixime, as a third-generation cephalosporin, will not work against this strain.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man in the third week of typhoid fever suddenly develops severe generalised abdominal pain, a rigid abdomen and absent bowel sounds. Pulse is 120/min. What is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Ileal perforation through ulcerated Peyer's patches is a classic complication of typhoid in the third week, presenting with peritonitis and needing resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgery. Typhoid can involve the gall bladder, but generalised peritonism with a rigid abdomen points to perforation.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with blood-culture-proven typhoid has been on an appropriate antibiotic for 3 days. Her fever persists but she is improving clinically. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Change to a different antibiotic class immediately
Continue the current antibiotic and monitor
questions.e: Fever in enteric fever commonly takes several days to settle even with an effective antibiotic, so a clinically improving patient on a drug to which the isolate is sensitive should continue treatment. Changing antibiotics so early is unnecessary, and dexamethasone is reserved for severe typhoid with shock or altered consciousness.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman who works as a cook has positive stool cultures for Salmonella Typhi 1 year after recovering from typhoid. Ultrasound shows gallstones. Which site is the usual reservoir in chronic carriers?
questions.e: Chronic typhoid carriage (shedding for more than a year) is usually from the gall bladder, especially when gallstones are present; carriers who handle food are a public health risk. Bone marrow is the best site for culture during acute illness, not the reservoir in carriers.

questions.s: Under the Pakistan EPI schedule, which vaccine against enteric fever is given to infants at 9 months of age?
questions.e: Pakistan introduced the typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) into its routine EPI at 9 months, in response to XDR typhoid. Plain Vi polysaccharide vaccine is poorly immunogenic below 2 years of age, and the oral Ty21a vaccine is not used in infants.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man with enteric fever has a pulse of 88/min with a temperature of 40 °C. What is this sign called?
questions.e: A pulse that is slower than expected for the height of the fever is relative bradycardia (Faget sign), classically seen in typhoid, as well as in some other infections such as legionella and brucellosis. It is not specific, but it is a useful clue in a febrile patient.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man is admitted with typhoid fever of 2 weeks' duration. He is now confused and muttering, picking at the bedclothes, and BP is 85/50 mmHg. Blood culture grows XDR Salmonella Typhi. What is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Severe XDR typhoid with encephalopathy and shock needs an intravenous carbapenem such as meropenem (often combined with azithromycin), alongside supportive care and consideration of dexamethasone. Ceftriaxone and ciprofloxacin are ineffective against XDR strains, and oral azithromycin alone is insufficient for a shocked patient.

questions.s: A 27-year-old man from rural Sindh has had fever with rigors every other day for a week. He is alert, eating and drinking. Hb is 11.5 g/dL. A thick and thin blood film shows Plasmodium vivax. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Uncomplicated vivax malaria is treated with chloroquine (or an ACT) to clear blood-stage parasites, followed by primaquine to eradicate liver hypnozoites and prevent relapse, after checking G6PD status. Primaquine alone does not reliably clear the blood stages, and IV artesunate is for severe malaria.

questions.s: Before giving primaquine for radical cure of vivax malaria to a 30-year-old man, which test should be done?
questions.e: Primaquine can cause severe haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, which is relatively common in Pakistan, so G6PD status should be checked before starting it. Haemoglobin electrophoresis detects thalassaemia, which does not contraindicate primaquine.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man has falciparum malaria confirmed by rapid diagnostic test in a BHU in Balochistan. He is alert, can take tablets, and has no features of severe disease. Parasitaemia is under 2%. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with an artemisinin-based combination therapy such as artemether-lumefantrine, recommended in Pakistan's national guidelines. Chloroquine resistance is widespread in P. falciparum, and parenteral treatment is reserved for severe malaria.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man with falciparum malaria becomes drowsy and then has a generalised seizure. Glucose is 40 mg/dL. Apart from correcting the glucose, what is the most appropriate antimalarial treatment?
o: Intramuscular quinine as a single dose
questions.e: Impaired consciousness, seizures and hypoglycaemia are features of severe falciparum malaria, which is treated with intravenous (or IM) artesunate for at least 24 hours, then a full course of an ACT once oral therapy is possible. Artesunate is superior to quinine in reducing mortality.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman is being treated for severe falciparum malaria. Which finding is a recognised criterion of severe malaria?
questions.e: Acute kidney injury (creatinine above about 3 mg/dL) is a WHO criterion of severe malaria, along with impaired consciousness, seizures, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, acidosis, shock, jaundice with other organ dysfunction and hyperparasitaemia. Mild thrombocytopenia, fever and splenomegaly are common in uncomplicated malaria.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy in Thatta has fever. The BHU has no microscope. Which test should be used to confirm malaria before treatment?
questions.e: WHO recommends parasitological confirmation of malaria before treatment; where microscopy is not available, a rapid diagnostic test detecting parasite antigens (such as HRP2 or pLDH) is used. Treating every fever as malaria leads to missed diagnoses and drug resistance.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman treated for vivax malaria 3 months ago with chloroquine alone presents with the same illness. She has not travelled or been exposed again. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Reinfection from a new mosquito bite
Chloroquine resistance of the blood stages
questions.e: P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant hypnozoites in the liver that can reactivate weeks to months later; chloroquine does not kill them, which is why primaquine is added for radical cure. Without new exposure, reinfection is unlikely, and P. vivax resistance to chloroquine is uncommon in Pakistan.

questions.s: A pregnant woman at 10 weeks' gestation has uncomplicated falciparum malaria. Which drug should be avoided?
questions.e: Primaquine is contraindicated in pregnancy because the fetal G6PD status is unknown and haemolysis may occur; for vivax, radical cure is deferred until after delivery. Current WHO guidance allows artemether-lumefantrine in all trimesters, and quinine with clindamycin is an alternative.

questions.s: A 23-year-old man in Lahore in October has had high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain and severe muscle and joint pains for 2 days. He has a flushed face. Platelets are 110,000/µL and WBC 3,100/µL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Post-monsoon high fever with retro-orbital pain, myalgia, leucopenia and falling platelets in Lahore is typical of dengue. Chikungunya also causes fever and severe joint pain, but leucopenia and thrombocytopenia are more characteristic of dengue, and typhoid has a gradual onset.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman with dengue has had fever for 4 days. Today the fever has settled but she has abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and is lethargic. Haematocrit has risen from 38% to 48% and platelets have fallen to 45,000/µL. What does this indicate?
o: She is recovering and can be discharged home tomorrow
Dengue with warning signs entering the critical phase
questions.e: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, lethargy and a rising haematocrit with a rapid fall in platelets around defervescence are WHO warning signs: plasma leakage is starting and she needs admission and careful IV fluids. The settling of fever is the start of the critical phase, not recovery.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has dengue fever with fever and body aches on day 2. He is drinking well and has no warning signs. Which drug should be used for his fever and pain?
questions.e: Paracetamol is the recommended antipyretic and analgesic in dengue. NSAIDs and aspirin should be avoided because they impair platelet function and increase the risk of bleeding and gastritis.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man with dengue on day 5 has cold peripheries, pulse 128/min, BP 90/78 mmHg (pulse pressure 12 mmHg) and capillary refill of 4 seconds. Haematocrit is 52%. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
o: Oral rehydration solution by frequent sips
questions.e: A narrow pulse pressure, tachycardia and delayed capillary refill with haemoconcentration indicate compensated dengue shock from plasma leakage; an IV crystalloid bolus with reassessment of haematocrit and vital signs is needed. Platelet transfusion is not indicated for thrombocytopenia without significant bleeding and does not treat shock.

questions.s: A 27-year-old woman has had fever for 2 days during a dengue outbreak in Rawalpindi. Which test is most useful for confirming dengue at this stage?
questions.e: NS1 antigen (or PCR) is positive in the first few days of fever, whereas IgM antibodies usually appear after about day 5. IgG indicates past or secondary infection, and the tourniquet test is a non-specific bedside sign of capillary fragility.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man with dengue was given large volumes of IV fluid during the critical phase. On day 8, with platelets rising, he becomes breathless with crepitations, raised JVP and a falling haematocrit. Pulse and BP are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Further rapid IV crystalloid boluses to maintain output
Reduce or stop IV fluids and consider a diuretic
questions.e: In the recovery phase, leaked plasma is reabsorbed; continued IV fluids cause fluid overload, shown by breathlessness, crepitations and a falling haematocrit with stable haemodynamics. IV fluids should be stopped or reduced and a diuretic considered; a falling haematocrit here reflects haemodilution, not bleeding.

questions.s: Which mosquito is the main vector of dengue in Pakistani cities?
questions.e: Dengue is spread mainly by Aedes aegypti, a day-biting mosquito that breeds in clean stored water in containers, tyres and coolers. Anopheles transmits malaria, Culex transmits filariasis and Japanese encephalitis, and Phlebotomus (a sandfly) transmits leishmaniasis.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man is newly diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. He has never been treated before and is HIV negative. What is the standard regimen?
questions.e: Drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is treated with isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months (intensive phase), then isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 months (continuation phase). Streptomycin-containing retreatment regimens are no longer recommended by WHO.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman on antituberculous therapy for 3 weeks reports reduced vision and difficulty telling red from green. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Ethambutol causes dose-related optic neuritis, typically with reduced acuity and red-green colour blindness; the drug should be stopped and vision assessed. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy and hepatitis, and rifampicin causes hepatitis and orange body fluids.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man started on HRZE for pulmonary TB 3 weeks ago now has nausea and jaundice. ALT is 420 U/L (normal under 40) and bilirubin 3.8 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Continue all drugs and add a hepatoprotective agent
Halve the dose of all drugs
questions.e: Drug-induced hepatitis with jaundice or ALT above three times the upper limit with symptoms requires stopping isoniazid, rifampicin and pyrazinamide until liver tests settle, then cautious sequential reintroduction. Ethambutol is not hepatotoxic, and continuing or reducing the doses risks fulminant hepatic failure.

questions.s: A 45-year-old diabetic man on isoniazid for tuberculosis develops burning and numbness in his feet. Which supplement would have prevented this?
questions.e: Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy by interfering with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) metabolism; pyridoxine is given prophylactically to people at risk, such as those with diabetes, HIV, alcohol use, malnutrition or pregnancy. Thiamine deficiency causes neuropathy but is not linked to isoniazid.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman on rifampicin-containing TB treatment says her urine and tears have turned orange-red. She also takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. What is the most important advice?
o: Stop rifampicin at once because this indicates toxicity
The colour change indicates liver damage
Her pill will be less effective, so use another method
Drink more water to clear the colour
questions.e: Orange-red discolouration of body fluids is a harmless effect of rifampicin, but rifampicin is a strong enzyme inducer that makes hormonal contraceptives unreliable, so a non-hormonal method such as a copper IUD is advised. The colour change is not a sign of toxicity and does not require stopping treatment.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man previously treated for TB has a relapse. Before starting treatment, which test should be done on his sputum to guide the regimen?
questions.e: Xpert MTB/RIF detects M. tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance within hours and is recommended for all presumptive TB, especially previously treated patients who are at higher risk of drug resistance. Smear microscopy cannot detect resistance, and IGRA cannot distinguish active from latent infection.

questions.s: A 33-year-old man has pulmonary TB with resistance to both isoniazid and rifampicin confirmed by molecular testing. How is this form of TB classified?
questions.e: Multidrug-resistant TB is defined as resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, and is treated with a second-line regimen under the national programme. Extensively drug-resistant TB additionally has resistance to fluoroquinolones and other key second-line drugs.

questions.s: A 4-year-old child lives with his father, who has smear-positive pulmonary TB. The child is well, with a normal examination and chest X-ray. What is the most appropriate management for the child?
questions.e: Child household contacts under 5 years of an infectious TB case should receive TB preventive treatment once active disease is excluded, for example isoniazid for 6 months or 3 months of isoniazid with rifampicin. A full treatment course is only for active TB, and BCG is not repeated.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man, a long-distance truck driver, has HIV diagnosed on a rapid test confirmed by the national algorithm. CD4 count is 450 cells/µL and he is well. When should antiretroviral therapy be started?
o: As soon as possible, regardless of CD4 count
Only when CD4 falls below 350 cells/µL
Only when he develops an AIDS-defining illness
After the viral load has been measured twice
questions.e: WHO recommends that everyone with HIV starts ART as soon as possible after diagnosis, irrespective of CD4 count, because early treatment improves survival and prevents transmission. CD4 thresholds for starting ART are no longer used.

questions.s: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV has a CD4 count of 80 cells/µL. Which prophylaxis should be started to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia?
questions.e: Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis prevents Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis in people with low CD4 counts (below 200 cells/µL in most guidance). Isoniazid prevents TB, and fluconazole is used for cryptococcal antigen-positive patients.

questions.s: A 36-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 60 cells/µL has 2 weeks of fever, headache and left-sided weakness. CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the grey-white junction and basal ganglia. Toxoplasma IgG is positive. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
o: Pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and folinic acid
questions.e: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in advanced HIV with positive toxoplasma serology are treated empirically for cerebral toxoplasmosis (pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine with folinic acid, or high-dose co-trimoxazole); clinical and radiological improvement within 2 weeks supports the diagnosis. Primary CNS lymphoma is the main alternative if there is no response.

questions.s: A nurse in a Larkana hospital sustains a needlestick injury from a patient known to have HIV. What is the most appropriate action regarding post-exposure prophylaxis?
o: Wait for her own HIV test result before deciding
Start PEP only if she becomes symptomatic
Start 3-drug PEP as soon as possible for 28 days
Give a single dose of nevirapine
questions.e: After a significant exposure, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis with a three-drug regimen should start as soon as possible, ideally within hours and no later than 72 hours, and continue for 28 days. Waiting for symptoms or results loses the window in which PEP works; baseline testing is done but should not delay the first dose.

questions.s: A pregnant woman at 24 weeks is newly found to have HIV. What is the most effective way to prevent transmission to her baby?
o: Elective caesarean section at 38 weeks alone
Treat the baby only after birth
Start lifelong ART for the mother now
questions.e: Starting lifelong ART in the mother as soon as possible to suppress the viral load is the most effective intervention to prevent mother-to-child transmission, together with infant prophylaxis. Caesarean section and feeding choices have smaller effects and are secondary to viral suppression.

questions.s: A 32-year-old woman with HIV is started on ART while being treated for TB. Two weeks later her fever returns, lymph nodes enlarge and a new pleural effusion appears, although she is adherent and her CD4 count is rising. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Paradoxical worsening of a known infection shortly after starting ART, with a rising CD4 count, is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome; TB and ART are usually continued, with NSAIDs or prednisolone for significant symptoms. Treatment failure would show a falling or static CD4 count and rising viral load.

questions.s: In Pakistan, recent outbreaks of HIV among children, such as in Ratodero, Larkana, were mainly linked to which route of transmission?
o: Vertical transmission from mother to child
Reuse of unsterile syringes and needles
questions.e: The 2019 Ratodero outbreak was attributed mainly to unsafe injection practices, with reuse of syringes and unsterile equipment by healthcare providers. Most affected children had HIV-negative mothers, which made mother-to-child transmission an unlikely main cause.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man has HBsAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive, HBeAg positive and ALT 1,200 U/L. He has jaundice and anorexia but no encephalopathy and a normal INR. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: HBsAg with IgM anti-HBc and very high transaminases indicates acute hepatitis B; most adults recover spontaneously with supportive care. A chronic carrier would have IgG rather than IgM anti-HBc, and vaccination gives anti-HBs only.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman found to be anti-HCV positive during screening before surgery feels well. Which test should be done next to confirm active infection?
questions.e: Anti-HCV indicates exposure but not necessarily current infection, since some people clear the virus; HCV RNA by PCR confirms viraemia and the need for treatment. ALT can be normal in chronic hepatitis C, and liver biopsy is no longer needed for diagnosis.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man has chronic hepatitis C with detectable HCV RNA. He has no cirrhosis. Which treatment is now standard?
o: Pegylated interferon with ribavirin for 48 weeks
questions.e: Chronic hepatitis C is treated with oral direct-acting antivirals such as sofosbuvir with velpatasvir or daclatasvir for 12 weeks, curing over 95%. Interferon-based regimens are obsolete, and tenofovir and lamivudine are hepatitis B (and HIV) drugs.

questions.s: A baby is born to a mother who is HBsAg positive. What is the most appropriate action for the baby?
o: Hepatitis B vaccine at 6 weeks with other EPI vaccines
Vaccine plus immunoglobulin within 12 hours of birth
questions.e: Babies of HBsAg-positive mothers need the birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine and HBIG within 12 hours, then the full vaccine schedule, which prevents most perinatal transmission. Breastfeeding is not contraindicated once the baby is immunised.

questions.s: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 30 weeks in rural Sindh develops jaundice, confusion and bleeding after a short febrile illness during a waterborne outbreak. INR is 3.2. Which hepatitis virus is most likely?
questions.e: Hepatitis E is spread by the faecal-oral route in outbreaks after contaminated water supply and carries a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure in the third trimester of pregnancy. Hepatitis A is also waterborne but rarely causes fulminant disease in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B, HBeAg negative, has HBV DNA 50,000 IU/mL and ALT twice the upper limit of normal. Which drug is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: Active chronic hepatitis B (raised HBV DNA and ALT) is treated with a potent antiviral with a high barrier to resistance, such as tenofovir or entecavir. Lamivudine is avoided because of frequent resistance, and ribavirin and sofosbuvir are hepatitis C drugs.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy in a village near Multan was bitten on the calf by a stray dog 2 hours ago, with bleeding through the skin. He has never had rabies vaccine. What is the most important first step at the BHU?
o: Apply a tight tourniquet above the bite wound
Wash the wound with soap and running water
questions.e: Immediate thorough washing with soap and water for about 15 minutes, followed by an antiseptic, greatly reduces the risk of rabies and is the first step, followed by vaccine and immunoglobulin. Bite wounds should not be sutured primarily, and tourniquets have no role.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man was bitten on the hand by an unknown dog, breaking the skin and drawing blood. He has never received rabies vaccine. Into which WHO exposure category does this fall and what is needed?
o: Category III: rabies immunoglobulin alone, no vaccine
questions.e: Single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, or contamination of mucous membranes or broken skin with saliva, are Category III exposures and need wound washing, a full course of rabies vaccine and rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into the wound. Category II (nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches without bleeding) needs vaccine without immunoglobulin.

questions.s: When giving rabies immunoglobulin for a Category III bite on the forearm, how should it be administered?
o: Infiltrated into and around the wound
Intramuscularly into the opposite deltoid only
In the same syringe as the first vaccine dose
questions.e: Rabies immunoglobulin is infiltrated into and around all wounds, as far as anatomically possible, to neutralise virus at the site of entry. It must never be mixed with the vaccine in the same syringe or injected at the same site, because it would neutralise the vaccine, and it is never given intravenously.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man who was bitten by a dog 2 months ago and received no treatment now has fever, agitation and painful spasms of his throat when offered water. He becomes terrified at the sight of water. What is the most appropriate management now?
o: Start a full course of rabies vaccine
Give rabies immunoglobulin into the old wound
questions.e: Hydrophobia with agitation after an untreated dog bite is clinical rabies, which is almost always fatal once symptoms appear; management is palliative, with sedation, analgesia and a calm environment, and staff protection. Vaccine and immunoglobulin are effective only before symptoms develop.

questions.s: A 28-year-old veterinary student in Lahore wants protection against rabies because she handles dogs regularly. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: No action until she is bitten
questions.e: People at continuing risk, such as veterinary workers and laboratory staff, should receive pre-exposure rabies vaccination; after a later bite they need only booster vaccine doses and no immunoglobulin. Immunoglobulin is used only after exposure in unvaccinated people.

questions.s: A 40-year-old farmer from Sargodha, who stepped on a nail 10 days ago, has difficulty opening his mouth, stiffness of the neck and back, and painful spasms triggered by noise. He is fully conscious. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Trismus, generalised rigidity and reflex spasms triggered by stimuli in a conscious patient after a contaminated wound is tetanus, caused by Clostridium tetani toxin. Meningitis causes fever, headache and altered consciousness rather than trismus and spasms.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man is admitted with generalised tetanus. Which measure is most important to neutralise toxin that is not yet bound to nerve endings?
questions.e: Human tetanus immunoglobulin neutralises circulating unbound toxin; it cannot reverse toxin already bound in the nervous system. Benzodiazepines and magnesium control spasms, and tetanus toxoid is also given because the disease does not confer immunity, but neither neutralises free toxin.

questions.s: A 7-day-old baby born at home in a village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa stops sucking, has stiffness and spasms. The cord was cut with an unsterilised blade and ghee was applied to it. The mother received no antenatal vaccination. Which measure would most effectively have prevented this illness?
o: Tetanus toxoid vaccination of the mother in pregnancy
questions.e: Neonatal tetanus follows contamination of the umbilical stump and is prevented by immunising pregnant women with tetanus toxoid (Td), which passes protective antibodies to the baby, together with clean delivery and cord care. The other birth interventions do not protect against tetanus.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has a deep contaminated wound from a farm accident. He received a full primary course of tetanus vaccine in childhood and his last booster was 12 years ago. What is the most appropriate tetanus prophylaxis?
o: A full new primary course of three toxoid doses
Td booster, plus immunoglobulin if high risk
questions.e: A tetanus-prone wound in someone whose last dose was more than 10 years ago needs a booster of tetanus toxoid (as Td), and immunoglobulin is added for high-risk wounds such as heavily contaminated ones. A full primary course is only for people who were never immunised or whose status is unknown.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman with a urinary tract infection is drowsy, with temperature 38.9 °C, respiratory rate 26/min, BP 88/50 mmHg and lactate 4.5 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate immediate step after taking blood cultures?
o: Wait for urine culture results before giving antibiotics
IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour
questions.e: Sepsis with hypotension and raised lactate requires blood cultures, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour, and an IV crystalloid bolus (around 30 mL/kg), with vasopressors if hypotension persists after fluids. Every hour of delay in antibiotics increases mortality.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman with a urinary tract infection is assessed in the emergency room of a THQ hospital. She is alert and oriented. Temperature is 39.2 °C, pulse 116/min and BP 96/60 mmHg. Her quick SOFA (qSOFA) score is being calculated. Which additional finding would raise her score to 2?
questions.e: qSOFA gives one point each for a respiratory rate of 22/min or more, altered mentation and a systolic BP of 100 mmHg or less; she already scores 1 for her BP, so a respiratory rate of 24/min makes 2 and flags a higher risk of a poor outcome from sepsis. Tachycardia, fever and the white cell count are SIRS criteria and are not part of qSOFA.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman is in septic shock from a perforated diverticulum. She is on noradrenaline and IV antibiotics. Which step is most important to control the source of infection?
o: Urgent surgical or radiological drainage of the source
questions.e: Source control, such as drainage of an abscess or surgery for a perforation, should be achieved as soon as practical in sepsis; antibiotics alone cannot sterilise a collection. Hydrocortisone is considered for shock needing escalating vasopressors, but it does not remove the source.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman with sepsis has received 2 litres of IV fluid. Which bedside measure best shows that her tissue perfusion is improving?
o: Falling serum lactate and urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/h
questions.e: Improving perfusion in sepsis is shown by falling lactate, adequate urine output (above 0.5 mL/kg/h), better mental state, capillary refill and mean arterial pressure. Temperature and white count reflect the infection rather than perfusion.

questions.s: A 38-year-old dairy farmer near Okara has had fever with drenching sweats, back pain and joint aches for 6 weeks. He drinks unboiled milk. He has hepatosplenomegaly and lumbar spine tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A prolonged undulant fever with sweats, arthralgia, sacroiliitis or spondylitis and hepatosplenomegaly in someone who drinks raw milk or handles livestock suggests brucellosis; treatment is doxycycline combined with rifampicin or an aminoglycoside. Spinal TB is possible, but the raw milk exposure and systemic features favour brucellosis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old butcher in Quetta develops high fever, myalgia and then bleeding from the gums and injection sites, 5 days after Eid-ul-Adha. Platelets are 18,000/µL and ALT is raised. A nurse who cared for him earlier is now febrile. Which infection is most likely?
questions.e: Fever with bleeding and severe thrombocytopenia in a butcher after animal slaughter, with spread to a healthcare worker, suggests Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever, a tick-borne Nairovirus endemic in Balochistan. It spreads through blood and body fluids, so strict barrier nursing is essential, and ribavirin is used in some centres.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man in a flood relief camp in Sindh has sudden profuse painless watery diarrhoea like rice water and vomiting. He is lethargic with sunken eyes and very slow skin pinch. What is the most important treatment?
questions.e: Rice-water stools with severe dehydration are typical of cholera; the priority is rapid IV rehydration with Ringer's lactate, followed by ORS once he can drink. Antibiotics such as a single dose of doxycycline or azithromycin shorten illness but are secondary, and antimotility drugs are not used.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy from Hyderabad has had fever for 3 weeks. Blood cultures taken on day 4 were negative, but he received antibiotics before they were taken. Which specimen gives the highest culture yield for enteric fever in this situation?
questions.e: Bone marrow culture has the highest yield for Salmonella Typhi and remains positive even after several days of antibiotics. Blood culture sensitivity falls with prior antibiotics and later in the illness.

questions.s: A family in Karachi asks how to prevent typhoid at home after their son recovered from it. Which measure is most effective?
o: Safe drinking water, handwashing and typhoid conjugate vaccination
questions.e: Typhoid is spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food and water, so safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene and vaccination with typhoid conjugate vaccine are the key preventive measures. Bed nets prevent mosquito-borne infections, and prophylactic antibiotics promote resistance.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman with falciparum malaria has fever, a parasitaemia of 12% and is jaundiced but conscious. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Hyperparasitaemia above 10% (and jaundice with organ dysfunction) defines severe falciparum malaria, which needs parenteral artesunate even if the patient is alert. Oral ACT is only for uncomplicated malaria.

questions.s: A 6-year-old child with severe falciparum malaria is treated with IV artesunate and improves. Two weeks later she becomes pale and tired with dark urine; parasites are no longer seen on film. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.e: Delayed haemolysis 1-3 weeks after IV artesunate for severe malaria is a recognised effect, caused by clearance of once-infected red cells, so haemoglobin should be checked after treatment. With no parasites on film, recrudescence is unlikely, and she received neither chloroquine nor quinine.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with dengue on day 3 has no warning signs, is drinking well and passing urine normally. Platelets are 95,000/µL. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Manage at home with oral fluids, paracetamol and daily review
questions.e: Dengue without warning signs in a patient who can drink and pass urine can be managed as an outpatient with oral fluids, paracetamol and daily review of symptoms, haematocrit and platelets, with advice on warning signs. Prophylactic platelet transfusion and steroids are not recommended.

questions.s: Which public health measure is most effective in controlling dengue in a city?
o: Indoor residual spraying against night-biting mosquitoes
Eliminating stagnant water in containers around homes
questions.e: Aedes mosquitoes breed in clean water in containers, tyres, flower pots and water tanks, so removing or covering these breeding sites is the cornerstone of dengue control. Aedes bites mainly during the day, so measures aimed at night-biting mosquitoes are less effective.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman has extrapulmonary TB of the cervical lymph nodes. She is not pregnant and has never been treated. What is the duration of standard treatment?
questions.e: TB lymphadenitis is treated with the same 6-month regimen as pulmonary TB (2 months HRZE, 4 months HR). Longer courses are reserved for TB meningitis and bone and joint TB.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man on TB treatment develops an acutely painful, swollen big toe. Serum uric acid is high. Which antituberculous drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Pyrazinamide reduces renal uric acid excretion and can cause hyperuricaemia and gout, as can ethambutol to a lesser extent. Pyrazinamide is the drug classically associated with acute gout and arthralgia during TB treatment.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with HIV on ART has a viral load of 15,000 copies/mL after 12 months of treatment, measured twice 3 months apart with adherence support in between. What does this indicate?
questions.e: A persistently raised viral load (above 1,000 copies/mL on two tests 3 months apart, after adherence support) after at least 6 months of ART indicates virological failure, and the regimen should be switched. A good response would give an undetectable viral load by 6 months.

questions.s: A 27-year-old man with HIV has a CD4 count of 150 cells/µL and white plaques on his tongue and buccal mucosa that can be scraped off. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: White plaques that can be scraped off leaving a red base are oral candidiasis, common in HIV with falling CD4 counts. Oral hairy leukoplakia, caused by EBV, forms white corrugated plaques on the lateral tongue that cannot be scraped off.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman is HBsAg negative, anti-HBc negative and anti-HBs positive. How should this be interpreted?
questions.e: Anti-HBs alone, without anti-HBc, indicates immunity from vaccination because the vaccine contains only surface antigen. Immunity after natural infection would show both anti-HBs and anti-HBc.

questions.s: A 9-year-old girl was bitten deeply on the face by a dog that later died. She completed a full course of rabies pre-exposure vaccination last year. What post-exposure treatment does she need?
o: Two booster doses of vaccine without immunoglobulin
A full course of vaccine plus immunoglobulin
No treatment, as she is already protected
questions.e: Previously vaccinated people need wound care and two booster doses of rabies vaccine (days 0 and 3), but immunoglobulin is not needed and may blunt the booster response. Face bites are high risk, so no treatment at all would be unsafe.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man with severe tetanus has frequent generalised spasms that interfere with breathing despite diazepam. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Intubation or tracheostomy with ventilation and muscle relaxation
questions.e: Severe tetanus with spasms compromising breathing needs a secured airway (often tracheostomy) with sedation, neuromuscular blockade and ventilation in an intensive care unit, with magnesium to help control spasms and autonomic instability. More toxoid does not affect current disease.

questions.s: Which set of findings meets the definition of septic shock in an adult with infection?
o: Fever above 38 °C, pulse above 90/min and respiratory rate above 20 per minute
White cell count above 12,000/µL with a confirmed bacterial source
Vasopressors to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg plus lactate > 2 mmol/L despite fluids
Systolic BP below 100 mmHg that corrects fully with one fluid bolus
questions.e: Septic shock is sepsis with persistent hypotension needing vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg and a serum lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Fever, tachycardia and leucocytosis are older SIRS criteria and do not define shock.

questions.s: A 32-year-old rice farmer in Sindh has fever, severe calf muscle pain, red eyes and jaundice a week after working in flooded fields. Creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL. Which organism is most likely?
questions.e: Fever with severe calf myalgia, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice and acute kidney injury after exposure to water contaminated by rodent urine suggests leptospirosis (Weil disease), treated with penicillin or doxycycline. Hepatitis A does not usually cause kidney injury or severe myalgia.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman, Rukhsana, has had pain and swelling of the small joints of both hands for 4 months, with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. The MCP and PIP joints are swollen and tender; DIP joints are spared. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis of the MCP and PIP joints with prolonged morning stiffness, sparing the DIP joints, is typical of rheumatoid arthritis. Osteoarthritis affects DIP joints with brief stiffness, and psoriatic arthritis often involves DIP joints asymmetrically.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has early inflammatory polyarthritis of the hands. Rheumatoid factor is negative. Which test is most specific for rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.e: Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies are highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis, can be positive when rheumatoid factor is negative, and predict erosive disease. ANA is sensitive for SLE but not specific, and ESR is a non-specific marker of inflammation.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman is diagnosed with active rheumatoid arthritis. Liver and renal function are normal and she is not planning pregnancy. What is the most appropriate first-line disease-modifying drug?
questions.e: Methotrexate is the anchor first-line DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis, often with a short course of steroid as a bridge. NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not prevent joint damage, and long-term steroids alone carry major toxicity without adequate disease control.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has taken methotrexate for a year. Which supplement is prescribed with it to reduce side effects?
questions.e: Folic acid is given on a different day of the week from weekly methotrexate to reduce mouth ulcers, gastrointestinal upset and bone marrow and liver toxicity. Pyridoxine is used with isoniazid, not methotrexate.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis is about to start infliximab (an anti-TNF drug). Which screening test is essential before starting it?
questions.e: Anti-TNF drugs greatly increase the risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis, so screening with history, chest X-ray and an IGRA or tuberculin test is essential, particularly in Pakistan; hepatitis B and C screening is also needed. The other tests are not mandatory before biologics.

questions.s: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has tingling in her hands and sudden electric-shock sensations in her limbs on bending her neck, and has become clumsy. What serious complication must be excluded urgently?
questions.e: Rheumatoid arthritis can erode the transverse ligament, causing atlantoaxial subluxation with cervical cord compression; Lhermitte-type symptoms and long-tract signs need urgent MRI, particularly before any general anaesthetic. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes median nerve symptoms in the hand only.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman has had painful joints, mouth ulcers, hair loss and a red rash over her cheeks and the bridge of her nose that spares the nasolabial folds and is worse after sun exposure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds with arthralgia, oral ulcers and alopecia in a young woman is typical of systemic lupus erythematosus. Rosacea has papules and pustules without systemic features, and dermatomyositis causes a heliotrope rash and proximal muscle weakness.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has suspected SLE with a positive ANA. Which antibody is most specific for the diagnosis?
questions.e: Anti-dsDNA (and anti-Smith) antibodies are highly specific for SLE, and anti-dsDNA levels track disease activity, especially nephritis. ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-histone antibodies suggest drug-induced lupus.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman with SLE now has frothy urine, ankle oedema and BP 150/95 mmHg. Urinalysis shows protein 3+ and red cell casts. Serum creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Proteinuria with red cell casts and rising creatinine in SLE indicates lupus nephritis; renal biopsy defines the histological class, which guides immunosuppression. Ultrasound shows kidney size but cannot classify the nephritis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has had three miscarriages at 10-14 weeks and a deep vein thrombosis last year. Her activated partial thromboplastin time is prolonged. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent pregnancy loss and venous thrombosis with a prolonged APTT (from lupus anticoagulant, which paradoxically promotes clotting) suggest antiphospholipid syndrome, confirmed by persistently positive lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Factor VIII deficiency causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man treated for many months with a drug for hypertension develops arthralgia, fever and pleurisy. ANA and anti-histone antibodies are positive; anti-dsDNA is negative. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Hydralazine is a classic cause of drug-induced lupus, which features arthralgia and serositis with anti-histone antibodies and usually negative anti-dsDNA; it resolves on stopping the drug. Procainamide, isoniazid and minocycline are other causes.

questions.s: A 32-year-old woman with SLE has joint pains and a malar rash but no organ involvement. Which drug should form the basis of her long-term treatment?
questions.e: Hydroxychloroquine is recommended for all patients with SLE unless contraindicated; it controls skin and joint disease, reduces flares and improves survival, with yearly eye screening for retinopathy. Cyclophosphamide and rituximab are reserved for severe organ-threatening disease.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man wakes at night with severe pain, redness and swelling of his right big toe after a wedding dinner with meat dishes. He cannot bear the bedsheet touching it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden, exquisitely painful inflammation of the first metatarsophalangeal joint after a purine-rich meal is typical of acute gout (podagra). Pseudogout typically affects the knee or wrist in older people, and septic arthritis is usually accompanied by fever and systemic upset.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man has an acutely swollen knee. Synovial fluid microscopy under polarised light shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Gram stain is negative. What are the crystals?
questions.e: Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals are monosodium urate, diagnostic of gout. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals in pseudogout are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.

questions.s: A 48-year-old man has an acute attack of gout in his ankle. He has peptic ulcer disease and normal renal function. Which treatment is most appropriate for this attack?
questions.e: Colchicine (or a short course of oral steroid) is preferred for acute gout when NSAIDs are contraindicated, as in peptic ulcer disease. Aspirin raises urate and can worsen gout, and allopurinol is not started during an acute attack without anti-inflammatory cover.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man has had four attacks of gout this year and tophi on his ear. Serum uric acid is 9.2 mg/dL. Which long-term drug is most appropriate?
questions.e: Recurrent attacks and tophi are indications for urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol, titrated to keep serum uric acid below about 6 mg/dL, with colchicine cover for the first months. Colchicine alone prevents flares but does not lower urate or dissolve tophi.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with gout on allopurinol is started on azathioprine after a kidney transplant. What is the main risk of this combination?
questions.e: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, which metabolises azathioprine (via 6-mercaptopurine); the combination greatly increases azathioprine levels and can cause life-threatening bone marrow suppression. If both are needed the azathioprine dose must be sharply reduced, or an alternative used.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has had low back pain and stiffness for a year, worse in the morning and after rest, improving with exercise. He wakes in the second half of the night with pain. Schober test shows reduced lumbar flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Inflammatory back pain in a young man, with morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, night pain and reduced spinal mobility, suggests axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis). Mechanical pain worsens with activity and improves with rest.

questions.s: A 27-year-old man has inflammatory back pain. Which investigation is most useful to confirm early axial spondyloarthritis when plain X-rays of the sacroiliac joints are normal?
questions.e: MRI of the sacroiliac joints can detect active sacroiliitis (bone marrow oedema) years before changes are visible on plain radiographs. Rheumatoid factor is typically negative in spondyloarthritis, and CT involves radiation without showing active inflammation.

questions.s: A 23-year-old man has pain and swelling of his left knee and right ankle, painful red eyes and dysuria, 3 weeks after an episode of diarrhoea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Asymmetrical lower-limb oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis a few weeks after a gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection is reactive arthritis, a spondyloarthritis associated with HLA-B27. Gonococcal arthritis presents with migratory arthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustular skin lesions.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with psoriasis has painful swelling of an entire finger (a 'sausage digit') and pitting of his nails. Which condition is most likely?
questions.e: Dactylitis (sausage digit) and nail pitting in a patient with psoriasis indicate psoriatic arthritis, which often affects the DIP joints. Gout can cause a swollen digit but is acute and very painful, and rheumatoid arthritis does not cause dactylitis or nail changes.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis develops a painful red right eye with photophobia and blurred vision. The pupil is small. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute anterior uveitis is the commonest extra-articular feature of ankylosing spondylitis, causing a painful red eye with photophobia, blurred vision and a small pupil; it needs same-day ophthalmology review. Angle-closure glaucoma causes a mid-dilated pupil and episcleritis is usually painless.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman has had pain and stiffness of both shoulders and hips for 6 weeks, worse in the morning, making it hard to get out of bed. Muscle strength is normal and ESR is 75 mm/h. CK is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness with a high ESR and normal CK in an older person is polymyalgia rheumatica, which responds rapidly to low-dose prednisolone (around 15 mg daily). High-dose steroids are for giant cell arteritis, which must be asked about.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has chronic sinusitis with bloody nasal discharge, haemoptysis and haematuria. Chest X-ray shows cavitating nodules and creatinine is rising. Which antibody is most likely positive?
questions.e: Upper airway disease, cavitating lung nodules and glomerulonephritis indicate granulomatosis with polyangiitis, strongly associated with c-ANCA against proteinase 3. Anti-GBM disease affects lung and kidney but not the upper airway, and p-ANCA is more typical of microscopic polyangiitis.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has had fever for 6 days with bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, red cracked lips, a strawberry tongue, a rash, swollen hands and feet and a cervical lymph node. What is the most important treatment to prevent complications?
questions.e: Kawasaki disease is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin, which reduces the risk of coronary artery aneurysms; echocardiography is needed. Antibiotics do not treat this vasculitis.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy has a raised purpuric rash over his buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain and painful swollen ankles, a week after a sore throat. Platelet count is normal. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with a normal platelet count, abdominal pain, arthritis and haematuria in a child is IgA vasculitis; renal involvement needs follow-up urinalysis and BP checks. In immune thrombocytopenia the platelet count is low and the purpura is not palpable.
