questions.s: A 24-year-old woman has tiredness, pain in her arms when combing her hair, and dizziness. The left radial pulse is weak and BP differs by 30 mmHg between the arms. A bruit is heard over the left subclavian artery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A young woman with arm claudication, unequal arm pulses and BP, and arterial bruits has Takayasu arteritis, a large-vessel vasculitis of the aorta and its branches. Giant cell arteritis occurs over 50 years of age, and coarctation causes radio-femoral delay rather than unequal arm pulses.

questions.s: A 63-year-old overweight woman has pain in both knees on walking and climbing stairs, relieved by rest, with stiffness for 10 minutes after sitting. There is crepitus and bony enlargement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Use-related joint pain with brief stiffness after inactivity, crepitus and bony enlargement in an older overweight person is osteoarthritis, which can be diagnosed clinically without imaging. Rheumatoid arthritis causes prolonged morning stiffness and soft-tissue synovial swelling.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man has osteoarthritis of the knee. He wants advice on non-drug treatment. Which measure has the best evidence for reducing pain and improving function?
o: Complete rest of the joint for several weeks
Wearing a soft knee brace at night
questions.e: Local muscle strengthening and general aerobic exercise, with weight loss if overweight, are core treatments for knee osteoarthritis. Rest leads to muscle weakness and stiffness, and glucosamine has not shown consistent benefit.

questions.s: An X-ray of a 66-year-old woman's knee is requested for long-standing pain. Which combination of findings is typical of osteoarthritis?
o: Narrowed joint space, osteophytes and sclerosis
questions.e: Osteoarthritis shows loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts. Periarticular osteopenia with marginal erosions suggests rheumatoid arthritis, and punched-out erosions with overhanging edges are seen in chronic gout.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has firm, non-tender nodules over the extensor surface of her forearms. What are these most likely to be?
questions.e: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, non-tender subcutaneous nodules over pressure points such as the extensor forearm, usually in seropositive disease. Heberden nodes are bony swellings of the DIP joints in osteoarthritis.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has dry eyes and a dry mouth, and needs water to swallow dry food. Which antibodies are typically associated with this condition?
questions.e: Dry eyes and mouth in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis suggest secondary Sjögren syndrome, associated with anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies. Anti-centromere and anti-Scl-70 are associated with systemic sclerosis, and anti-Jo-1 with myositis.

questions.s: A 29-year-old woman with SLE is planning pregnancy. She is anti-Ro positive. Which complication in the baby should she be counselled about?
questions.e: Maternal anti-Ro antibodies cross the placenta and can cause congenital heart block and neonatal lupus rash, so fetal heart rate is monitored in pregnancy. Hydroxychloroquine is continued in pregnancy and may reduce this risk.

questions.s: A 27-year-old woman with known SLE has a flare with fatigue and joint pain. Which pair of blood results best reflects active lupus nephritis or a major flare?
o: Rising anti-dsDNA and falling C3 and C4
Rising ANA titre and normal complement
questions.e: Active SLE, especially nephritis, is associated with rising anti-dsDNA titres and consumption of complement (low C3 and C4). ANA titre does not track activity, and CRP is often normal in a lupus flare unless there is serositis or infection.

questions.s: A 68-year-old woman has an acutely painful, swollen knee. X-ray shows linear calcification of the meniscal cartilage. Joint fluid contains rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray with rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals indicates calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, presenting as pseudogout. Gout crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man on allopurinol for gout asks what else he can do to reduce attacks. Which lifestyle change is most appropriate?
o: Reduce alcohol, especially beer, and sugary drinks
questions.e: Reducing alcohol (especially beer and spirits), fructose-sweetened drinks and excess purine-rich foods, losing weight and keeping well hydrated lower urate levels. Low-dose aspirin reduces urate excretion and can raise serum urate.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with ankylosing spondylitis has back pain and stiffness despite exercise. What is the first-line drug treatment?
questions.e: NSAIDs at full dose are first-line drug treatment for axial spondyloarthritis, combined with regular exercise and physiotherapy; anti-TNF or IL-17 drugs are used if NSAIDs fail. Methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs are not effective for axial disease.

questions.s: Which genetic marker is most strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
questions.e: Most patients with ankylosing spondylitis carry HLA-B27, although most people with HLA-B27 never develop the disease. HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis, HLA-DQ2 to coeliac disease and HLA-B51 to Behçet disease.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has fever, weight loss, testicular pain, a new mononeuritis multiplex (foot drop) and hypertension. He is hepatitis B surface antigen positive. ANCA is negative. Angiography shows microaneurysms in the renal arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Medium-vessel vasculitis with mononeuritis multiplex, testicular pain, hypertension, renal microaneurysms, negative ANCA and hepatitis B association is polyarteritis nodosa. Microscopic polyangiitis is a small-vessel, usually p-ANCA-positive vasculitis without microaneurysms.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman has painful bony swellings at the distal interphalangeal joints of both hands. Which name is given to these swellings?
questions.e: Heberden nodes are osteophytes at the DIP joints in hand osteoarthritis, while Bouchard nodes occur at the PIP joints. Rheumatoid nodules are subcutaneous and not bony.

questions.s: Ayesha, a 34-year-old schoolteacher in Multan, has had low mood for most of the day, loss of interest in her usual activities, early morning waking, poor appetite with weight loss and feelings of worthlessness for the past 6 weeks. She has never had a period of elevated mood and does not use alcohol or drugs. Thyroid function and blood count are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Pervasive low mood and anhedonia with biological symptoms and worthlessness for more than 2 weeks meet criteria for a major depressive episode, and the absence of mania makes it unipolar. Dysthymia is a milder chronic low mood lasting at least 2 years, and adjustment disorder needs an identifiable stressor with less severe symptoms.

questions.s: Bilal, a 30-year-old bank officer, has had moderate depression for 2 months that has not improved with guided self-help. He has no medical illness and takes no other medicines. He agrees to start an antidepressant. Which drug is the most appropriate first choice?
questions.e: SSRIs such as sertraline are first-line antidepressants: they are effective, better tolerated and much safer in overdose than older drugs. Amitriptyline works but has anticholinergic and cardiotoxic effects and is dangerous in overdose, while MAOIs such as phenelzine need dietary restriction and are reserved for resistant depression.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man developed persistent low mood, anhedonia and poor sleep 6 weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction. He meets criteria for moderate depression and wants medication alongside cardiac rehabilitation. Which antidepressant is the most appropriate?
questions.e: Sertraline has been shown to be safe after myocardial infarction and is the preferred antidepressant in heart disease. Tricyclics such as amitriptyline and imipramine are pro-arrhythmic and cause postural hypotension, and venlafaxine can raise blood pressure.

questions.s: A 62-year-old widow in Hyderabad has severe depression. Over the past week she has stopped eating and drinking, lies mute in bed and says her intestines have rotted away. She has taken sertraline at full dose for 6 weeks. Her blood urea is rising. What is the most appropriate treatment now?
questions.e: Severe depression with nihilistic delusions and refusal of food and fluids is life-threatening, and ECT gives the fastest and most reliable response. Switching or augmenting antidepressants takes weeks she does not have, and psychological therapy is not possible in a mute, psychotic patient.

questions.s: Rukhsana, 40, started fluoxetine 20 mg daily for moderate depression 8 days ago. She says she feels no better yet and has mild nausea that is settling. She has no suicidal thoughts and is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Switch today to a different SSRI
Continue the same dose and review
questions.e: Antidepressants usually take 2 to 4 weeks to show benefit, so lack of response after 8 days is expected and the dose should be continued with review. Switching or increasing the dose this early only adds side effects without allowing time for a response.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman attends the emergency department for the fourth time in 2 months with sudden attacks of palpitations, breathlessness, chest tightness, tingling fingers and a fear that she is dying. Each attack peaks within 10 minutes and settles within half an hour. Between attacks she worries about having another. ECG, blood glucose and thyroid function are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recurrent unexpected attacks of intense fear with autonomic symptoms that peak within minutes, plus persistent worry about further attacks, define panic disorder. Generalised anxiety is continuous rather than episodic, and SVT is unlikely with repeatedly normal tests and the prominent fear of dying.

questions.s: Imran, 45, has worried excessively about his business, family and health on most days for a year, with muscle tension, irritability and poor sleep. Psychological therapy has helped only partly and he would like medication. Which is the most appropriate long-term drug treatment?
questions.e: An SSRI such as sertraline is the first-line drug for generalised anxiety disorder. Benzodiazepines such as alprazolam cause tolerance and dependence and are only for short-term crisis use, and propranolol eases physical symptoms without treating the worry.

questions.s: A 22-year-old university student in Karachi washes her hands up to 50 times a day because of intrusive thoughts that she will contaminate her family with germs. She knows the thoughts are excessive and tries to resist them, but her anxiety rises until she washes. Her studies are suffering. Which psychological treatment is most effective?
questions.e: Obsessive-compulsive disorder responds best to CBT with exposure and response prevention, in which the patient faces the feared trigger while resisting the compulsion until anxiety falls. Psychodynamic therapy and supportive counselling have little evidence in OCD.

questions.s: Three months after surviving a bomb blast at a market in Peshawar, a 35-year-old shopkeeper has vivid flashbacks and nightmares of the event, avoids the market area, startles easily and sleeps poorly. He has been unable to return to work. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Re-experiencing, avoidance and hyperarousal lasting more than a month after a life-threatening event define PTSD. An acute stress reaction settles within days to weeks, and adjustment disorder follows ordinary stressors without the intrusive re-living of a trauma.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man with thalassaemia trait needs regular blood tests but has a lifelong intense fear of needles. He becomes panicky at the sight of a syringe and avoids appointments, although he knows the fear is excessive. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Specific phobias are treated with graded exposure (systematic desensitisation), working up a hierarchy of feared situations while anxiety settles. Long-term benzodiazepines cause dependence and medication has little role in a single specific phobia.

questions.s: Kashif, a 22-year-old student, has become withdrawn over 8 months. He hears voices discussing him in the third person, believes his thoughts are being broadcast on television and has stopped bathing. He does not use drugs and has no prominent mood symptoms. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Third-person auditory hallucinations, thought broadcasting and negative symptoms persisting for months without a mood disorder or substance cause indicate schizophrenia. A brief psychotic disorder resolves within a month, and delusional disorder lacks prominent hallucinations and functional decline.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man is newly diagnosed with schizophrenia at a teaching hospital in Lahore. He has never taken antipsychotic medication and has no medical illness. Which drug is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.e: A second-generation antipsychotic such as risperidone is a standard first-line treatment for a first episode of schizophrenia. Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant illness because of the risk of agranulocytosis, and lithium and fluoxetine do not treat psychosis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with schizophrenia has not responded to adequate trials of risperidone and then olanzapine. She is started on clozapine. Which investigation must be monitored regularly throughout treatment?
questions.e: Clozapine can cause agranulocytosis, so the neutrophil count is checked weekly at first and regularly thereafter, and the drug is stopped if it falls. Prolactin is rarely raised by clozapine, and creatine kinase is measured only if neuroleptic malignant syndrome is suspected.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has believed for a year that her husband is having an affair. She checks his phone daily and follows him, though there is no evidence. She works, manages her home well and has no hallucinations, disorganised speech or mood symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A single fixed, non-bizarre delusion (here jealousy) lasting more than a month, with preserved functioning and no hallucinations or disorganisation, is delusional disorder. Schizophrenia would show other psychotic features and decline, and paranoid personality is a lifelong suspicious style rather than one fixed false belief.

questions.s: Which of the following is a negative symptom of schizophrenia?
questions.e: Negative symptoms are a loss of normal function: alogia, blunted affect, avolition, anhedonia and social withdrawal. Thought insertion, hallucinations and delusions are positive symptoms, adding abnormal experiences.

questions.s: Sana, a 25-year-old, has slept only 2 hours a night for 10 days without feeling tired. She talks rapidly, says she has been chosen to lead the country and has spent her family's savings on gold. She does not use drugs and has no medical illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, pressured speech, grandiosity and reckless spending for more than a week with marked impairment is a manic episode, which defines bipolar I disorder. Cyclothymia involves milder mood swings, and grandiose ideas that match the mood favour mania over schizophrenia.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man with a first manic episode is agitated, grandiose and has not slept for several nights. He takes no regular medicines and has no medical illness. Which is the most appropriate first-line drug to control the mania?
questions.e: An antipsychotic such as olanzapine, haloperidol or quetiapine is first-line for acute mania in a patient not already on a mood stabiliser. Lamotrigine has no antimanic effect and is used for bipolar depression, and an antidepressant could worsen the mania.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man stable on lithium for 10 years was started on a new antihypertensive 2 weeks ago. He now has vomiting, diarrhoea, a coarse tremor, unsteady gait and confusion. Which new drug is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Thiazide diuretics reduce renal lithium clearance and commonly precipitate lithium toxicity, shown here by gastrointestinal upset, coarse tremor, ataxia and confusion. ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs act similarly, whereas atenolol, doxazosin and hydralazine do not meaningfully raise lithium levels.

questions.s: A 44-year-old woman has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 6 years. She reports tiredness, weight gain, constipation and feeling cold. Her serum lithium is within the therapeutic range. TSH is 18 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) and free T4 is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lithium inhibits thyroid hormone release and commonly causes hypothyroidism, confirmed by a high TSH and low free T4, which is why thyroid function is monitored. Lithium toxicity is excluded by a therapeutic level, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus would cause polyuria and thirst.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder stopped his lithium. He became depressed and his GP prescribed sertraline alone. Three weeks later he is overactive, irritable, sleeping 2 hours a night and making grandiose business plans. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Continue sertraline and add night-time diazepam
Stop sertraline and start an antipsychotic
questions.e: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can trigger a switch into mania, so the antidepressant should be stopped and the mania treated with an antipsychotic or mood stabiliser. Adding diazepam may help sleep but leaves the cause in place, and switching to a tricyclic carries an even higher switch risk.

questions.s: Two days after admission for a fractured femur, a 48-year-old man becomes confused, sweaty and tremulous. He is picking at the sheets and says insects are crawling on the walls. Pulse 118/min, temperature 37.9 °C. His wife says he drinks heavily every day. What is the most appropriate drug treatment?
questions.e: Confusion, tremor, autonomic overactivity and visual hallucinations 2 to 3 days after stopping heavy drinking indicate delirium tremens, treated with a benzodiazepine plus parenteral thiamine. Haloperidol does not treat withdrawal and lowers the seizure threshold, and naltrexone and disulfiram are for relapse prevention.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with long-standing heavy alcohol use is brought in confused and unsteady on his feet. He has horizontal nystagmus and bilateral lateral rectus weakness. Capillary glucose is 72 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
questions.e: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in a heavy drinker indicate Wernicke encephalopathy, which needs urgent parenteral thiamine to prevent permanent Korsakoff syndrome. Giving glucose first can worsen thiamine deficiency, and his glucose is normal anyway.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man is found unresponsive in a park in Rawalpindi with a syringe beside him. Respiratory rate is 6/min, pupils are pinpoint and there are needle marks on his arms. After airway support and oxygen, which drug should be given?
questions.e: Coma, respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils in an injecting drug user indicate opioid overdose, reversed by the opioid antagonist naloxone. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and can provoke seizures, and atropine is used for organophosphate poisoning.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man admitted with cellulitis becomes restless on day 2. He is yawning, has watery eyes and a running nose, goose flesh, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea and dilated pupils. Pulse 104/min. He admits to daily heroin use. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Yawning, lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, cramps, diarrhoea and mydriasis are typical of opioid withdrawal, which is distressing but rarely dangerous. Alcohol withdrawal features tremor, sweating and possibly seizures or hallucinations rather than piloerection and rhinorrhoea.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man who has completed alcohol detoxification chooses disulfiram to help him stay abstinent. He is warned that drinking alcohol while taking it will cause flushing, nausea and palpitations. What is the mechanism of this reaction?
questions.e: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so acetaldehyde builds up after drinking and causes an unpleasant reaction. Alcohol dehydrogenase is inhibited by fomepizole, mu-receptor blockade is how naltrexone works, and acamprosate modulates glutamate transmission.

questions.s: Zubaida, 78, is brought to hospital by her son because over the last 2 days she has become confused, at times drowsy and at times agitated, and worse at night. She cannot keep her attention on a conversation. A week ago she was managing her household normally. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute onset over days of fluctuating confusion with inattention and a disturbed sleep-wake cycle, with a likely urinary infection as a trigger, is delirium. Alzheimer disease develops over months to years with preserved attention early on.

questions.s: On the second day after a hip replacement, a 74-year-old man becomes disoriented and restless and keeps pulling at his drip. He was cognitively normal before surgery. Which is the most appropriate first step in management?
o: Apply wrist restraints to keep the drip in place
Look for and treat the underlying cause
questions.e: Delirium is a symptom of an underlying problem such as hypoxia, infection, pain, urinary retention, constipation or drugs, so the first step is to find and correct it alongside supportive care. Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium (except in alcohol withdrawal) and restraints increase agitation and injury.

questions.s: A 72-year-old retired teacher has had gradually worsening memory for 2 years. She repeats questions, misplaces things and recently got lost in her own neighbourhood. Examination is otherwise normal, and blood tests including vitamin B12 and thyroid function are normal. CT shows atrophy most marked in the medial temporal lobes. Which class of drug is first-line for her symptoms?
questions.e: Gradual progressive memory loss with medial temporal atrophy suggests Alzheimer disease, for which acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil are first-line symptomatic treatment. Antipsychotics are avoided where possible because they increase stroke and death risk in dementia.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man has had a year of fluctuating attention and alertness, with well-formed visual hallucinations of children in his room. He has a mild resting tremor and a slow, shuffling gait. After a single dose of haloperidol for agitation he became severely rigid and more confused. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fluctuating cognition, vivid visual hallucinations and parkinsonism appearing together, with severe sensitivity to antipsychotics, are the core features of dementia with Lewy bodies. In Parkinson disease dementia the motor disorder precedes cognitive decline by more than a year.

questions.s: A 69-year-old man has a 6-month history of a broad-based, slow, magnetic gait, urinary urgency with incontinence and slowly worsening forgetfulness. CT head shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to cortical atrophy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline with ventriculomegaly is the triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus, a potentially reversible cause of dementia treated by CSF shunting. Progressive supranuclear palsy causes falls and vertical gaze palsy without ventricular enlargement.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man is seen in clinic with depression. He lost his job last month, drinks alcohol most evenings and lives with his wife. Two years ago he was admitted to intensive care after taking a large overdose of his tablets. Which factor in his history most increases his risk of completed suicide?
o: Recent loss of his job and income
questions.e: A previous suicide attempt, especially a medically serious one, is the strongest single predictor of eventual suicide. Job loss and alcohol misuse add to his risk but less so, and living with a partner is protective rather than a risk factor.

questions.s: A 23-year-old woman is medically fit for discharge 2 days after a paracetamol overdose treated with acetylcysteine. She tells the doctor she still wants to die, regrets being found and has saved more tablets at home. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Discharge with a GP appointment next week
Start sertraline and discharge her home
Urgent psychiatric assessment before she leaves
Discharge to her family with outpatient follow-up
questions.e: Ongoing intent, regret at survival and access to means indicate high immediate risk, so she needs a specialist psychiatric assessment before leaving hospital. Discharge with later follow-up, even to family, leaves her exposed during the highest-risk period, and an antidepressant takes weeks to act.

questions.s: A GP in Faisalabad sees a 35-year-old man with moderate depression. She is unsure whether to ask about suicide because she fears the question may put the idea into his head. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Avoid the topic unless he raises it himself
Ask him directly about thoughts of suicide
Ask only his family about any suicidal talk
Give a helpline number without asking further
questions.e: Asking directly and sensitively about suicidal thoughts does not increase risk and often relieves the patient; it is essential to assessing risk. Avoiding the subject or relying only on relatives misses people who are at risk and need a safety plan.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man is admitted after taking an overdose of his mother's tablets. When assessing suicidal intent, which feature of the attempt most strongly suggests high intent?
o: He took the tablets impulsively after an argument
He told his brother immediately after taking them
He had been drinking alcohol beforehand
He left a note and chose a time he would be alone
questions.e: Planning, precautions against being discovered and a final note show that death was intended and predict higher future risk. An impulsive act after an argument followed by telling someone suggests lower intent, although every attempt still needs full assessment.

questions.s: A 19-year-old woman with moderate depression is started on fluoxetine by her GP. She has no current suicidal plans and lives with her parents. Given her age, when should she be reviewed first?
questions.e: Young people under 25 starting an antidepressant have a higher risk of suicidal thoughts in the early weeks, so they should be reviewed about 1 week after starting. Older adults without increased risk are usually reviewed after 2 to 4 weeks.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man started on haloperidol for a first psychotic episode 5 days ago now complains of an unbearable inner restlessness. He cannot sit still, repeatedly crosses and uncrosses his legs and paces the ward. Temperature, muscle tone and creatine kinase are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Akathisia is a subjective inner restlessness with an urge to keep moving, usually within days to weeks of starting or increasing an antipsychotic; it is managed by reducing the dose or switching drug, and propranolol often helps. It is easily mistaken for worsening psychosis. Tardive dyskinesia appears after months to years and causes involuntary orofacial movements.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman taking sertraline was given tramadol for back pain. Within a day she is agitated and sweating, with diarrhoea, tremor and a temperature of 38.4 °C. Which examination finding best supports serotonin syndrome rather than neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
questions.e: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability, with clonus and hyperreflexia most marked in the legs, distinguishes serotonin syndrome, which also develops within hours. Fever, sweating and autonomic instability occur in both syndromes, while lead-pipe rigidity points to neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man was given IM haloperidol in the emergency department for agitation. Six hours later his neck is twisted to one side and his eyes are fixed upwards. He is fully conscious and afebrile. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Torticollis and oculogyric crisis within hours of a high-potency antipsychotic is an acute dystonic reaction, which responds quickly to an anticholinergic such as procyclidine. Dantrolene and bromocriptine are used in neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and propranolol treats akathisia.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman has taken haloperidol for schizophrenia for 15 years. Her family notice repetitive lip smacking, tongue protrusion and chewing movements of which she seems unaware. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Involuntary orofacial movements after years of antipsychotic treatment are tardive dyskinesia, which may be irreversible. Acute dystonia occurs within days, akathisia is inner restlessness, and parkinsonism causes tremor, rigidity and slowness rather than choreiform movements.

questions.s: An 81-year-old woman started citalopram 3 weeks ago. She is now confused and unsteady. She is clinically euvolaemic, serum sodium is 121 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality is low and urine osmolality is inappropriately high. What is the most likely mechanism?
questions.e: SSRIs can cause SIADH, especially in older people in the first weeks, giving euvolaemic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine. Primary polydipsia produces maximally dilute urine, and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus causes high rather than low sodium.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man has moderate depression with marked insomnia, poor appetite and weight loss. He asks for an antidepressant that might also help him sleep and eat. Which drug is most suitable?
questions.e: Mirtazapine is sedating and stimulates appetite through histamine and serotonin receptor blockade, which can be useful in depression with insomnia and weight loss. Fluoxetine and bupropion are activating and may reduce appetite.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has felt anxious and on edge for 3 months, with palpitations, a fine tremor, weight loss despite a good appetite and heat intolerance. Before an anxiety disorder is diagnosed, which investigation is most appropriate?
questions.e: Weight loss with increased appetite, tremor and heat intolerance suggests hyperthyroidism, a common physical cause of anxiety symptoms that must be excluded with thyroid function tests. Cortisol testing is for suspected Cushing syndrome, which does not cause weight loss.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman taking risperidone for schizophrenia develops amenorrhoea and a milky nipple discharge. Her pregnancy test is negative. Which mechanism explains these effects?
o: Dopamine D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway
Dopamine D2 blockade in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways
questions.e: Dopamine from the hypothalamus inhibits prolactin release through the tuberoinfundibular pathway, so D2 blockade there causes hyperprolactinaemia with galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea; risperidone does this markedly. Mesolimbic blockade produces the antipsychotic effect, not endocrine changes.

questions.s: A woman with bipolar disorder took lithium throughout the first trimester of an unplanned pregnancy. Which fetal cardiac abnormality is particularly associated with this exposure?
questions.e: First-trimester lithium exposure is linked to Ebstein anomaly, a downward displacement of the tricuspid valve, so a detailed fetal echocardiogram is advised. Valproate, by contrast, is best known for neural tube defects.

questions.s: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after 3 nights without sleep at a party. He is agitated and paranoid and clenching his jaw, with dilated pupils, pulse 130/min, BP 170/100 mmHg and temperature 38.6 °C. Which substance is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Sympathomimetic toxicity with insomnia, paranoia, jaw clenching, mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia points to a stimulant such as methamphetamine. Heroin causes pinpoint pupils and sedation, and cannabis rarely causes hyperthermia or marked hypertension.

questions.s: A 74-year-old man with hypertension and diabetes has had three episodes over 2 years after which his memory and planning suddenly became worse, with no recovery in between. He has a mild residual right-sided weakness and brisk reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Stepwise decline after discrete events, vascular risk factors and focal neurological signs suggest vascular dementia from repeated infarcts. Alzheimer disease progresses gradually without focal signs, and frontotemporal dementia presents with personality or language change.

questions.s: An 82-year-old man is 3 days after surgery for a fractured hip. Nurses say he is quiet and sleeps much of the day. When awake he cannot count backwards from 20, drifts off mid-sentence and is disoriented, but for some hours he seems almost normal. Before surgery he lived alone and managed independently. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute onset, inattention, drowsiness and fluctuation after surgery indicate delirium; the quiet hypoactive form is common in older people and easily mistaken for depression. Depression does not cause fluctuating attention and disorientation, and he was independent before surgery.

questions.s: During a review, a 45-year-old man with depression says he has recently thought that his family would be better off without him. What is the most appropriate next question?
o: Whether he has made a plan or has the means
Whether any relative has had a depressive illness
Whether he has been sleeping well recently
Whether he is worried about losing his job
questions.e: Once suicidal ideation is disclosed, the next step is to explore how far it has gone: plans, preparations and access to means, which determine immediate risk. Family history and sleep are relevant to the overall assessment but do not judge current danger.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman with bipolar disorder is started on lithium once daily at night. When should blood be taken to measure the serum lithium level?
o: Immediately after any dose is taken
At any time, as levels are steady
questions.e: Lithium levels are standardised to a sample taken 12 hours after the last dose, usually the next morning, so results can be compared with the therapeutic range. Samples taken soon after a dose catch the absorption peak and overestimate the steady level.

questions.s: A 66-year-old woman taking an antidepressant reports palpitations and a brief faint. ECG shows a corrected QT interval of 520 ms, and electrolytes are normal. Which antidepressant is most likely responsible through a dose-dependent effect?
questions.e: Citalopram (and escitalopram) cause dose-dependent QT prolongation, which is why maximum doses are lower in older people. Sertraline has little effect on the QT interval and is preferred in cardiac disease.

questions.s: Two months after her husband died suddenly, a 58-year-old woman in Quetta feels sad, cries often and sometimes sleeps poorly. She still cooks for her family and visits relatives, has no guilt, worthlessness or suicidal thoughts, and says the pain comes in waves when she is reminded of him. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Waves of sadness linked to reminders, with preserved functioning and no worthlessness or suicidal ideas, are a normal grief reaction that needs support and review rather than medication. Antidepressants are considered only if a depressive episode develops, and benzodiazepines can delay adjustment.

questions.s: Ten days after delivering her first baby in Lahore, a 27-year-old woman becomes confused and agitated, sleeps very little and says her baby has been replaced by an evil double. She has no fever, and her blood glucose and sodium are normal. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Urgent psychiatric admission, ideally with her baby
Reassure the family that this is baby blues
Start sertraline and review in 4 weeks
questions.e: Rapid-onset confusion, agitation and delusions about the baby in the first weeks after delivery indicate postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency with risk to mother and baby that needs urgent admission, ideally to a mother-and-baby unit. Baby blues are mild tearfulness in the first days without psychosis.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy has had itchy, dry, red patches in the creases of his elbows and behind his knees for months. His father has asthma and hay fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Itchy dry eczematous patches in the flexures of a young child with a family history of atopy is atopic eczema. Psoriasis favours extensor surfaces with silvery scale, and seborrhoeic dermatitis affects the scalp, face and nappy area in infants.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl with known atopic eczema suddenly develops painful, punched-out erosions and clustered vesicles over her eczematous face, with fever and malaise. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Rapidly spreading painful clustered vesicles and punched-out erosions over eczema with fever is eczema herpeticum, a dermatological emergency treated with aciclovir (IV if severe). Increasing topical steroids would worsen the viral infection.

questions.s: A 34-year-old woman who works as a cleaner has itchy, red, fissured skin on the backs of her hands, which improves on holidays. What is the most important measure to prevent recurrence?
questions.e: Hand eczema that improves away from work suggests irritant contact dermatitis from detergents and water; avoidance, protective gloves and regular emollients are the key measures. Antihistamines do little for eczema itch, and antifungals treat tinea, not dermatitis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has well-demarcated red plaques with thick silvery scale on his elbows, knees and scalp. His nails show pitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and scalp, with nail pitting, are typical of chronic plaque psoriasis. Tinea has an active scaly edge with central clearing, and lichen planus produces purple polygonal papules.

questions.s: A 17-year-old boy develops many small, drop-like scaly red papules over his trunk 2 weeks after a sore throat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Guttate psoriasis presents with numerous small teardrop scaly papules on the trunk, typically 2-3 weeks after a streptococcal throat infection in young people. Pityriasis rosea starts with a single herald patch followed by oval patches along skin lines.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man with psoriasis was started on a drug for another condition, and his psoriasis has become much worse. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials such as chloroquine, and withdrawal of systemic steroids are well known to worsen psoriasis. Paracetamol, omeprazole and amlodipine are not typical triggers.

questions.s: Several children in a madrassa hostel in Peshawar have intense itching that is worse at night. Examination shows papules and burrows in the finger webs, wrists and around the waist. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Oral cetirizine at bedtime for all
Topical hydrocortisone 1% to all itchy areas
questions.e: Nocturnal itch, burrows in the finger webs and wrists, and spread among close contacts indicate scabies; permethrin 5% applied from the neck down, repeated after a week, is used to treat all contacts at the same time, with washing of bedding. Antihistamines and steroids only relieve itch and do not kill the mite.

questions.s: A frail 80-year-old woman in a care home has thick, crusted, scaly plaques on her hands and feet with little itching. Several staff members now have an itchy rash. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Crusted scabies occurs in elderly or immunocompromised people, with hyperkeratotic crusts teeming with mites and often little itch; it is highly contagious, explaining the staff cases. It requires oral ivermectin with topical treatment and infection-control measures.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man was treated correctly for scabies with permethrin 2 weeks ago. He still has some itching but no new burrows. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Itching may persist for weeks after cure
Repeat permethrin every week for 2 months
Treatment has failed, so start oral ivermectin
Start a potent topical steroid on the whole body
questions.e: Post-scabetic itch can persist for 2-6 weeks after successful treatment, as a hypersensitivity reaction to dead mites; emollients and an antihistamine help. New burrows or lesions would suggest treatment failure or reinfection.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man in Karachi has an itchy, ring-shaped rash on his groin and inner thighs, spreading outwards with a raised scaly edge and central clearing. The scrotum is spared. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An itchy, annular lesion with an active scaly edge and central clearing in the groin that spares the scrotum is tinea cruris, a dermatophyte infection. Candidal intertrigo often involves the scrotum and has satellite pustules.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man has many pale and light brown, finely scaly patches on his upper back and chest that became more obvious after sunbathing. Skin scrapings show 'spaghetti and meatballs' hyphae and spores. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: Pityriasis versicolor, caused by Malassezia yeast, gives hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches on the trunk with a 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on microscopy, and is treated with topical azoles or selenium sulfide. Griseofulvin is ineffective against Malassezia.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy has a scaly, itchy patch of hair loss on his scalp with broken hairs, and a tender boggy swelling on the scalp has now developed. Fungal culture grows Trichophyton. What is the most appropriate treatment?
o: Incision and drainage of the swelling
questions.e: Tinea capitis, including a kerion (inflammatory boggy swelling), needs oral antifungal therapy because topical agents do not penetrate the hair follicle. A kerion is not a bacterial abscess and should not be incised.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man returned to Lahore after working in a village in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. He has a painless nodule on his cheek that slowly enlarged over 2 months and has ulcerated, with a raised edge and a crust. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A slowly enlarging, painless nodule on exposed skin that ulcerates with a raised edge, in someone from an endemic area, is typical of cutaneous leishmaniasis ('oriental sore'), spread by sandflies. Basal cell carcinoma grows over years and is rare at 26.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has a suspected cutaneous leishmaniasis ulcer on his forearm. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Slit-skin smear from the ulcer edge
Swab of the ulcer base for Gram stain
questions.e: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is confirmed by finding Leishman-Donovan bodies (amastigotes) in a slit-skin smear, scraping or biopsy from the active edge of the lesion, with PCR where available. Serology is usually negative in localised cutaneous disease.

questions.s: A 9-year-old child has a single small cutaneous leishmaniasis lesion on the arm, not near a joint or the face. Which treatment is commonly used in Pakistan?
questions.e: Small, uncomplicated cutaneous leishmaniasis lesions are commonly treated with intralesional pentavalent antimonials such as sodium stibogluconate or meglumine antimoniate, or with cryotherapy. Topical steroids worsen the infection and antibiotics treat only secondary bacterial infection.

questions.s: A 16-year-old girl has open and closed comedones on her forehead and a few small inflamed papules. There are no nodules or scars. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
o: Oral doxycycline alone for 6 months or more
questions.e: Mild acne with comedones and few papules is treated with topical therapy, such as a topical retinoid combined with benzoyl peroxide. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulocystic or scarring acne, and oral antibiotics should not be used alone.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman with severe nodulocystic acne and scarring has failed oral antibiotics and is to start oral isotretinoin. Which measure is mandatory before and during treatment?
o: Weekly full blood count with blood film
questions.e: Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic, so women must use effective contraception with regular pregnancy tests before, during and for a period after treatment; liver function and lipids are also monitored. Patients should avoid excessive sun because of skin sensitivity.

questions.s: A 23-year-old woman has acne, irregular periods and excess facial hair. She is overweight. Which underlying condition should be considered?
questions.e: Acne with hirsutism and irregular periods in an overweight woman suggests hyperandrogenism from polycystic ovary syndrome; a combined oral contraceptive can help both acne and cycles. Hypothyroidism and Addison disease do not cause androgen excess.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man started carbamazepine 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, painful mouth ulcers, red eyes and dusky target-like lesions with blistering and skin detachment over 8% of his body surface. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Continue the drug and add an antihistamine
questions.e: Fever, mucosal involvement and blistering with skin detachment under 10% of body surface after a new drug is Stevens-Johnson syndrome; the culprit drug must be stopped immediately and the patient managed like a burn, with eye care. Carbamazepine is a common cause, especially in carriers of HLA-B*15:02.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a single round, dusky red-violet patch on his lip that blisters, and it recurs at exactly the same site each time he takes co-trimoxazole, leaving brown pigmentation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: A fixed drug eruption recurs at the same site each time the drug is taken, often on the lips, genitals or hands, and heals with hyperpigmentation; sulfonamides, NSAIDs and tetracyclines are common causes. Herpes labialis recurs but with grouped vesicles and no drug link.

questions.s: A 4-year-old child has mild atopic eczema with dry skin and occasional itchy patches. What is the mainstay of long-term management?
o: Potent topical steroid applied daily for months
questions.e: Liberal, regular emollients and avoiding soap are the foundation of eczema care, with short courses of mild topical steroids for flares. Long-term potent steroids cause skin atrophy, and oral steroids are not used for mild eczema.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with chronic plaque psoriasis covering 25% of his body has not improved with topical treatment and phototherapy. Which drug is a standard first-line systemic option?
questions.e: Methotrexate is a first-line systemic agent for extensive psoriasis not controlled by topical therapy and phototherapy, alongside ciclosporin and acitretin. Systemic corticosteroids are avoided because withdrawal can trigger severe pustular or erythrodermic flares.

questions.s: An 18-month-old child has scabies with lesions on the palms, soles and scalp. How does the presentation in infants differ from adults?
o: Lesions may involve the face, scalp, palms and soles
Burrows are never seen in infants
Lesions are confined to the genitals and buttocks in infants
questions.e: In infants and young children, scabies can involve the face, scalp, palms and soles, which are usually spared in adults, and may present with vesicles or pustules. Permethrin is applied to the whole body including the scalp and face in this age group.

questions.s: A 45-year-old diabetic man has a thickened, yellow, crumbling big toenail. Fungal culture grows Trichophyton rubrum. He wants treatment. Which is the most effective option?
questions.e: Dermatophyte onychomycosis of the toenail responds best to oral terbinafine for about 12 weeks, after checking liver function. Topical creams do not penetrate the nail plate, and short courses are not sufficient.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man treated in childhood for visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) now has multiple hypopigmented macules and nodules on his face. Slit-skin smears show Leishman-Donovan bodies. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis develops months or years after treated visceral leishmaniasis, with hypopigmented macules, papules and nodules, often on the face; the lesions contain parasites. Leprosy can look similar, but smears would show acid-fast bacilli rather than amastigotes.

questions.s: A 17-year-old boy has moderate inflammatory acne with many papules and pustules on his face and back, not improving after 3 months of topical treatment. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Oral isotretinoin at full dose straight away
Oral doxycycline alone for at least a year
questions.e: Moderate inflammatory acne not responding to topical therapy is treated with an oral tetracycline such as doxycycline for up to about 3 months, combined with a topical retinoid or benzoyl peroxide to reduce resistance. Isotretinoin is reserved for severe or scarring acne or failure of these measures.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with pyelonephritis has BP 78/45 mmHg, pulse 120/min, cool mottled skin and a lactate of 5 mmol/L. He has received 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid, and blood cultures and IV antibiotics have been started, but his mean arterial pressure remains below 65 mmHg. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.e: Septic shock with persistent hypotension after adequate initial fluid needs a vasopressor, and noradrenaline is first-line, targeting a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg. Large further fluid volumes risk overload without restoring vascular tone, and dobutamine is an inotrope for poor cardiac output, not a first-line pressor.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man is 6 hours into an extensive anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. BP is 80/50 mmHg, his hands are cold and clammy, the JVP is raised and there are crackles to both mid-zones. Urine output is minimal. What type of shock is this?
questions.e: Hypotension with cold peripheries, a raised JVP and pulmonary congestion after a large infarct indicates pump failure, which is cardiogenic shock. Hypovolaemic shock also gives cold peripheries but with a low JVP and clear lungs.

questions.s: After diving into a shallow canal, an 18-year-old man has a cervical spine injury with weakness of all four limbs. BP is 76/40 mmHg, pulse 50/min and his feet are warm and pink. A FAST scan shows no free fluid and the chest is clear with equal air entry. What is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
questions.e: Cervical cord injury interrupts sympathetic outflow, causing hypotension with bradycardia and warm, vasodilated peripheries, which is neurogenic shock. Haemorrhage causes tachycardia and cold peripheries, and a tension pneumothorax would give unequal air entry.

questions.s: On day 5 of a febrile illness during the dengue season in Lahore, a 24-year-old woman's fever settles but she develops abdominal pain and lethargy. Her hands are cold, capillary refill is 4 seconds, BP is 100/90 mmHg and haematocrit has risen from 38% to 48%. Platelets are 40 × 10⁹/L and she is not bleeding. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: Narrow pulse pressure, cold extremities and a rising haematocrit at defervescence indicate dengue shock from plasma leakage, which needs prompt IV isotonic crystalloid with close monitoring. Platelet transfusion does not correct leakage and is not indicated without significant bleeding.

questions.s: A 19-year-old woman took 30 tablets of paracetamol 500 mg exactly 4 hours ago, all at once, after an argument. She feels well apart from mild nausea. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start acetylcysteine and stop if LFTs are normal
questions.e: After a single timed overdose, the paracetamol level taken at 4 hours or later is plotted on the treatment nomogram to decide on acetylcysteine, and the result is available well within the 8-hour window. Activated charcoal helps only within about an hour of ingestion, and stopping acetylcysteine on normal early LFTs is unreliable.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman is brought in after taking a large number of her amitriptyline tablets. She is drowsy, with dilated pupils, dry skin and pulse 130/min. She has a seizure, and the ECG shows a QRS duration of 140 ms. Which treatment is most appropriate for the cardiac toxicity?
questions.e: Tricyclic overdose blocks cardiac sodium channels, widening the QRS and causing arrhythmias, and IV sodium bicarbonate reverses this. Flumazenil and physostigmine can precipitate seizures or asystole in tricyclic poisoning and are contraindicated.

questions.s: On a winter morning in Quetta, a family of four is found drowsy in a closed room where a coal heater burned all night. The father has headache, vomiting and confusion, and his pulse oximeter reads 98% on air. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.e: Headache, vomiting and confusion in several people exposed to a fuel-burning heater in a closed room suggest carbon monoxide poisoning; high-flow oxygen shortens the half-life of carboxyhaemoglobin. Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy in a village near Sukkur swallowed kerosene oil stored in a soft-drink bottle an hour ago. He coughed and choked at the time and is now breathing fast. Which is the most important complication to anticipate?
questions.e: Kerosene has low viscosity and spreads easily into the airways, so the main danger is chemical aspiration pneumonitis, especially after coughing or choking. Vomiting must not be induced for this reason, and stricture is a complication of corrosives such as acids and alkalis.

questions.s: Within minutes of an IV dose of ceftriaxone, a 40-year-old woman develops widespread urticaria, stridor, wheeze and a BP of 70/40 mmHg. After calling for help and lying her flat, which drug should be given first?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis with airway, breathing and circulatory compromise is treated first with IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1,000) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 minutes if needed. Antihistamines and steroids act too slowly and are not first-line life-saving treatment.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with anaphylaxis after a wasp sting has received two correctly given doses of IM adrenaline 5 minutes apart and an IV fluid bolus. He remains hypotensive with wheeze. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Start a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion
questions.e: Anaphylaxis that persists after two doses of IM adrenaline is refractory and is treated with a low-dose IV adrenaline infusion under expert guidance, alongside further fluids. Hydrocortisone and antihistamines do not reverse the life-threatening features and should not delay adrenaline.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman has recovered from a suspected anaphylactic reaction during dental treatment. To help confirm the diagnosis and guide later allergy assessment, which blood test is most useful?
questions.e: Mast cell tryptase rises after anaphylaxis, peaking 1 to 2 hours after onset, and timed samples help confirm the diagnosis. Total IgE does not confirm an acute reaction, and complement levels are used when hereditary angioedema is suspected.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man collapses on the cardiac ward. He is unresponsive and not breathing normally. CPR is started, and the monitor shows ventricular fibrillation as soon as the defibrillator is attached. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Continue CPR for 2 minutes before the first shock
Deliver a single shock, then resume CPR at once
questions.e: VF is a shockable rhythm, and early defibrillation with minimal pause in compressions is the key to survival; CPR resumes immediately for 2 minutes after the shock. Adrenaline and amiodarone are given only after the third shock in VF.

questions.s: During resuscitation of a 70-year-old woman in cardiac arrest, the rhythm is asystole. Chest compressions and ventilation are under way and IV access has just been obtained. Which drug should be given now?
questions.e: In non-shockable rhythms, adrenaline 1 mg IV is given as soon as access is obtained and then every 3 to 5 minutes. Amiodarone is for shock-refractory VF or pulseless VT, and atropine is no longer recommended in asystole.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest witnessed by two bystanders trained in basic life support. No airway device is available. What compression-to-ventilation ratio should they use?
questions.e: Adult basic life support uses 30 compressions to 2 breaths at 100 to 120 compressions per minute and a depth of 5 to 6 cm. The 15:2 ratio is used by healthcare providers for children.

questions.s: A 32-year-old farmer in southern Punjab is brought in after spraying a cotton crop without protective clothing. He is sweating and drooling, with pinpoint pupils, wheeze with copious bronchial secretions, vomiting and pulse 48/min. Which drug should be given first?
questions.e: Organophosphate poisoning causes a muscarinic crisis, and the life-saving first drug is atropine, titrated to dry the bronchial secretions. Pralidoxime is at most an adjunct, and physostigmine is itself a cholinesterase inhibitor and would worsen toxicity.

questions.s: A 20-year-old woman who drank an organophosphate insecticide is being treated with repeated doses of IV atropine. Which clinical end point is most important in deciding that she is adequately atropinised?
o: Clear chest with drying of secretions
questions.e: Atropine is titrated to a clear chest with dry secretions, along with heart rate above 80/min, systolic BP above 80 mmHg and dry axillae. Pupil size changes late and is unreliable, and aiming for marked tachycardia causes atropine toxicity; cholinesterase levels do not guide dosing.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man is recovering in hospital from organophosphate poisoning; his cholinergic features settled with atropine. On day 3 he develops weakness of neck flexion, proximal limb muscles and several cranial nerves, with a falling vital capacity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Intermediate syndrome develops 1 to 4 days after organophosphate poisoning, after the cholinergic crisis, with neck flexor, proximal and cranial nerve weakness that can cause respiratory failure needing ventilation. A recurrent cholinergic crisis would bring back secretions, miosis and bradycardia.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man was bitten on the foot by a snake while working in a rice field in Sindh 3 hours ago. The foot is painful and swollen to the knee and his gums are oozing blood. Which bedside test is most useful to confirm venom-induced coagulopathy?
questions.e: In the 20-minute whole blood clotting test, blood in a clean dry glass tube that fails to clot after 20 minutes shows venom-induced consumption coagulopathy and is an indication for anti-snake venom. Bleeding time and the tourniquet test assess platelets and capillaries, not clotting factors.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy sleeping on the floor of his home in rural Sindh wakes before dawn with abdominal pain. By morning he has bilateral ptosis, difficulty swallowing and weak breathing. No snake was seen, and there is no swelling at a faint mark on his hand. Which snake most likely bit him?
questions.e: Krait bites typically occur at night in people sleeping on the floor, are often painless with little local reaction, and cause abdominal pain followed by descending paralysis. Cobra bites are also neurotoxic but usually cause marked local swelling and tissue necrosis, while vipers cause local swelling and bleeding.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man is bitten on the leg by a snake in a village 2 hours from the nearest hospital. Which first-aid measure is most appropriate?
o: Tie a tight tourniquet above the bite
Cut the wound and suck out the venom
Immobilise the limb and transport him urgently
Apply ice packs to the bite site
questions.e: First aid is reassurance, immobilising the bitten limb to slow venom spread, and rapid transport to a facility with anti-snake venom. Tight tourniquets cause ischaemia and gangrene, and cutting or sucking the wound adds infection and bleeding without removing venom.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman with septic shock from pneumonia is started on noradrenaline after initial fluid resuscitation. What initial mean arterial pressure target is recommended?
questions.e: Sepsis guidance recommends an initial mean arterial pressure target of 65 mmHg in septic shock. Aiming higher increases vasopressor exposure and arrhythmias without improving survival in most patients, while 50 mmHg risks organ hypoperfusion.

questions.s: Acetylcysteine is started for a woman after a significant paracetamol overdose. How does it protect the liver?
o: It replenishes glutathione to detoxify NAPQI
It blocks cytochrome P450 conversion of paracetamol
It increases renal excretion of paracetamol
It binds paracetamol in the gut
questions.e: In overdose, paracetamol is increasingly converted to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which exhausts hepatic glutathione; acetylcysteine restores glutathione so NAPQI is conjugated safely. It does not block P450 metabolism or bind the drug in the gut, which is what activated charcoal does.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man develops anaphylaxis after eating peanuts. He is conscious with no breathing difficulty but feels faint, and his BP is 75/40 mmHg. While adrenaline is being prepared, how should he be positioned?
o: In the recovery position on his side
Standing and walking to keep alert
Lying flat with his legs raised
questions.e: A hypotensive patient with anaphylaxis should lie flat with the legs raised to improve venous return; sudden sitting or standing can cause fatal cardiovascular collapse. Sitting up is reserved for those whose main problem is breathing difficulty without hypotension.

questions.s: In organophosphate poisoning, what is the intended action of pralidoxime?
o: It blocks muscarinic receptors at the end organs
It increases acetylcholine release from nerve endings
It reactivates phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase before ageing
It binds free organophosphate in the bowel
questions.e: Oximes such as pralidoxime remove the phosphate group from acetylcholinesterase and restore its activity, but only before the bond ages and becomes permanent. Muscarinic receptor blockade is the action of atropine, which remains the mainstay of treatment.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man bitten by a cobra develops ptosis, difficulty swallowing and pooling of saliva despite anti-snake venom. Which complication is the most likely cause of death if it is not managed?
questions.e: Neurotoxic envenoming causes descending paralysis, and death results from airway obstruction and respiratory muscle failure, so early intubation and ventilation are vital. Acute kidney injury and bleeding are features of viper envenoming.
